A PLEA FOR SHOP ASSISTANTS. Sir,—l have for some time thought of appeal- ing to you to open your columns to a corre- spondence on behalf of shopkeepers and their assistants against the long hours we are at pres- ent compelled to work. I am encouraged to do so now by reading a letter of "A Watcher," which appeared in the February number of the local "Labour Gazette," which, if it really represents the views of the Labour party is a most hopeful and encouraging sign of the times. The letter referred to is a strong protest against the 12 to 16 hours per day we are now working, and ends in a threat to boycott shops whose doors are not closed at a reasonable time. I am delighted to find this attitude on the part of a class who, rightly or wrongly, has been considered the cause of long hours owing to their late shopping, and if trade unionists act in the spirit of the letter referred to, and com- pel shopkeepers to close earlier, they will earn the gratitude of all shop assistants. I commend the views of "A Watcher" to the Health Comisnittee of our Town Council, who for many months have had before them a peti- tion from at least one trade in the town to make an order to close at 7 p.m. Mondays and Tuesdays, 8 p.m. Wednesdays, 9 p.m. Fridays, and 10 p.m. Saturdays. Nothing has yet been done. It is a sad reflection on our boasted 20th century humanity and progress that a trained, intelligent body of workers have to plead—so far, in vain—for such a limitation of their work- ing hours, which would still be unnecessarily long. L for one, see no reason why all shops cannot close much earlier without loss to the shop- keeper or serious inconvenience to the public. Many shopkeepers would gladly close earlier, only for the thoughtless late shopper and a few of their own class, who are afraid they will miss some trade if they don't keep open all their working hours. Our present hours leave us no leisure for recreation, and Sundays often find us too used up and exhausted after the long rushing Satur- day for anything but resting ready for the coming week. Is it any wonder our churches complain that young people seek the fields and lanes in pre- ference to Sunday services, and Sunday schools plead in vain for teachers and retaining elder scholars? This question so closely concerns our church life that I wonder our Free Church Councils have not taken up the matter. I hope they will use their influence and join trade unionists in an effort to do something towards improving the lot of an overworked class, who at present are at the mercy of the late shopper on the one hand, and the grasping shopkeeper on the other.
EARLY CLOSER.

div.head: ROMANIST CLAIMS.
div.p: THE ROMANIST CLAIMS.

regret that it is once more necessary to restate the objections we Protestants have to the Roman Church. We deny its claim to be either Apostolic, Catholic, or Orthodox. I main- tain that it has utterly gone astray from the pure faith; that it has no claim or title to call itself either universal or infallible; that its doc- trines and precepts are not founded on, but against, Scripture; that it teaches false doc- trine and leads men astray from the true path of righteousness. This lays down a sufficiently definite issue for either " J.D." or any other Romanist to tackle. We are reminded in "J.D.'s" letter that the Roman Church was supreme up to the close of the 15th century, but let me remind him that the Roman Church is not the Church Apostolic of the early centuries of the Christian era. The Roman superstition Lind heresy had not made much progress at the close of the fifth century, but from that for the next thousand years it made sad havoc in the Christian Church. You may trace through those ten centuries a lurid flame of fire and sword, stamping out all that was good and noble in the Christian doctrine and the Word of God, even the latter being com- pletely suppressed, until its rediscovery by Wycliffe in England, Huss in Bohemia, and Luther in Germany. No credit attaches to Romanism for the preservation of the Bible, and now, even in our day, they do their best to mutilate and misquote it. It is an interesting study to refer to and compare the quotations given by " J.D." with those in the Authorised or Revised Versions. ".Y.D." writes of the fundamental questions of religion, but does he know' himself what is fundamental and what is not? He need not conclude his letter by that foul slander that Protestants and Free Churchmen do not read their Bible. If he would read his Bible a bit more he would find out how much the worship of relics and saints and other forms of idolatry are condemned in it. If he would read and study history he would find out how much of the doctrines of his church dated their origin from the Council of Trent, and would ,be sur- prised to find how modern are the chief'dogmas of his church. I ',would invite " J.D." to read and ponder well the events of Europe during the critical days of the 16th century. Let him study well what reduced Charles V. in 25 years from the most handsome and most powerful prince in the world to a decrepit old man at the age of 55, and made him glad to seek the shelter of aeon- vent cell. Let him study the no less active reign of Philip the Catholic, and he will be able to realise the horror with which modern Protest- ants view the revival of Papal ascendency. Who is responsible for the Reformation? Is it not the Church of Rome for maintaining its anti- Christian darkness? Nearly all the leaders of the Refbrmation received their first impressions in the Roman Church. Martin Luther was a Romish monk; William the Silent was a Romish prince; and many other leaders learned their first lessons in that Church. Then if "J.D.'s" Church had shown a little of the Christian spirit there need to have been no change, only a revival. We are practically told in the Good Old Book that neither in this place nor that shall they worship, "But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall- wor- ship the Father in spirit and in truth." And again, "Where two or three are gathered to- gether in My Name there am I in the midst of them." Let me, in concluding, point out that Protestantism is not our religion, it is only an accident in that religion, and a very important landmark in its history; our religion is Chris- tiaality, and that in its purest and freest sense. PIIIL SQUOD.

LOGIC. Sir,—The President of the Warrington Liberal Association, Mr. C. E. Parker, said, at the annual meeting of the association: "That dur- ing many visits to Ireland he had spoken to all sorts of men on the Irish Question. On his last visit lie met ten Ulster men and one Home Ruler, and that Home Ruler impressed him a great deal more than the ten." One is irresistibly reminded of the story of the perverse Jlll7Marl, who, pressing his indi- vidual and contrary opinion on the unanimously agreed eleven, said.: 'He had never met with , such a stubborn, ignorant, prejudiced lot of men in his life." RALPH DONE. 62, Elaine-street, Warrington, March 19th, 1914.

div.head: DISCLAIMER.
div.p: A DISCLAIMER.

sir,—According to the report in "The. Exam. iner" of the Liberal annual meeting, on Tues- day, March 10th, Mr. Delaney, "to show the loyalty of the Irish people, for whom he spoke, , proposed a vote of confidence be forwarded to the Government." This statement, coming from a man belonging to no Irish Society. or organisation in the town, is very misleading, and is strongly resented by the officials of the United Irish League. The vote of confidence in the Government is unchallenged.

The officials of the U.LI. are quite capable of issuing any further statements coming from the Irish people in Warrington. JAMES FAY (For the officials of the United "Irish League). 25, Winsvick-street.

div.head: THR DECREPIT HORSE TRAFFIC.
div.p: THR DECREPIT HORSE TRAFFIC.

1 Sir,—May I once more remind your readers that a Bill to prevent the worst cruelties of the old horse traffic will come -up for discussion in the House of Commons on April sth, and I beg them to do all they can to influence their Members to support the measure? An eye-witness writes: "There are great sausage manufactories at Ghent, and no horse is too old or too thin for sausage-making. Some that arrived were such scarecrows that I cannot think where in England they had been hidden. Several were freshly clipped. It was freezing hard. A bitter wind blew and the ground was slippery with frozen snow. Slowly the stiff, feeble old horses walked the short distance to the quarantine stable. One fell, but was got up again." .. . .. _

--.- The present regulations have proved quite in- adequate to purify this horrible traffic, and our honour as a humane nation is at stake. EDITOR, "The Animals' Friend." Portugal-street, London, March 10th, 1914.

div.head: IRISH LIFEBOAT DISASTER.
div.p: THE IRISH LIFEBOAT DISASTER.

Sir,—ln acknowledging the receipt of a num- ber of donations which have been sent to me, and which I have forwarded to the Dublin branch of the Royal National Lifeboat Institu- tion, on behalf of the fund which is being raised to provide for the 27 dependents of the nine lifeboatmen who recently lost their lives off the Wexford coast in an attempt to rescue the crew of the Norwegian vessel Mexico, the secretary informs me that the various appeals have so far been generously responded to, but that another thousand pounds is still required if the sufferers are to be provided for on as liberal a scale as has been the case in connec- tion with similar lifeboat disasters.in the past. As has already been stated, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution has made the usual grant to the relief fund, and the Norwegian Parlia- ment has contributed the sum of of." 500.

I sincerely hope the sum still required will be forthcoming. Contributions are still being senb to me, and among those just received is one of ..k25 from a firm of Manchester merchants, who were inter- ested. in the cargo of the wrecked vessel. I understand that the various funds which have been opened will bepaid into one central fund, and that this central fund will be admin- istered systematically, as has been the case with previous lifeboat disaster funds. CHARLES W. MICARA. Ardmore, St. Annes-on-the-Sea, March 9th, 1914.

The subscribers to the land had an idea that the new Parish Council would waken up to their responsibilities; but no, we find they have not even awakened. As a trustee for the open space. I wrote the Latchford Parish Council on March 15, 1913, suggesting they should take over the control of the land for the use of the neighbourhood in just the way your correspondent wishes, and if they agreed I would call a meeting of sub- scribers for the purpose of getting their con- speanrtiesl tshhealleobpeypolefas my to show any interested letter. I received a Postcard, after several weeks, saying the Coun- cil had decided not to accept the offer. Of course, the poor souls cannot help it, but still I should like the residents themselves to recog- nise the fact that the responsibility is, after all, theirs. They will, when the next election of councillors comes along, have an opportunity of putting people in power who not only recognise it really is the 20th century, but also have at least an ordinary anticipation of what will be , required in the future.
W. H. BELLIAN. The Spinney, Grappenhalt.

div.head: WORKERS, CAPITALISTS, AND DEPORTED LEADERS.
div.p: WORKERS, CAPITALISTS, AND DEPORTED LEADERS.

Sir,—No doubt we may all agree with Mr. Waterson that the South African Government have done a very wrong thing in deporting him and his colleagues from their homes upon such charges as have been stated. And perhaps we may all agree that the conditions of labour in South Africa were becoming such that a general revolt of the working class was amply justified. But r think we should lose the pith of the lesson in South Africa if we allow our senti- ment to hide our. reasoning faculties, so that we cannot see the position of things in the right perspective.

Where we may express surprise with such sweet reasonings as I, for one, was pleased to hear from such a person as Mr. Waterson the other evening at the Parr Hall, is that he should be. indignant at the attitude of the capitalist class towards the revolt. It is here that I again say that quite a lot of trade union leaders make a fatal mistake. The average trade union leader makes elaborate plans to attack the capitalist citadel. He advises the strike weapon, some advise sabotage, some advise political action; in fact, advise every position that is likely to take advantage over the capitalist. This is done in a state of cool complacency. But, my word, if the capitalist should do likewise, what a superheat they get into. Do our trade union industrial-political friends expect that when he has made his plans and operated accordingly, the capitalist is just going to hand over the booty and say or do " nothink "? If he does, where is the ;logic of his position? If life is a war between two social elements, there must be fighting upon both sides, and if one-side have so premeditated their plans so as to win; call- ing that side names is not a sensible thing to do; at least, I think so. We are told that in South Africa the competi- tion of Chinese and Kaffir labour with white labour is bringing conditions down so badly, that the white man has been forced into revolt against those conditions, and that that revolt has taken the form of a strike. The capitalist may be awfully wicked to take advantage of this factor, but that does not alter the fact that wages are brought down by an economic factor known as the supply exceeding the demand, and I ask where is the logic of the strike leaders' case when tho only thing that they can advise as a counter-balance is a cessa- tion of production or political action? I should think that if excess of labour power was the cause of low wages, it should be upon that fac- tor that the workers should rivet their atten- tion. For I have not come across the person as yet who has dared to try to prove that political and industrial action will reduce excess of sur- plus labour. A far more sensible proposition to me than strikes or political action would be for trade unions to provide first-class hotels for the unemployed man, so as to keep him off the labour market, thereby enhancing the value of labour. Another lesson to be drawn from South Africa is the incapacity of the workers and leaders to understand simple economics. Does it ever dawn upon our South African brothers of what they are revolting against? Does it ever cross their minds that if they get good con- ditions of labour, what is the result of their labours? _ _ _

The chief productions of South Africa are diamonds and gold. The labour of those in re- volt is used to produce these commodities. Although the market value of these things is high, 'does the South African worker ever ask himself what is the actual value of his product to himself? Diamonds are used to adorn my lady in London, Paris, Berlin or Vienna. Gold is used in a small degree for the same purpose, but in a far greater degree as a metal shaped for use as a means of exchange. What I wish to impress is that no matter what the quan- tity of these things produced, the world is actually none the richer. To illustrate what I mean with greater emphasis, suppose some kind of paint was fashionable for ornamentation, the same as we find in some places, and that shells were the means of exchange, and that the workers of South Africa were the producers of these things, is not it a feasible proposition to say that they would question whether their energies were used rightly in producing such commodities? I do not say a word against the production of these things as such. But the point I wish to draw attention tolis that the worker's difficulty is in getting the elemental needs of life, and that if he wishes to get the physical demands satisfied he must do it for himself. I say the first duty of the working class is to see that there is sufficient supply- of food, clothing, and shelter provided for himself and his kind, and that be must see to it that these things if he areprfo produced and distributed. ,No one else The whole fault lies, I think in the fact that he concentrates all his energies upon getting a mythological thing called wages. Consciously or unconsciously, the economic disadvantages of the worker has been commercialised, just as the capitalist .has commercialised the supply of the people's needs. One is just as faulty as the other. It is quite an easy task to advise the worker that an Elysium life lies within easy reach, either by putting a cross upon a piece of paper against a particular name, or merely putting his hands in his pockets and doing noth- ing. No change in history has been accom- plished by these means. Unless the worker wants to be always in pawn to the capitalist, he must understand his correct economic posi- tion. Anyways I, for one, shall oppose any- thing that I consider is economically unsound, from whom or what source it comes. Just at present I think the greatest stumbling blocks are those persons considered the workers' leaders.
LABOR OMNIA VINCIT.

MODERN INTER-DEPENDENCE.
By C. E. PARKER.
Three years ago Mr. Norman Angell stirred he thought of EuroPe by his striking work .

' The Great Illusion." No single book has for I oany years created such a world-wide interest. t has been the subject of much thought, has teen through the fires of criticism, and has come ut practiCally unscathed. The main purpose f the book was to prove that war under modern onditions is not alone destructive to the aaterial advancement of the conquered nation, out that the victorious nation suffers out of all droportion to any material advantage gained; in other words that one nation cannot enrich itself by defeating, subjugating anether. The book we have now before us, "The Foundations of International Polity," follows the same line of arguments as, "The Great Illusion," but the matter is new. The author acknowledges his ' debt to writers, both here and on the Continent, who have outlined the theory, and forecast its application to our modern conditions. Ile Pays a tribute to Cobden, who, he says, presented the case long ago with incomparable lucidity. But the case has become much stronger as the years have advanced, and the factors which made war unprofitable to the victor, which Cobden recognised seventy years ago, are new much more potent. Mr. Angell says: "We are now in possession of facts which enable us to crystalise into a definite and comprehensive social and political doctrine, of a quite simple nature, likely to affect public opinion, the principle of the futility of military force as applied to the things for which the world is striving. Modern conditions have made war irrelevant to the issue it has in view."

- Opportunity is here taken to deal with the objections to the main contention that have been made since the issue of "The Great Illu- sion." It is worthy of note that the objectors do not attack the main thesis; in fact, the general chorus is "There is a good deal in it. Adverse critics have been forced to adopt the plan not of answering, but of belittling, as far .as possible, the arguments, and claiming that they do not, as is contended, cover the whole ground. In Chapter VI. and Appendix B. we have an interesting account of the organisation of the Garton Foundation, formed to promote the study of international polity along the hues of thought in these books. Perhaps the simplest way of indicating the line of argument in both works is to borrow an illustration supplied by Mr. Angell. He cites an incident from a book of adventure : Two men in a leaky boat, the sea heavy, the shore a long way off; it takes all the efforts of one man to row and of the other to bale, if either ceases worlc`both are drowned. At one Point the rower • threatens the baler if he does not bale with more energy he will throw him over- board, to which the baler makes the obvious reply: "If lie did, he. the rower, would certainly drown also." As the rower is dependent on the baler, and the baler on the rower, neither can advantageously use force against the other. Here, then, we have the relation, in pictorial form, of civilised countries at the present day in reference to the use of force. Through the division of labour due to differences of climate, natural resources, &c., every country produces the greatest possible value of useful products with the least possible expenditure of effort, and it exchanges, or rather the individual producers, exchange through international trading and banking, the surplus products for goods of a different character which they require. As this interchange grows in volume and complexity, the element of physical compulsion in national relations declines in effectiveness, and is re- placed by agreement based on mutual recogni- tion of advantage. This important point is reasoned out in detail.

GERMANY AND GREAT BRITAIN. Mr. Angell says some good things about the position between Germany and our own ' country. He cites the general British attitude, which Winston Churchill has put in concise I words: "The way to make peace secure is to be so strong that victory over your enemy will he certain." Here is a political idea which we in England parade with a serene dogmatism. But the difficulty is how to obtain the sole right to apply this axiom. There is no patent right' in ideas. How are we to Prevent Germany, Russia, or France from adopting the same prin- ciple to their military and naval preparations? If two or more nations adopt the axiom, attain- ment is impossible, since each cannot be stronger than the other. Mr. Angell was asked at an English meeting if he suggested that we be stronger than our enemies, or weaker? He replied that the last time he was asked this question .was by a German in Berlin, and naturally asked his English questioner how he was to reply to his GerTnan friend. He empha- sises the necessity of putting ourselves in the other fellow's place. To the German the affirm- ation of Churchill's axiom implies that we do not accord to the German the right we claim for ourselves. The Englishman claims superior- ity, hut only, as he says, for defence against attack. A nation can always argue itself into the belief that it is the attacked party. I suppose Englishmen would say we were the attacked party in the Boer War; the Boers entertain the opposite opinion. The German demands the right to make himself sufficiently powerful for it to be dangerous for the English to attack. The Englishman claims superiority of two to one in naval armaments; this means, from the German point of view, that it is not, dangerous for England to attack Germany. England can make this attack with absolute' security. Germany does not even claim equality of armaments; only the right to build such armaments as will make the result of England's aggression doubtful. To the German, England appears to demand a proportion of armaments that will make aggression on Germany a mere naval picnic, which will not leave her even a fighting chance. But the Englishman advances the idea that what is a vital necessity to Eng- land is merely a luxury to Germany.. He says we have no intention of attacking Germany, and Germany says the ss.ame about attacking Eng- land. Each nation is confident of its own p veracity, but doubts that of the other. We claim that our fleet is designed, amongst other things, to protect otir commerce. Germany's oversea commerce is extending equally as r eTa B They e y n great supremacy asr our acy own. of G t auena Britain's power, two keels to one, means a possible menace to the that the , safety of Germany's increasing trade, • and so they go on building and so does England. Neither party feels safe. If for a time one secures a margin of safety, this is the very thing that makes the other unsafe. Both countries will keep up the fight to the point of exhaustion; neither will be frightened by the other's threats, or satisfied by the other's peace- ful assurances. The only way to bring about an end of this mad rivalry is to show how useless it all is. A holiday year, a reduction in size of ships, are only palliatives that do not touch the heart of the problem. What Englishmen and Germans must be made conscious of is that war with its guns and Dreadnoughts is a ludicrously ineffective instrument in accomplishing what each nation has in view.
DISASTER TO THE "CONQUEROR." But why is war ineffective? Take the case be- tween Germany and England. Look at the possibility pictured by recent writers, wherein

German derigibles rained hell upon London, blew up the Bank of England, and a raiding force in some wonderful way captured the gold forming the Bank Reserve. This is a picture drawn not long ago in the London Press, and we are asked: " What would then happen?" This, since Germany's financial stability de- pends nearly as much upon our bank reserve as does our English finance, Germany would suffer nearly as much as we. The first effect of such action would be a run on every bank in Eng- land, and many could not stand the strain. Simultaneously German bankers, many with credits in London, and all under financial obli- gations, would feel the effect, merchants the whole world over, threatened by ruin through the financial collapse in London, would imme- diately call in all their credits in Germany, and German finance would present a condition of things hardly less chaotic than that in Eng- land. Very much the same conditions would result from a declaration of war between the two countries, and this without any fanciful pictures of a hell rain, or act of burglary on the bank reserve. Germany's capital and credit, because of the inter-nationalisation and political inter-dependence of our modern financial system, would also suffer severely. Not only would the individual Germans trading with England suffer, but the whole commercial community would lose heavily. To show how thoughtful men are moving in this direction, Norman Angell quotes the words of Dr. Jayne Hill, some time the American Am- bassador at the German Court. The Doctor says:—

International spoliation has ceased to be a trade. Yet all the old traditions of depre- dations from beyond the border, of peaceful commerce exposed to capture at sea, of crushing indemnities to be paid by the van- quished to the invading conqueror, are kept alive, and serve to thrill the readers of sensational publications, and to force the assent of Parliamentary Committees to ex- travagant military appropriations. •• . . . "But no," it will be said, "the light of Yesterday has not departed. These fears are well grounded. Our natural enemy is stronger than we, and he will therefore avenge himself upon us." Acting upon this assurance we strive to become stronger than he; and now this " natural enemy" says, with all honesty, "An assault is imminent; we must prepare to resist it." And so by a process of endless circular reasoning the illusion of hatred and hostility is kept alive. • • • • And so it happens that the modern State, the embodiment of law and the pro- tagonist of justice, whose simple promise to pay is bought by the million in the open market by the shrewdest interpreters of human intentions—the bankers and mcneY- lenders—permits itself to be discredited by a dogma of diplomacy which sounds to every honest man like a calumny on human decency. It is not necessary to prove that human nature has changed, or will change, or that men are in any degree less self-regarding, or inspired by a loftier altruism, than pre- veiled in former times. It is simply that humanity has discovered a new path and is disposed to follow it. It is perceived that happiness can be obtained more easily and more surely lq industry than by plunder, by commerce than by piracy, by intercourse between the nations than by isolation.

This last paragraph suggests the line of cleavage between what Angell calls the "pacifists," or what is generally known as the "peace party." They base their claims for peace on Christian principles, plead for a loftier altruism, for an improved nature, and a truer conception, of the sacredness of human life. Angell admits the power of these, but they leave him cold; he contends that they are ineffective, because they do not bring to their aid the economic aspect of the question. Ile calls for correct thinking in the practical plane. lie instances the passing away of religious wars through a realisation of their ineffectiveness, and because it was found that truth was out: side the scope of physical conflict. As this realisation grew, religious wars declined, and finally ceased. In like manner he says that security of life and property, like the security of truth, is not derived from military force; that military force is as ineffective as irrelevant in the end for promoting prosperity as for pro- moting truth. When people realise this politi- cal wars will cease, as religious wars have ceased, for the same reason and in the same way, this not necessarily from any change in the character of the persons forming communities, but from a change of their conceptions.

HOW IS THIS TO BE BROUGHT ABOUT? Sir Edward Grey, shortly after "The Great Illusion" was published, said: Another force at work on the side of peace was that people were beginning to realise war between two great nations was bound increasingly to become a disaster not only to themselves, but to other nations that were taking no part, and even as between the two nations themselves it was quite possible in the most successful war the victor might lose More than he gained. When I read that book (" The Great Illusion") I was reminded of the !saying of a thinker a great many years ago that not things that matter so much, but peoples opinions,about things. True as the state- ment of that book may be, it does not be- come an operative movement in the minds and conduct of nations until they are con- vinced of its truth, and it has become a commonplace to them. Mr. Ure is convinced of the truth, for be said in connection with the Ulster trouble : Assuming a Provisional Government were set up in the four north-eastern counties, what would happen? The first consequence would be a panic run on the local banks. The banks of Ulster depended for their credit on Lombard-street in London, and Lombard-street would act in the same way SS they would do in the ease of a South American Republic in the hands of revolu- tionaries—their rate of interest would be put up. Then the Ulster banks would immediately raise their rates and would call in their loans right and left, and the Irish farmers in the south and west would instantly with- draw their deposits. The Provisional Gov- ernment would find itself faced with rising prices and languishing credit. - -

Mr. Angell recognises the truth of what Sir Edward Grey says, and refers to it in the fol- lowing passage: It cannot be too often repeated that the necessary profitlessness of war between civil- ised nations, the necessary inter-dependence of nations, will not stop war.- It is the general recognition a profitlessness and inter- dependence that will stop war. Impersonal • forces, the Stock Exchange, and the rest of it, will certainly push these truths molt) and more into our notice. But the rapidity with' which we shall arrive at a better condition I of things depends, as every. other part of man's struggle for life depends, on the extent to which he brings his intelligence to bear on the matter. The rate of real pro- gress is the rate of improvement in ideas. And when our ideas as to the real relation- ship of nations have become somewhat saner, it will no longer be possible for intriguing statesmen or concession-hunters to explode these magazines of ignorance and passion. All their intrigues will fizzle out as harmlessly as a wax vesta on a cement floor.
*The Foundations of International Polity. By Norman Angell. London: W. Heinemann, 21, Bedford-street; W.C.

div.p: THE FORCE OF THE WIND.

Towards the end of 1911 our coasts were visited by severe gales, and the papers were provided with abundant news in the shape of. reports of numerous shipwrecks. One paper had a column headed "Great Storm. Gale blows 80 miles an hour." Probably few people have the remotest idea of what a gale of eighty miles an hour means. The follow- ing figures may amuse those who take any interest in the matter. The day is calm when the wind is blowing at less than 2 miles an hour. At such times the smoke from the chimneys rises vertically. When the wind is moving at four miles an hour its direction is shown by the drift of the smoke but not by the wind vanes;- at seven miles an hour it is felt on the face, leaves are rustled and an ordinary vane is moved; at ten miles an hour leaves and small twigs are set in motion and light flags are extended; at nineteen miles an hour small trees in leaf begin to sway and wavelets form on inland waters; at thirty- one miles an hour whole trees are set in mo- tion and inconvenience is experienced in walking against the wind. At thirty-seven miles an .hour we get what sailors call a 'Fresh Gale.' This breaks twigs of trees and generally impedes progress. A Strong Gale is a wind moving at 44 miles an hour, a speed sufficient to result in the removing of chimney pots and slates; at 63 miles an hour we have a Whole Gale. This is very seldom experienced inland and when it is, trees are uprooted and considerable structural damage is done. We are still a long way from the newspaper's 80 miles an hour and we have finished the catalogue of gales as known to the sailor.

div.head: HURRICANE.
div.p: THE HURRICANE.

If the wind has a velocity of 64 miles an hour it is a Storm while if it has a velocity of 77 miles an hoar it is a Hurricane. Both Storm and Hurricane are rarely experienced even on the sea and when they are, wide- spread damage is the ,result. It is possible that the wind in question did blow 80 miles an hour but if that were the case then the storm was of extraordinary strength and the wonder is not that so many vessels were wrecked but that so few escaped destruc- tion.

The West Indies suffer from hurricanes in the months of August, September, and Octo- ber. They are dreaded by the captains of ships and if sufficient warning of their ap- proach can be obtained the vessel is put offt of its ordinary course in the endeavour to escape, for a conflict with the violent wind is sure to result in great damage if not in tlbe total loss of the vessel. The tales that are told of the loss of life and property when one of these hurricanes passes over the land are not ex.aggerated. The hurricane leaves a path as clean as if cut with a knife. Some of the smaller islands are literally swept clean, crops, houses, buildings and trees, collapse as if uprooted by a gigantic earthquake. Along the coasts the damage is even more terrible, for there the effects of wind and wave are • combined. The water is heaped up in a great tidal wave and death by drowning becomes the lot of many of those who have escaped the falling of bricks and mortar and the bom- bardment of uptorn trees.

THE DREADED TORNADO. But worse than the hurricanes of the West Indies are the Tornadoes. These move alonrlg at the rate of about 40 miles an hour fortunately, rarely last more than T a spiral wind They fire small violent cyclones.. in them moves towards the centre in p two hours. motion, and the rate of moveme it towards the centre of the swirl has been known to reach as much as 200 to 400 miles _ the onset hour. The only thing that can withstand sooflidinenaur itself. nwth rahie trains ins of isesuchis alikfoercteheis rtohaer over a gigantic bridge. forest The tornado cuts a of a path through a e Loose soil like that mow r through a meadow- is removed from fields, water from s ponds. Large boulders are caught up and carried hundreds of feet away. No building, whatever be its can escape demolition, and animals have been lifted up and carried for strength, menglefneth' mile or more. Professor Dryer says ~itaavy. structures are removed from their foundations and locomotive engines lifted from their rails. The smaller work of the tornado is equally impressive such as the stripping of feathers from fowls and the clothing from persons. Wire hairpins have been driven through fence boards, and straws driven into oak wood. Almost any story of a tornado's energy may be true, be- cause the truth is beyond the power of human imagination to invent. A part of a house may be reduced to fragments while the rest is left undisturbed. People have been car- ried long distances and deposited unhurt. Heavy objects are remelted and light and fra- gile ones left in the place. Fragments of furniture from the same room or from the same piece are often widely scattered in op- posite directions. These and other mysteri- ous freaks are probably due to irregular and confused currents in the general whirl. The walls of buildings are often thrown outwards as if by an explosion."

If our weather be Often described as abom- inable, at any rate we usually escape such visitations as these. And yet, there are times when we get a touch of gales that must he first cousins to a tornado. Thus on March 24th, 1895, a storm traversed England from South IVales to Norfolk. At Cambridge hun- dreds of trees were blown down in the short space of two hours, and in other places the wind cut a clean path similar to those which are caused by the tornadoes of the United States of America. THE GREAT STORM.
The most terrific storm we ever experienced in these Islands occurred in November, 1703. :ts results were so disastrous that it has ever

since been referred to as 'The Great Storni. It was almost as violent as a typhoon, hilt instead of lasting for a few hours it blew for a whole week. On Saturday morning, tbe 27th. of the month, the people of London had got so frightened that they tumbled out klf, bed and took refuge in. the cellars. Many 0, them thought that the end of the world ha° come. When the wind abated a little and tile most courageous ventured outside, theY found the streets thickly strewn with bricks. tiles, stones, lead, timber and all kinds a building material. Twenty-one people were killed by falling chimneys and the house were often mere skeletons of their former selves. Boards, tarpaulins, old sails, all,d straw were requisitioned with which to repair the damage. Tiles rose from one guinea 0, six guineas per thousand and bricklayers wages rose in ,proportion. In London. th Temple and Christ's Hospital presented an al" most ludicrous appearance with their patch' ings of straw, reeds and other thatching mat' erials. At Wells the bishop and his wife were kill- ed in bed by a stack of chimneys that dis- turbed their night's rest. Defoe tells that in Kent alone over a thousand dwellini houses and barns were levelled to the grouill and five hundred old oak trees were destroyej in the park at Penshurst. On the Thames the watermen lost 500 whet: Iries and the bargemen 120 of their craft. :WY ' other vessels were also destroyed and tile number of the drowned was never asce tained. It was during this storm that Eddystose, 'lighthouse collapsed. It had been erectel 'four years before by Winstanlev, and he fire qlf his fr‘ends were in the lig,hthouse s' the time of its destruction. In this case se have to add the force of the waves to those °f the wind but, as the waves are caused by rile wind, it is still the former of the two agenh. that we have chiefly to reckon with when se wish to account for the disaster. Many parts of the world suffer from o(4' sional but none the less fearful winds whit are, however, purely local in character. I° certain parts of southern France there is lt wend that comes r from the east, and is knolre, as the avian. When this blows, carriage are apt to be precipitated into the val 4 and pedestrians have to lie flat on the groull° to prevent themselves bein.g carried away.

MEASURING THE FORCE. The force of the wind is measured exPeriP mentally, on land, by means of an instrf inent called an Anemometer. Many Pe°llo4; are familiar with the most commoti form this, which consists of four hieinispherical cups which spin round and round withilt wind and are Dlaced on She too of some niZ-% building. Tile axis on wrnen rue cups revo;fi is connected with a ntunlx,r of wheels whiell record the number of revolutions in a gives time. Robinson, the inventor of this lustre,' ment, ' supposed that the cups revolved wit! about a third of the velocity of the win 4 1310' his theory has been shewn to be wrong. A later form of anemometer is not quite °!' striking to the eye but is much more ingelll' ous. In this apparatus the wind blows acrooe the top of a tube in such a way that it sue° tbg: the air out of the tube, the amount of suct depending on the force of the wind. Atiee ; bottom of the tube there is a little float in reservoir of water and "t• as the wind sucks Oa the air this float rises and falls. To the el': of the float there is attached a pen which re:, cords its nuitions on a revolving drum, that by day and by night, the instrument re; corcls the slightest variation in the force the wind.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1914.
FARM AND GARDEN.
FLOODS AND STORMS.
Bad for Seeding Time but Good for
Water Supply.

'The forebodings expressed when March opened, so pleasantly are being fulfilled, says "The ' Times." The past 10 days have been produc- tire of some of the most tempestuous and dis- agreeable weather of the season.. The rainfall throughont the southern half of England has been abnormal for the time of year, and north of the Trent there has been an equivalent in rain, sleet and snow combined. Rivers and their tributaries have risen to a higher level than'was readied at any time during winter. Many of them have overflowed on to grass and arable land in a manner which recalls the early months of last year, and the freedom of the herds and flocks, as well as the progress of field work, has been hampered somewhat seriously. The prospect of an early and auspicious seed- ing season is less reassuring now than at the beginning of the month, but the position is not yet irreconcilable with a 'satisfactory finish of spring sowing. The land is sodden at pres- ent, but it dries quickly under the influences of the sunshine and winds of March. Little headway was made last week with the prepara- tion and the seeding of the land, but work was already so forward that the interruption has been accepted with equanimity, all the more pronounced in that something of the kind was expected. The wet spell has not been devoid of redeeming advantages. The many aistricts of uncertain water supply will find in the replen- ishment of the wells and springs substantial recompense .for the temporary discomforts and suspension of Work;

THE'-EXPENSE OF FENCES. To turn to pasture farming, here, too, there are signs to those who can read them that the present state of affairs Cannot last much longer and the first thing \that s4ikes me in a grass c,ounty like Somerset is the hedges. If you took 1,800 acres of the country round here in one farm it would cost in labour more actual cash

to keep and Maintain the fences on it than it costs to work the 1,800-acre arable farm I men- tioned. altogether:-- During the last twenty years it has cost me double the amount of time and money to make and maintain the hedges on the various lands I have farmed than it has to harvest and thatch the whole of the crops grown on the same land, and it is the same throughout Somerset and some adjoining counties. These hedges, two-thirds of which are

quite unneeessary, cost farmers up and down the country millions a year. A dertain number of hedges are very necessary for shelter and fence, but our forefathers seemed to have a mania for hedges, and thousands of them would be got rid of at once if it were not for the back- breaking labour of grubbing them. In faet, it is a puzzle how they are to be get rid of, for go they must before any great economy of farming can be practised about here. Farmers here in North Somerset have brought economy of labour to a fine art. The labour trouble, acute...for years, is getting worse; and in engag- ing men it is not at all a question as to whether a man suits you or not. Whether or not he stays over a fortnight depends upon whether you and your work suit him.—" A Somerset Farmer" in "Farm and Home."

div.head: SEVEN YEARS FOR RICK FIRING.
div.p: SEVEN YEARS FOR RICK FIRING.

•, Mr. Justice Darling, in sentencing to seven years' penal servitude Henry Ives, 29, labourer, for setting fire to a corn rick belonging to Mr. Dance, a farmer, near Uxbridge, said the pris- oner had been four times indicted for setting fire to ricks; he had been convicted twice, the grand jury threw out the bill once, and he was acquitted once. •• He must expect .a severe sen- tence, because he had been convicted before. Ile was an idle and worthless person: The proper sentence which lie would-pass-if lie. had power to do so Would be some sort of sentence which they bad power to pass in America, that was that lie be kept in prison until the authorities were sat- isfied he was a reformed character. If he could pass a sort of .indeterminable:sentence like that lie would do so. If prisoner did that kind of thing again be would probably be sent to penal servitude for life.

DISEASE. There were four cases of foot-and-mouth disease reported in the week ended March 7. Thirty-two cattle were attacked in the Liver- pool case and one pig in the Carnarvon case. There has since been no spread of the disease and the outlook is again reassuring. Swine fever was reported from 64 new centres in 21 English counties, the pigs slaughtered number- ing 506. The fresh outbreaks of anthrax totalled 24, attacking 24 cattle and one dog.

WOMEN STAMPEDED BY RABBITS. The sudden appearance in a Berlin tramcar of nine rabbits which issued from a basket car- ried by a sleeping passenger caused a stampede among the women travellers, during which the conductor was knocked down and seriously in- jured and two windows were shattered.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Herbaceous plants may be divided where necessary. Such plants as Michaelmas daisies, harpaliums, and phloxes soon outgrow their positions, and division is necessary to prevent deterioration of the flowers. • For the making of new plants select the out- side growths, as being more likely to grow well and flower better. If the ground is not over moist plant tubers of anemones and ranunculus, covering them with a little sand before earthing over.

Climbing plants may be got in, after due pre- paration of the soil, and adding decayed manure. t Prepare sites for sweet peas by deep digging or trenching, and do not spare the manure in the under soil.

Plant fruit trees; dig and manure rhubarb beds. Remove weeds from strawberry beds, and make firm young plants. Fruit trees may be pruned and trained. Make sowings of early broad beans, parsnips, radish, mustard and cress and lettuce. A first sowing may be made of early peas if the soil is not .too wet. Plant shallots.

div.head: ON SOWING PEAS.
div.p: ON SOWING PEAS.

In sowing early peas leave room for two or three rows of early potatoes between each row of peas. Many sow their peas too thickly; not only .wasting the seed but spoiling the crop. After prearing the' soil by deep digging and manuring, draw drills six inches wide and two to three inches deep, placing the early sorts at a uniform distance of two inches apart all over the drills. Later varieties should not be less than three inches apart, and the drills three inches deep, or a little more in summer. div.head: 'THE END OF THE WORLD."
div.p: 'THE END OF THE WORLD."
Forecast of What Will Happen in the World to Come.
ERA OF LOVE AND JUSTICE.

A forecast of the doom of this earth, and the advent of a better world, in which organised sin and selfishness would give .place to all era of love and justice, was given at a meeting, Sutuuddeerntts' he auspices of the International Bible Association, held in the Park Picture P Warrington, on Sday evening. The speaker tin was Mr. Alexander Kirkwood, of Glas- gow. The object of the lectures, he said, was to stimulate faith in and to increase the systematic study of the Bible. In this our day when know- ledge is being so marvellously increased in re- spect to all the various sciences, fresh light we believe is due also upon the science of Divine revelation. We are living in an age of pro- gress. Advancement is being made all along the line. Carried along by the current of the times: old land marks are • gradually fading away; estab- lished .ideas are being unrooted ; creeds. and theories centuries old are being thrown into the melting pot to be fashioned, afresh. Indeed, ao great is the general feeling.- of :unsettlement, that many are in danger of losing, and many have already lost their faith in. the Bible as the infallible Word of clod. What was needed was niiire Veal. Bible study and that the Bible should be studied in its own light.

div.head: End—And After.
div.p: The End—And After.

What did Ile mean by !'fillet itte:of "Tho End of dm World—And After "? -There were three great worlds in the plan of God. The first, be- ginning at the creation of man. elided at the flood. It lasted for a period of 1,656 „years. The second great world, the present one, Which was then introduced, will confinne rtill the second advent of Christ, when the third great world, " The world to come," will be ushered in. Un- like its predecessors, it will e "World 'with- out end." The expression " the end of the world," is coninionly.; used in reference to this material globe upon which we live, the thought being that there will be by-and-bye a great catastrophe to this planet, and amid the wreck of matter and the crash of worlds, it will be utterly destroyed together with everything upon it. This, however, is not the Biblical use of the expression. The first world is said to have come to an end at the time of the flood, yet the planet still exists. So will it be when the second world, this present evil world will terminate. This same earth will continue in the world, to come. When the end of the world is spoken of in the Scriptures it means simply the end of the age, or dispensation, or the end of the existing order I of things. I - ' World-Wide Anarchy.

of Parallel in world-wide a The return of Christ, which will end this present world and usher in the new dispensatioit is always associated in the Scriptures with a ghiu•ematantiinalistm tlrtouisbtleo,bwie h timetlout anarchy and confusion in which the then exist_ Mg order of things, social, political, industrial and ecclesiastical, will be revolutionised. Many e of r. figures are employed to describe or picture these conditions. Sometimes it is spoken of as a "great flood"; again as a "great storm," again as a "great earthquake"; again as a " great battle," the battle of Armageddon. The best known, and perhaps the most mis- understood, is the picture the Alostle Peter gives in the third chapter of his second epistle. He describes it there in the language of a great conflagration which burns up the heavens and the earth at the second coming of Jesus. The language is, Of course, symbolical. The phy- sical sky, and literal earth are not going to be burned up when Jesus comes. He is coming to set up His kingdom upon the earth and intro- duce that time, we have all prayed for, sayieg "Thy kingdom come; Thy will be done on earth as it is done in heaven."

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
The Proper Time for the Overhauling O f Tyres.
A DANGEROUS OCCUPATION?

I wonder how many of our readers have ever realised that cleaning a bicycle has a right to be classed among the dangeraus occupations of to- day. At all events, such is the view expressed recently to the Postmaster-General by one of his numerous staff. In the course of an inquiry respecting the status of night messengers and their duties, a witness contended that cycle cleaning, one of his nocturnal duties, was really dangerous, as the fine dust from the unclean mount penetrates to the lungs with disastrous results. What a glorious chance for the lazy cyclist, who at once is provided by a really good excuse for refusing to clean either his own or anybody else's machine, and what an oppor- tunity for the makers of all black cycles to introduce one which does not require cleaning. But, seriously, such statements are absurd in the extreme, as probably every member of the Inquiry Committee in question had often cleaned a machine, and all members of the general public are merely amused by the guile- less assertion.

div.head: Inflaters.
div.p: Inflaters.

He will confer a real boon on the cycling fraternity who places on the market a genuinely reliable inflater. Since the advent of the pneu- matic tyre every conceivable variety seems to have been tried, and we are as far from perfec- tion as ever. First came the heavy metal arrangement, heavy short and stumpy, requir- ing a considerable effort to induce air to enter the tyre, and usually attached to the cross-bar by thick, elastic bands. Practi- cally every single feature was unsatisfac- tory, and the long, narrow inflater of metal which succeeded it was a definite improvement. The now universal celluloid pump seems very prone to leak at the bottom of the barrel unless made in one entire piece, while the -larger pat- terns are liable to depart from the perpendicu- lar after much use. The clips are now more satisfactory, and at least one prominent firm of makers have made these part of the frame itself. A good foot pump at home is a great conveni- ence, as the doubtful inflater attached to the average machine can then be used only in times of emergency. Take Care of Your Tyres.

Now is the time to make a thorough examina- tion of your tyres before the commencement of the cycling season, an event which is usually Considered to coincide with the date of the Easter holidays, although our proverbial climate has the caking vote in the matter. As a natural result of the extra wear and tear the back tyre always requires the most attention and more frequent replacement, particularly as it is all- important that the greatest weight should be accompanied by the greatest strength. Any tyres by a reliable maker are good for at least two years, but at the beginning of the second season it is a good plan to transfer the compara- tively unworn tyre on the front wheel to the back, and vice versa. A few minutes spent in renovation will be well spent, and ensure tyre comfort for a whole season. Remove all par- ticles of grit, &c., from the inside of the cover with a damp cloth, as these are liable to work through the inner tube, causing punctures and carefully patch any weak places with canvas. Holes on the outside of the cover may be re- paired by filling with cotton wool, soaked in rubber solution.

An Interesting Vessel. .."1•11e Sylmastian, .the first British:built motor- driven tank ship,:arrived in the Thames a few dais ago. On her maiden voyage from Dundee to the: Black Sea. For several reasons the event is noteworthy in the annals of British shipbuild- ing, but particularly as the Admiralty have ordered five vessels of the same class. Time new ship is driven by twin screws worked by two sets of Swedish two-cylinder Diesel engines. Both main engines have six cylinders of 16in. diameter and 221 in. stroke, generating 1,600 horse power, on a daily consumption of oil amounting to 71 tons. The Sebastian is 310 ft. long by 45ft. beam, and has an average speed of 111 knots, rather higher than that of time average •cargo steamer. It is difficult to forecast time future development of the oil-driven vessel, and the extent to which it will supersede the ordinary steamer. Just at present, however, the price of oil is unnaturally high, but with the probable expansion of the supply and improved facilities for its transport, the use of the Diesel engine for overseas traffic seems likely to increase in the near future.

Legal Notes. Just at present the Royal Automobile Club and the Automobile Association and Motor Union have under consideration a number of Private Bills introdnced into Parliament in the present session, which, if carried, may prove hostile to the motoring community. Various local authorities, for example, are seeking powers to charge extra for water used in wash- ing priate motor cars, a procedure diametric- ally opposed to the general practice of including water so used under the " domestic purposes" clause. Other Bills are Railway Bills, with reference to level crossings, and applications from various tramway authorities in connection with the various undertakings. It should be emphasised that none of the motor organisations desire any preference or privilege hostile to the public at large, but, unfortunately, there still exists a mass of biassed opinion even among Corporations and powerful trading concerns, as well as among private individuals. At present, at any rate, careful supervision of all proposed enactments is a very necessary precaution prior to active..., opposition to more objectionable measures.

The Best Place for the Petrol Tank. In the early days of the motor car the fuel tank was placed almost universally underneath the driving seat, the spirit being fed to the car- buretter by gravity. Such arrangement has many advantages: it can be made sufficiently large to hold five, ten, or even twenty gallons, according to the size of the car, and, what is even more important. is comparatively immune from. damage either from fire or collision. Of course, to fill the tank involves disturbing the passenger, but as a general rule enough spirit can be run in at the commencement of a journey to last until the next stop. During the last two or three years the rear tank has found increas- ing favour, despite annoyance caused by clogged pressure pipes, filters and valves. But here the chief danger is the grave risk of collision, and a tank ornamented with several dents is becoming quite a common sight in the Metropolis and elsewhere. A protective cover of wooden laths is sometimes employed, but the liability to damage is only lessened and not by any means abolished. On the whole the former type seems the more satisfactory.

The meeting joined with the National Federa- tion special praise service on Sunday, when at 3.30 the hymn "Fling out the banner" was sung most heartily, as it was all over the country at the same time. The occasion was most inspir- ing. Mr. Farrar presided, and explained the National Brotherhood's request for a little extra contribution to carry on their work. There were no paid officers, everything was done vol- untarily, but printing was a great cost, and that expenditure needed to be met. This year the National Federation was going in for a big campaign in the country to reach all working amen and the women. After the special hymn and the collection, Mr. Wright addressed the meeting on " Person- ality." He referred to' the men and women of the past, who had laboured earnestlY, and mentioned the work of Elizabeth Fry and others. Mr. Yearsley read the lesson and Mr. A. Healey led the prayer. Two new members received a hearty wlcome.

div.head: BAPTIST SUSTENTATION SCIIEME.
div.p: BAPTIST SUSTENTATION SCIIEME.

At the special services and collection for the sustentation fund at Golborne-street Baptist Church, the preacher was the Rev. H. Ogden, who took for his text Romans x. 14, " How shall they hear without a preacher?" The preacher is called upon to make known pre-eminently and conspicuously that "Whosoever will call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." The preacher's pre-eminent commission is to tell all men that there is room in this busy life, and there must be a place, if life is to be kept sweet for fellowship and communion with God. A preacher may be tempted by the immediate life around him to feel. and to speak furiously about the very bad conditions. Mr. Ogden said that at least thrice daily he passed through a portion of the town, which he first saw on a November day more than two years ago. The anger he then felt has in no way diminished. The horror of a first sight, though now seen thrice daily, has not been lessened. How long ' will a Christian community, though more hap- pily environed, endure it? And yet there are distinct factors in the life of that unhappy region which will never be cured without the power of a personal Saviour in those people's lives. The preacher must point to "Him" who transforms men and women morally. The Baptist Church in England is striving to place the man who preaches in a position of decency. The man in the slum shall not merely have com, forting words, but be shall have practical as- sistance. The country minister wearing out his life on £7O a year shall have behind him not only the moral support of the Baptist Union, but also its financial aid. The Strong shall bear the burdens of the weak:, How much we owe to village churches can never be calculated. Our best ministers, our choicest deacons have been, many of them, village men. The little Baptist Bethel has been the only place in the whole village that dared to assert its independ- ence against the squire. Such terms as liberty of conscience, political freedom, and the liberty of the mind were and are championed by the dweller in the village manse. Hithertolie had to do it on his £7O a year. Now he shall he assured of his £l2O to £l5O per annum, with the Baptist Union ever behind him. Our de- nominational statesman, the Rev. T. 11. Shakes- peare, has appealed for A,20,000. Any contribu- tion received by the preacher would be for- warded to our Union Committee in London.

div.head: BOLD-STREET MEN'S CLASS. " The Lawful Use of the Sabbath."
div.p: BOLD-STREET MEN'S CLASS. " The Lawful Use of the Sabbath."

The essayist appointed to deal with the cur- rent lesson for Sunday afternoon was Mr. Peter Woods. The passages of Scripture down for consideration illustrated the attitude of Christ towards the rigid Sabbath observance which characterised the Jewish religion. Mr. Woods suggested that the Pharisees had purposely ar- ranged for the presence of the man suffering with dropsy in order to ensnare the Saviour, and
S.

confound Him before the multitude. Christ, however, accepted the challenge, and, curing the unfortunate, routed His enemies by illustrating the fact that it was ever the spirit, and 'never the letter of the law, which determined a sin- cere man's action.

Evidently legitimate occupations on the Sab- bath day came under three heads, acts of piety, acts of charity, and acts of necessity. The court of appeal which decided the lawfulness of any deed must finally be the individual con- science. When a man was guided by the spirit of Christ there would be no fear of his abusing the dictates of that conscience. _

The discussion which followed was of a brisk and critical order.- It was pointed out that the liberty of conscience must not be allowed to interfere with another individual's freedom of action. Tolerance must be tempered with jus- tice. Emphatic exception was taken to the attitude displayed by certain members of the Christian Church towards the Sunday tram ser- vice. The unanimous opinion seemed to be that the intolerance displayed by "the self-appointed deputation" was a serious reflection upon the sincerity of Nonconformity, and should have been met with an official reproval. Mr. Woods, in reply, agreed with the plea for justice, but said it was not his place to sit in judgment on the tramway deputation.

div.head: Höli
div.p: Höli
TO EVERY MAN.

A " Campaign to Every Man in England" is being arranged to open pn November Bth to the 15th of this year by the National Brotherhood Council. The "Campaign Manual" (Brotherhood Pub- fishing House, 6d.), which the Council ha a just issued, gives a very clear outline of the forth- coming " Campaign." The Brotherhood Move- ment, of which the Council is the representative body, now includes in this country some 2,300 societies, with an aggregate membership of up- wards of half a million.

The movement has also spread to the Conti- nent, and has met with remarkable success in France and Belgium. Canada, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand have each taken up the movement, and it is gaining ground steadily. American sympathisers are arranging for a Convention- at Buffalo with a view to starting the movement in the United States.

The Brotherhood Movement, according to the " Manual," aims at uniting men of all Churches, parties and classes in common action for social well-being and the public good. It holds that while differing in their views as to doctrines, church systems and policies, they can all agree on the basis of the Fatheihood of God and the brotherhood of man, and can, as men of good will, work out the social and moral logic of this position. in order. that .the "Message" shall reach "Every Man in England" much work will have to be done, and the movement welcomes suggestions and offers of help from till who can in any way give some service. The " Manual" explains bow the "Message" will be delivered to all classes of people, and also how the workers will be trained for their great work. It works out in detail the gospel of the Brotherhood Movement, and is, we think, a most interesting and instructive little book.

div.head: BLOOD PURIFYING EXTRAORDINARY.
div.p: BLOOD PURIFYING EXTRAORDINARY.

Professor J. Abel, Drs./ L. G. Rountree and, B. B. Turner, all of Jotuts Hopkins University,' have (says " Science Siftings") just conducted a remarkable experiment on a living dog. They took the blood out of the dog's body and sent it coursing through a coil of tubes measuring nearly 50ft. The scientists who watched the

demonstration saw the entire circulation of the dog going on in the glass tubes, being propelled through the tubes by the action of the animal's heart, which never stopped beating while they watched it. At the same time, by the use of a salt solution through which the blood was cours- ing, the vital fluid was being purified of sugar, urea, and all diffusible materials. By passing . it through chemicals of different sorts other kinds of blood poisons, it is claimed, can be re— moved. The dog, thoroughly antesthetised, lived throughout the wonderful experiment, which may some day be applied to man.

div.head: KIMOC: ITS lIISTORY.
div.p: KIMOC: ITS lIISTORY.
The Adventures of a United States Government Scout.

Some years ago Mr. Charles Bigelow, now one of the proprietors of the famous Kimoc Indian Remedies, was acting as a Government Scout in the Indian Territory, and while on one of his expeditions was taken ill with a fever, and foi some time lay at death's door. During his ill- ness he was cared for by an Indian Chief and his family. He was visited by an Indian doctor, who gave him that now famous Indian remedy, Kimoc Tonic, and by its use he was snatched from the jaws of death, and restored to health, owing his life to the wonderful efficacy and curative power of this medicine. He then en- deavoured to persuade the Indians to give him their secret of its ingredients. This, at first, they refused to do, but after, much persuasion and many discussions, they at last partially yielded to his request, and the chief of the tribc allowed five of his most renowned medicine-men to accompany Mr. Bigelow, together with an ample supply of the roots, herbs, gums, barks, &c., used in the manufacture of their medicines. What started thus in a small way has now grown into a large business, and to-day theii famous Kimoc remedies, which have done so much to alleviate sufferipg of every description, are known throughout England and America. Throughout the civilised world there is no more potent remedy known for diseases result- ing from a disordered condition of the kidneys. liver, stomach, or blood, than Kimoc Blood Tonic. The address of Messrs. Healy and Bigelow, the proprietors of the Kimoc Remedies, is 27, Col- quitt-street, Liverpool. Their remedies can also be obtained from all chemists and stores.

GETTING AGATE. In 1877 I went to a farmyard to see the men start work at a threshing machine. A labourer, a newcomer from Norfolk, stood looking, when the farmer shouted to him, "Get agate." The man walked down the stackyard, and presently returned carrying a five-barred gate. The farmer shouted, "What the d— are you doing?" The man replied, "Master, you told me to get a gate, and I have fetched one." The farmer, of course, meant "start work."

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY CONCERT.
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY CONCERT.
"Hymn of Praise". to be Rendered
Next Wednesday.
THE 4th PRINTING CENTENARY.

At the Warrington Musical Society's con- cluding concert of the season on Wednesday next Mendelssolin's "Hymn of Praise" is the chief item in the programme. It is some 18 years since this work was last heard in War- rington, and in the interval much water has passed under the bridges. Music of the modern school has eclipsed, partially at all events, the shining lights of thel Lobgesang and kindred favourite works by the same composer. But a return to loyalty to the works of the old and well-tried masters of oratorio, such as Mendelssohn, Haydn, Handel and Beethoven, has been often predicted, and there are not wanting signs that these prophe- cies are already beginning to be realised. That an old favourite like "The Hymn of Praise" will attract a good audience in Warrington there is little reason to doubt, for the work is hardly second to " The Elijah" in point of popularity. For the following interesting and informative "note" in regard to " The Hymn of Praise" we are indebted to Mr. F. H. Crossley, the Musical Society's conductor, under whose baton the performance of nearly two decades ago was given. The "Hymn of Praise" was written in 1840, and was specially composed for the fourth cen- tennial celebration of the invention of printing which was held in Leipsic in that year. At first sight this may appear rather a prosaic occasion to have inspired such a magnificent work; but it must be remembered that Ger- many prides itself very much on the invention of printing, and Leipsic is especially regarded as being the birthplace of books. Mendelssohn was commissioned by the Corporation to write a work to celebrtite the event. Musical works written ,on commission are not always satisfac- tory. A composer is bound down to time, and I he is more or less influenced by the circum- stances under which he knows his composition mLill be performed. Under these circumstances rr is natural that works written to order, so to speak, should often lack spontaneity and appear more or less laboured. However, in the "Hymn of Praise" we have a brilliant example of how Mendelssohn was superior to these influences. From beginning to end the music flows on as if it had cost the composer no trouble at all to think it out. As usual Mendelssohn selected his own words, and they appear most appropri- ate for celebrating the invention of that art which has done so much towards creating Light out of Darkness. On the title page of the score the "Hymn of Praise" is described as a "Symphony—Can- tata," which at once gives us the idea that the orchestra has an equal share with the chorus in depicting the composer's ideas. In construC- tion the only work with which the " Ilymn of Praise" can be compared is Beethoven's last Symphony, " The Choral Symphony," as it is called, but the resemblance is only slight. In Beethoven's work the chorus only- comes in to- wards the close, and has, compared with the orchestra, little to do. Mendelssohn has given •,a much more important part to the chorus, and besides this there are several solos for soprano and tenor voices. The symphony commences with a very striking phrase which forms, as it were, a text to the whole work. This is first iven out by three trombones in unison, and is afterwards repeatedly heard in various forms throughout the entire cantata. Perhaps the finest aml most telling chorus in the work is Whenlo;l t this i:ohrek: the Night is departing," which concludes with he e chorale "Let all men praise the Lord." was first produced in England tat Birmingham, under the composer's direc- flulteirainumber. - The as so impressed with this ceiotrale that they simultaneously rose to their ahieneud.asstsainding until the conclu- sufio'elisi Powers ao truly be regarded as " Hymn of Praise" written during the zenith of Mendelssohn's years of age and must indeed, it is one of the sagnificent cibeeateiavile wrote, not even excepting the "Elijah," which is only more important on account of its greater length.

div.head: CHRISTIAN SOCIALISM.
div.p: CHRISTIAN SOCIALISM.
Necessaries of Life Before Preparation for Beulah Land.
STRIKING ADULT SCHOOL PAPER.

Christian Socialism " was the subject at the. Academy-street Men's on Sunday. Mr. Price said Christian Socialism is none other than the application of the golden rule—the capacity of placing ourselves in the position of the wrong- doer and considering his difficulties and tempta- tions before we condemn—and this is Christian- ity; and such a Socialist was Jesus Himself. We are forced to admit that sometimes people who make no pretence to Christianty and who never enter a place of worship, put us to shame. The poor get nearer to the heart of things than those who are wealthier, and their actions are of a very Christlike order, when trouble and necessity occur amongst them. Churches are now awakening to the import- ance of providing the necessaries of life before Preparing souls for Beulah Land. Ignorance, dirt, squalor, starvation and hunger are not essential to civilisation as we have been wont to believe, and if the Church or Adult School • can restore a sense of their value and possibili- ties to those who have, trod slippery, miry paths, giving them a new determination and a new hope, a great thing will have been achieved. There will come a time, not Very distant either, when our successors will marvel at the apathy of this age towards social questions, and this time can be .hastened by united efforts of Churches, Brotherhoods and Adult Schools, who would send to Parliament men of high resolve, who would strive not for personal honour nor power, but to bring into being such laws as • will exalt a nation and make her free indeed. STOCKTON HEATH WOMEN'S. The last two Thursday evening meetings have been of a musical character, the first being of second uo f a social kind, 'when an excellent musical and dramatic programme was provided by the Hill Cliffe Concert Party. It was highly appreciated y lecturette on all e educational of b Theeing a music by Mr. Levi Richardson. After a short history of the rise" of hymn sing- ing and singers, the lecturer gave many hints as to voice training, breathing and phrasing, l • ustrating his points by examples and by many fi felicitous asides, which humorously enforced his teaching. A number of illustrative pieces were sung by members of the Men's Choir, which wa recently formed. A most delightful and Profitable time tinues to me was spent. The School con- Progress, and is now the centre of much interest and activity.

STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S. On Sunday morning Mr. W. J. Rowland gave a lecturette on "John Woolman, Quaker, of New Jersey.? Woolman was born in 1720, and died in 1772. Early in life he devised a more humane way of slaughtering animals. His love for the dumb creation was thus expressed. Much of his leisure time was devoted to writing many valuable essays, and.lie undertook many jour- neys through the States in the service of the slaves. It is Possible his work was an import- ant factor in the ultiinate abolition of slavery. The whole life of Woolinan was a protest against superfluities. He saw with singular clearness that every degree of luxury had some connec- tion with evil. Ile carried his principles into even the smallest etails of life. SANKEY BRIDGES MEN'S. Following on the two lectures given by Mr. William Landon on "Shakespeare, the 'play- wright and the man," during the last fortnight, a lecturetje was given on Sunday by a member of the School on one of the tragedies, " Macbeth," The speaker pointed out that Shakespeare's plays were written primarily to be acted, not read, and in order to understand them fully the Movement of the characters must not be lost sight of.

LONGFORD. The members of this School moved into their new premises in West-street on Sunday. Every- body present was saying what a fine school it would make when the membership increases. It is to be hoped the residents in the neighbour- hood will take full advantage of the educational facilities and fellowship afforded them by join- ing the School. On Sunday the members dis- cussed the Bible lesson on " Training in spiritual insight." Next Sunday a commence- ment will be made of i series of lecturettes of an edtmational character.
