THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1914. " TERRIERS " 100 YEARS AGO, WORKERS AND T)iE INFIRMARY.
Quaint and Curious Orders of the Old Volunteers.
CENTURY-OLD DOCUMENTS.
I EXAMINER" SPECIAL.

In the days of Napoleon Volunteer Corps were raised all over the country in view of possible hostilities with France and Spain, and Warrington's sons responded to the appeal in a ready manner. The following article deals with the formation of the corps and other interesting items in its history. " In many towns, less opulent than this, they are raising Volunteer Corps, the rich contri- buting their purses, the lower orders their Per- sonal services.

"The inhabitants of Warrington are full of loyalty and spirit, and wait only to be called into action by some principal townsman. "Are you determined to confine your exer- tions to the cold and compulsory measures of the Act of Parliament, or will you come forward to awake the energies of your country, and by a combination of powers erect a tower of strength impregnable by any enemy?" This appeal, signed by "An Inhabitant," in 1797, was part of the endeavours at that time to raise a Volunteer Corps in the town.

BOOMING THE VOLUNTEERS. On the sth June, 1797, Mr. Pickmere made " a celebrated" speech on the motion for raising a Volunteer Corps in Warrington, and in Gore's Liverpool paper of, the Bth June, 1797, he is re- ported as saying, amongst ether things, " Sen- sible I am, gentlemen, that if the measure Pro- posed shall go forward, it will be a puff in the scale that will make the balance of Europe pre- ponderate in our favour.

"We must be as hot fts mustard, fierce as Pepper, pungent as snuff, and stiff as starch, in our opposition to these torrent-like over-run- ners of the earth. Gentlemen, the •crisis has arrived and the corps must be made." The worthy gentleman then made the appeal that if they had no property to defend they could make their fortunes, ostensibly, for it is obviously suggested, from France and Spain.

"BLUE BACKS" FORMED. Now in face of such allurements, couched in such powerful oratory, what could the people of "The good old town" do? "The Loyal War- rington Volunteers," alias "Blue Backs," were', formed, and the history of the movement Up to 1898 is excellently set out in the book by Walter Crompton and George Venn, in the pages of which we find that in 1803 there were "the War- rington Volunteers alias Robin Redbreasts." It might also be interesting to know that in 1806 a court-martial was held at the Old Assembly Room, Warrington. In 1808, from the recommendation of, his Majesty's ministers, the Volunteer Regiments were induced to transfer their services to the Militia, or to form themselves into Militia , Regiments, subject to certain conditions laid , down by Lord Derby. The Warrington Corps became amalgamated with the Wigan Rifle Corps, and became known as "The Warrington Regiment of the local Militia." In the book we also find that about a century ago "The late regiment of Warrington' Volun- teers were thanked for their services." •

div.head: Contributions Slightly Lower but Future Prospects are Brighter.
div.p: Contributions Slightly Lower but Future Prospects are Brighter.
RADIUM TREATMENT IF REQUIRED.

The Mayor presided at the annual meeting of of the Warrington Working Men's Infirmary Committee held in the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon. There was a large attendance of representatives from the various works, in addition to Alderman Burton (chairman of the committee), Mr. G. Walker (vice-chairman), Mr. J. H. J. Harapson (secretary), Honorary Sur- geons, and others. Apologies for non-attendance were read from Sir Gilbert Greenall, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Councillor Henry Roberts, Messrs. John Fair- dough (chairman of the House Committee), W. p. Rylands, Ziba Armitage, J. C. Parr, F. W. Monks, and J. A. Ransoms.
FOOTBALL NO RIVAL

-......-. The MAYOR said he was pleased to preside over that great gathering of working men, and their attendance in such large numbers, in spite of the football matches taking place in and around Warrington, reflected great credit on them, and showed their interest in the Infirmary, which was such a useful institution. They found from the balance sheet that there was a decrease in the income, but after all was said and done the amount collected from the various works, in view of the difficulties they had experienced, was very satisfactory. Alderman Burton and he (the Mayor) had accompanied Mr. Hampson to Messrs. Rich- mond's works, and he was struck by the enthu- siasm that prevailed. He was glad to be able to thank the men of those works for having col- lected the large sum of £76 16s. 7d. The Insurance Act had, in a degree, affected the working classes in regard to the Infirmary. A lot of the firms in the town had sick clubs in the works, and he was informed that through those sick clubs some of the contributions to the Infirmary had suffered to a slight extent. He was informed that everything was now in proper working order, and when the men got properly adapted to the Insurance Act the con- tributions to the Infirmary would be of the normal average. However, the men were to be congratulated on their success, in spite of those difficulties. The hearty co-operation of the men was necessary to the working of that committee. (Applause.)

interest in the Institution was increasing very rapidly. Personally, he was one of those who, believing in democracy, was not sorry they had no big endowments. They regretted it, to the extent that it deprived them of doing more work, but the inhabitants of the borough made every effort to provide the funds necessary. (Hear, hear.) He could assure them that the claim of the Infirmary was a just one—(hear, hear)—and he hoped for the time to come when it would not be necessary to go asking for money for that Institution. When they considered the work that was being done, and the provision 'made, it formed an argument that they coulii not deny. (Hear, hear.) He deplored the fact that the subscriptions from Messrs. Pearson and Knowles were only ..e7 17s. 2d., as against ..tlO5, and whether that was due to the Insurance Act or not it was regrettable. (Hear, hear.) They only hoped, whatever the reason was, that not only the works, but all the others in the town would fall into line. They were glad there had been no necessity for complaints; for the Board of Man- agement had done all they could to keep up the efficiency of the Institution. They had a splen- did staff and they all knew the value of the senior house surgeon. (Hear, hear.) They would always endeavour to maintain efficiency, and although he did not say they would get radium for Warrington, still they would do their best for the patients. (Applause.)

div.head: SUBSCRIPTIONS KEPT UP.
div.p: SUBSCRIPTIONS KEPT UP.

Mr. HAMPSON submitted the statement of On- tributions, and said the total contributions from the works was .21,093 lie. 2411., as against .21,157 10s. 3id. for the previous year, and he was glad to say that the majority of the firms had kept up their subscriptions very well. The outside contributions amounted to .2140 ss. 3id., as against .2108 Os. Old. the previous year. This time there had been a contribution from the butchers, who had come to 'their help with a football match and handed 0230 Bs. 3d. to the Institution. (Applause.) The total amount collected was £1,233 16s. 6d., as against £1,265 10s. 4d. After expenses had been paid, the amount handed to the treasurer of the Infir- mary was .21,215 17s. 5d., as against .21,248 18s. 10d.

The majority of the employes in the town, con- cluded Air. Hampson, paid one penny per week, but others who had difficulties to contend with did not pay that Amount. As far as the Insti- tution was concerned, he thought they compared favourably with those in other towns. (Ap- plause.)

11,531 PATIENTS TREATED. Alderman BURTON, making a statement in re- gard to the work of the Infirmary, said that the number of patients actually treated at the Infir- mary and their own homes was 11,531. Person- ally, he was rather disappointed with last year's work. The reduction in the contributions from the works—about £64—was a very serious item. The deficiency had, however, been made up to some extent by other people, and they were not alone in regard to the deficiency in contribu- tions, for the collections in neighbouring towns had come out worse than theirs. He submitted that the members of the com- mittee were not to blame for the decrease, for they had done their best during the year to keep up the subscriptions, and Mr. Hampson had also done all he could with a view to keeping up the subscriptions by visiting many of the works and addressing the men. This was invaluable help. (Hear, hear.) The committee had done their best and the year's work was deserving of better results than had been obtained. They set out at the beginning of the year with the determination to keep up the subscriptions, and no opportunity had been missed in that endea- vour. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Insurance Act Effect.
div.p: Insurance Act Effect.

After giving an extensive and interesting re- view of the year's work and having made sug- gestions to the committee, Alderman Burton dealt with the general work of the committee, and said when it was formed they set out with the purpose of getting all those employed in the town to contribute a small sum weekly. They .did fairly well until the Insurance Act made its appearance. He had nothing to say about the Insurance Act, either for or against it, but he thought it had been the cause of the diminution in subscriptions during the last two years. He hoped some system would be arranged now, whereby the workpeople could pay their subscriptions every week. Ten years prior to the formation of that committee the übscriptions to the Infirmary from the indus- trial classes of the town amounted to .2734 Is. Bid., or an average of £73 Bs. 2d. for each of the ten years. Since the formation of that commit- tee they had handed to the Infirmary ..t23,713 12s. sd. or an average over the 33 years of £7lB 12s. The amount contributed during the first year of the committee's existence was £165 19s. 4d. That was a small beginning, but every- thing had to have a beginning. During the lest five years a sum of over £1,200 had been contri- buted each year. (Applause.)

div.head: INFIRMARY'S NOBLE WORK.
div.p: INFIRMARY'S NOBLE WORK.

Mr. G. WALKER also paid a tribute to the excel- lent work done by the committee. He was of the opinion that they needed large endowments. Mr. SMETHURST spoke of the noble work the Infirmary was doing. The large attendance of working men that afternoon proved that their

div.head: SPLENDID EXAMPLE.
div.p: A SPLENDID EXAMPLE.

Mr. BERRY, a member of the committee, men- tioned that the contributions at Mr. Harry Fairclough's were twopence each from all re- ceiving 30s. and over per week. That was a splendid contribution from the workpeople. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURTON said the committee appre- ciated that contribution from Mr. Fairclough's men. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. T. T. JAMES said the Working Men's Committee was doing excellently in regard to the Hospital in the town. He trusted they would be still more successful in their efforts. (Ap- plause.) The Secretary's statement of accounts and Alderman Burton's report were adopted unani- mously.

div.head: OFFICIALS ELECTED.
div.p: OFFICIALS ELECTED.

. ._...__ Alderman Burton was re-elected chairman of the committee, Mr. Walker vice-chairman, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes honorary auditor, and Mr. Hampson honorary secretary. Suitable replies having been made, Mr. GREAVES proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, Vice-chairman, Honorary Auditor, and Honorary Secretary, which was carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. T. WESTON a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the Honorary Sur- geons.

div.head: RADIUM COULD BE SECURED.
div.p: RADIUM COULD BE SECURED.

In reply Dr. JOSEPH said he had been con- nected with the Institution for 40 years and it had always been conducted in a proper manner. National provision had been made for the cure and prevention of certain ailments, but still there were cases which had to be treated at such institutions as the Infirmary, and he was glad to find they were helping that Institution, which received nothing through legislature. He be- lieved that if radium should be considered of paramount importance at that Institution that Warrington would provide it under those cir- cumstances. (Applause.) Dr. SUTHERLAND also replied. A vote of thanks was also unanimously accorded the Corporation, Chief Constable, Press, Mr. Down's Band, Crosfield's Band, Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd.; Mixed Voice Choirs, Mr. Edward Wallington, Staff and Pupils of People's College, and the Warrington Butchers.

div.head: EDUCATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE EDUCATION QUESTION.

Mr. G. WALKER then gave his report as a mem- ber of the Education Committee. He said that education had been one of the prevalent subjects discussed in the Town Council since Councillor Peacock had been appointed Mayor, and with as much of the vehement spirit the Council could put into such things. After referring to • the increased cost of education he said he was on the School Attendance and Sites and Build- ings Sub-committees, which seemed to get their fair share of criticism, not always honest, but certainly very vigorous. At one meeting the extravagant expenditure was attributed to co- opted members, but if the business of the Edu- cation Committee was to be done, it was to be done by the co-opted members. (Laughter.) The islAyou : I suppose you except the Deputy. Mayor and myself? (Laughter.) Mr. WALKER said present company was always excepted. Mr. Richard andFairclougho okl. werehimself a twon- and were the co-opted members. They innocent men. They were innocently he was sure they would not credit themng'with being the desperadoes they wereeTow written clown to be. (Laughter.) They et . b morepepowerfulm l than they thought they were have their own way was mysterious they could to him.

New Schools Required. In regard to the new schools he could not understand where they were going to add three- halfpence to the rates, because money borrowed for the schools was repayable over 30 or 40 years. If they were going to look for expenditure they would have to look in a different way altogether. New schools were not the cause, and if they were Warrington was suffering from its indo- lence of past years. During the past week the Corporation had been fined £5O for overcrowding in schools. After other details of the Committee's work had been given, Mr. Walker concluded by remarking that so far they were not thoroughly convinced they were getting value for money in regard to education generally. (Applause.) The MAYOR said he had had more pleasure in presiding over that meeting than over a gather- ing of his fellow-councillors, who all seemed to be pulling in different ways. Members of that committee were pulling in one way, cordially supporting one cause. (Applause)

Outburst by Councillor Pemberton Abruptly Ends
Committee Meeting.

div.head: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS VACATES THE CHAIR.
div.p: COUNCILLOR ROBERTS VACATES THE CHAIR.
There was an exciting scene at the meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday, which brought the business to an abrupt end.
A deputation was proposed to go and interview the Board of Education about the stopped grants, and it was over this that the friction arose.
After a few passages-at-arms had taken place, the meeting came to the climax point in the comedy-drama, and then the curtain fell.
Mr. Plipston had referred to something Coun- cillor Pemberton had said at the Council meeting about education as " tommy rot." This raised the Councillor's ire.
Councillor Pemberton characterised some con- 'duct of the Education Committee as a type which would not be tolerated " in a third- class gambling hell."
ThA Chairman (Councillor Roberts) asked him to apologise for such "an abominable expres- sion.': This Councillor Pemberton refused to do.
Then the Chairman told him to sit down, but the Councillor declined, and finally, amidst intense excitement, the Chairman adjourned the meeting and vacated the chair.
The business of the Education Committee was not completed, although it had then sat for thirty-five minutes, but the matters held over will be taken prior to the next monthly meeting.
• The trouble arose over the minutes of the Sites and Buildings Sub-committee, which stated :

"A letter was read from the Board of Educa- tion with reference to their continued recogni- tion of the Wycliffe, Temporary Council School premises, and asking for the date by which the committee expect that the new school in Lovely- lane will be completed, and to be informed what is the earliest date by which the committee can undertake that it will be ready for occupation; and with regard thereto it was resolved that the Chairman of the Committee (Mr. Richard T. Fairclough), his Worship the Mayot (Mr. Coun- cillor Peter Peacock), Mr. Councillor John Pemberton and the Director of Education be appointed a deputation to interview the Board of Education in connection with ihis matter, and also with reference to the supply of school accommodation in the borough generally." Mr. FAIRCLOUGH (the chairman of the sub- committee) moved the adoption of the minutes, and hoped the proposed deputation would get something satisfactory out of the Board of Education.

I IS THE DEPUTATION ILLEGAL? Councillor Witxissox : I rise for an explana- tion in reference to the deputation. I notice the Mayor, ,Mr. Fairclough, Councillor Pember- ton and the Director of Education are appointed to go on this deputation. In our Council we have a Standing Order which says deputations ' shall not Consist of more than two members and an official, and, as chairman of the Finance Com- mittee of the Council, I say to allow a deputa- tion of three members and an official is quite contrary to our Standing Orders. How will 'thel public auditor take it?

The committees of the Corporation pass ac- counts at various times, but they finally come to the Finance Committee, and if we pass an account for these three members having gone on a deputation we on the Finance Committee will be surcharged. We have an instance where an important committee was surcharged, three years ago, for sending an Art Master to some conference, and it took a lot of correspondence on the part of the Town Clerk to get the auditor to say he forgave us, but we must never do it again.

could go on a deputation without the Mayor's sanction. He thought it was essential to have a. strong deputation. The same thing had been done by the Warrington Council without any objection being raised. Councillor WILKINSON: We had no time. Councillor ARCHER: I say '6 Yes !"
Councillor Wzmussos: Wre had no time to take it before the Council.— Councillor ARCEIER : I distinctly say "Yes, Yes!" (Laughter.)

div.head: Must_ Have a Safeguard.
div.p: Must_ Have a Safeguard.

I have always had a feeling -that I must safe- guard the members of the Finance Committee, who are the parties to be surcharged. I move the minute be referred back for the considera- tion and the'opinion of the Town Clerk upon it. Mr. H. KmosoN : Unless the members pay their own expenses. Councillor WILKINSON : I have nothing to do with that. It appears to we an irregularity, and I would like it referred back to get the opinion of the Town Clerk. Mr. J. JARMAN : I move that the name of Coun- cillor Pemberton be omitted frOm the deputa-

tion. The CHORMAN (Councillor 11. Roberts) : I can- not accept a second amendment unless the pre- vious one has been first disposed of by the meeting. Councillor JessiNs : I second Councillor Wil- kinson's amendment.

div.p: START OF THE BREEZE.

Councillor ARCHER,: I ami surprised at the poirits raised by the Chairman of the Finance Committee, lie must know, when weighty pro- blems are before a committee, it is within the jurisdiction of the committee to appeal to the Mayor, or the Deputy-Mayor, for acquiescence that any deputation may reach any number.

The CHAIRMAN: That is in case there is no time to get special sanction by special resolution of the Council. There is plenty of time for this before the deputation goes. Councillor ARCHER: Perhaps Councillor Wil- kinson has been on as many deputations as any member of the Corporation._

Councillor WILKINSON : No. I have never been on a deputation of over two and an official. Councillor ARCHER: No! I say Yes, Yes! I do not think it is right to raise this question when such a difficult problem is before the Warrington ratepayers as at the present time. "Nonsense.") I know for a fact there are, questions at issue of the most vital importance to the borough. Warrington is placed in a diffi- cult position in regard to its education, and surely' Councillor Wilkinson is not going to be a stumbling block. _ _
Councillor WILKINSON t I'm fiothing of the kind.
THE BREEZE GAINS FORCE.

The CHAIRMAN: Councillor Wilkinson's amend, ment only goes to the extent of asking the opinion of the Town Clerk on the legality of ap- pointing more ,members than the Standing Orders permit. Councillor ARCHER : I agree, but the more we have on the deputation the more chance we have of getting redress. Councillor WILKINSON.: I am merely making myself right with my committee. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JENKINS : It is as a member of the Finance Committee that I am seconding; I have no animosity against any gentleman proposed on the deputation. Mr. G. WALKER: I think Councillor Wilkinson is quite justified in raising the point. Councillor OSBORNE read the Standing Order, which showed that not more than two members

div.head: LULL BEFORE THE STORM.
div.p: LULL BEFORE THE STORM.
Councillor OSBORNE : I cannot contend with these interruptions. If we feel as a committee it will add to the weight of the deputation to send an extra representative we ought to agree to it.
Councillor WILKINSON: In answer to Council- lor Archer, when Warrington sent deputations of three, four, five or six members we had no public auditor as we have now.

The CHAIRMAN: There is a provision to get the permission of the Mayor if there is no time to obtain the sanction of the Council. The MAYOR: There is no special sanction needed. The deputation does not intend to go until the minutes are confirmed by the Council. So far as I am concernecl, I do not want to go on this deputation. I am against deputations, and have been so sitice I have been on the Coun- cil. To refer this back for the authority of the Town Clerk is all piffle and nonsense. We do not want the Town Clerk's ruling at all, as the Standing Order is quite clear. Alderman Brz.narr thought the Standing Order conflicted with the special Act of Parliament.

div.head: STORM BREAKS. Deputation Thought a Joke.
div.p: THE STORM BREAKS. Deputation Thought a Joke.

Mr. an.arrox : I thought the whole recommon-1 dation: was a joke. We have been neglecting thei gchool accommodation to such a degree that we have been penalised, and, the sub-committee, some members of which are 'responsible for the lack of procedure, are put upon a deputation to do what? We have the Chairman of the Sub- committee, " a fanatic and spendthrift" (Mr. Plinston here was quoting from a previous speech made by Councillor Pemberton). Mr. FAIRCLOUGII Are you referring to me? (Laughter.) Mr. PLINSTON't Yes. We have the Mayor and we have Mr. Pemberton, who absolutely opposes the procedure in any way, shape or form, and who condemns wholesale the work of the Board of Education, and unless he is going to London with proper arguments, instead of the "tommy rot" we hear in this room, we are going to make a laughing-stock of the Warrington, Education Committee before the Board of Education and its officials. (One laugh .\

div.head: Whining Over Punishment.
div.p: Whining Over Punishment.

Oh, Councillor Archer laughs. He may well laugh at the position we ought to have seriously considered some time ago. I do not believe in a committee getting punishment and then whining. It is a pitiable position for the tducation Committee to be in. I hope we shall look this matter plainly in the face, come to the conclusion that we deserve the punishment, and proceed properly with the accommodation which we admit seriously we ought to provide. (Hear, hear.)

THE HURRICANE OF WORDS. , Councillor PEMBERTON (angrily) : It was not my intention to speak at all, but a personal attack has been made on me. I leave it with the people of Warrington generally to say whether I talked " tominy rot" or not. I did not ask to go on this deputation. NO one was more surprised than myself when the committee put me on. I have been told many times I am the odd man out on a committee. The charge by Mr. Plinston is untruthful. I have not delib- erately stopped schools from being built. Councillor WILKINSON: You have stopped the plans.
Councillor PEMBERTON : I have stopped what I considered unfair and improper treatment of people outside.
C-ouncillor—* n.Kissow : That is what you al- ways do.
"THIRD-CLASS GAMBLING HELL."

- --------••-- ••---- Councillor PEMBERTON : That is my opinion. I back my opinion against that of anybody else. (Hear, hear.) Ido what I consider right. I answer for my own conscience. There are some things done in this committee that would not be tolerated in a third-class gambling hell. The CHAIRMAN : Are you referring to the con- duct of this committee?

Councillor PEMBER-T-O-N. : I am referring to the matter Mr. Plinston referred to. The CHAIRMAN : If it is anything to do with the work of this committee I will not allow it to pass. I will not allow you to be heard. Councillor PEMBERTON : I don't care. You allowed him to attack me. The CaAnimAN: I will not submit to it. Councillor PEMBERTON : I am only— The CHAIRMAN : It is a charge against the con- duct of this committee, and, as chairman, I am not going to submit to it.

div.head: "I DON'T CARE."
div.p: "I DON'T CARE."

Councillor PEDIBERTON : I don't care. The CHAIRMAN: Then I shall not allow you to be heard. Councillor PEMBERTON : You've allowed others to say things. I say this committee has passed unfair conditions and—

The CHAIRMAN: You have said the action of the committee in regard to some of its affairs is characteristic of a third-class gambling hell. Councillor PEMBERTON : And worse. The CHAIRMAN: I will not allow you to make such a, statement.
Councillor PEMBERTON : I made it and I shall stick to it.
"I WILL NOT SIT DOWN."
The CHAIRktAN : You will not make any such statements here. I will not allow you to speak. You must sit down.
Councillor PEMBERTON : I will not Bit down. The CHAIRMAN: Then I will vacate the chair. Councillor PFXBEHTON : You can do it if you like, but you can't stop me.
The CHAIRMAN : Members of the committee, do you wish to hear Mr. Pemberton any further?
' This query was greeted with loud cries of "No." s

The CHAIRMAN: Then I declare this meeting adjourned until he sits down and apologises for that abominable expression. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON (angrily) : I shall do nothing of the kind.' You allowed Plinston to make a personal attack upon me. The CHAIRMAN: Then so far as I am concerned this meeting is adjourned. Councillor PEMBERTON remained standing until nearly all the members had left the room, and then, gathering his papers, followed them out. The extraordinary incident was discussed amongst the members in the lobby, and later "The Examiner" representative was informed that it had been arranged to finish this month's business a the commencement of ,the next monthly meeting.

Pity Instead of Blame.—Gertrude Fleetwood (16), 36, Old-road, was charged on remand with stealing a pair of boots, value 6s. 11d., the pro- perty of Benedict Tyrer, 100, Buttermarket- street.—The Chief Constable said the girl stole the boots from the -shop doorway and the theft was discovered when she tried to pawn the boots for is. to another pawnbroker, who recog- nised Mr. Tyrer's private mark. She then said she was pawning them for a lady in Wellington - street. Further taxed she went away. The girl alleged that she was badly treated at home, and he thought there was truth in that allegation. The father had promised to leave the woman he was living with, and to make a home for the girl and her sister. That he thought was a happy solution. lie thought the girl should be pitied rather than blamed.—The girl was bound over for 12 months.

Four Policemen Necessary.—James White, a fo„rm labourer, of Stockley Farm, Arley, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, arid with assaulting P.C. John Reyes and P.C. John Gibbs.—On Sunday night P.C. Heyes was on point duty in Arpley-road, when he saw the prisoner in Bridge-street in a very drunken con- dition. He went to two gentlemen, who were standing opposite the Old Academy, and after using filthy language he struck at them, but missed. He was taken into custody by P.C. Heyes and when in Arpley-road the prisoner became very violent. The officer closed with him, and both fell to the ground. P.C. Gibbs was summoned and prisoner also assaulted him by kicking his legs. Two other police officers had to be called before the prisoner could be carried ta the Police Station.—White said he did not know what he was doing. He was fined 20s. and costs, or one month's imprisonment.

Theft of Bricks.—James Henry Clarke, 59, flume-street; William Bolton, 68, Dallam-lane, and John Lomax, 29, Crossley-street, were charged with stealing 6,000 old bricks, value the property of Messrs. John Lunt and Sons, Knutsford-road, on the 11th or 12th March.— Supt. Williamson said the men were employed as carters, and they were carting bricks from the old Bedstead Works, which were being pulled down. The bricks should have been taken to Grappenhall-road. Inquiries were made on the previous Wednesday, and it was found that a Mr. Owen had purchased the bricks. They received 245. between them.—The prisoners were sent to prison for one month.— Mr. Owen was ordered to return the bricks to Mr. Lunt.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

Before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), A. J. Jolley, W. Roberts and Dr. Naden. Slot Meter Thief.—Edward Mullen, of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing 10s. 3d. Pram two slot gas meters at 12 and 14, Stanley-street on the 9th and 11th March.—Supt. Williamson said prisoner had slept at 12, Stanley-street, and left early in the morning without having paid. He was seen the worse for drink on the second occasion, and muttered "I must have another slot to-night." He was seen to go in the cup- board where the meter was, and it was after- wards found that the meter money had been taken. Prisoner had admitted the offences, and said he had been drinking.—Prisoner submitted a long statement to the Bench in which he said he did not know what he did when he was drunk. He was sent to prison for one month with hard labour. Mat Mender in Trouble.--Joseph Lowe, mat mender, of no fixed address, was charged with withme stealing unaknown.—Supt. piece of beef, stealing 7s. 6d. from a drawer in the provision shop, 55, Sharp-street, the moneys of Mary Ann Williamson said that whilst there was no one I in the shop prisoner was seen to go to the drawer and take , the money. A Quiet and Orderly Dispute.

div.head: By "A Worker."
div.p: By "A Worker."

Councillor H. Roberts, the chairman of the Bench, who heard the case against Mr. Adam Bennett, the leader of the strikers at Messrs. Fletcher, Russell's works, on a charge of alleged intimidation, took a very sensible view of the whole matter, and the Bench rightly dismissed the case, which was of a most trifling character. Rad there been a conviction it would have been stretching the terms of the Trades Dispute Act to breaking point. There was no conviction, and in coming to the decision they arrived at the magistrates have earned the gratitude of all trade unionists in Warrington, who feel that they can expect justice from our local Bench. As the Chairman said, the strike is being most peacefully conducted. In all my experience of strikes I cannot recall one which was so quiet and orderly.

div.head: I.L.P. Coming-of-age.
div.p: I.L.P. Coming-of-age.

The Independent Labour party comes of age at the Easter Conference, to be held in Brad- ford, where the first conference was held 21 years ago, although the party saw its birth in Manchester when Blatchford was rather a powerful factor in its foundation. He is now ploughing his lonely furrow with sympathies leaning towards the B.S.P. The first chairman u-as Keir Hardie, who will preside at • the coming-of-age meeting. He had been asked to stand for another term, but refused, owing to pressure of Parliamentary work. Councillor Tom Fox, the chairman of the Labour party and leader of the Labour Group in the Maliches- ter City Council, was then invited, but he declined. The candidates in the running are Messrs. Philip Snowden, F. W. Jowett, J. Bruce Glasier, Joseph Burgess, Harry Dubery, and Dick Wallhead. The first three have occupied the chair before, and there is a strong opinion in favour of Snowden.

div.head: CLERKS MAKE MERRY.
div.p: CLERKS MAKE MERRY.
Railway Employes Hold a Smoking
Concert.

There is no disputing the fact that the rail- way clerks of Warrington are enthusiastic in their cause, for they realise that the principles for which their association stands are well worth supporting. That whole-heartedness which characterises their work is also perceiv- able in the social side of the association's pro- gramme. ,

A peep into one of the upstair rooms at the Royal Oak Hotel on Saturday evening would have revealed this fact at once, for there, under the presidkmcy of Mr. Holloway, a large num- ber of members of the Warrington Branch of the association were thoroughly enjoying a smoking concert.

The entertainment was excellent in every respect. Songs, humorous and sentimental, as well as the duets, were all rendered in pleasing style by the following artistes: Mr. J. 11. Mark- ham (tenor), Mr. J. W. Hughes (baritone), Mr. R. A. Lee (bass), Mr. Torn Smith and Mr. J. B. Richardson (humorists). Mr. A. E. Trow was an efficient accompanist. The diversion pro- vided by Mr. Baxteau in the way of illusions proved very popular, for most of his tricks were exceptionally smart and executed with a neat- ness and rapidity that defied even the most alert. - -

At an interval, Mr. Blanchard, of Liverpool, addressed the gathering, and in the course .of his appeal on behalf of the association he said there was no reason why anyone employed by the railways should not join the association. Men were joining at such a rate that they had now fully 27,000 members, and that was no mean achievement, and they had .a,OOO carried forward in the balance sheet. After enumer- ating the various benefits of the association he appealed to them all to go forward conquering and to conquer. (Applause.) The Chairman said there, was no member who could say he had not benefited by the associa- tion. He proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Blanchard. Mr. Blanchard said the best thanks they could give him was to join the union and see that someone else came in by their solicitations. Hearty votes of thanks to the Chairman and artistes concluded the programme.

div.head: TAILORING TRADE BOARDS.
div.p: TAILORING TRADE BOARDS.
Several New Appointments Made.

The term of office of the Tailoring Trade Board (Great Britain), established on 23rd November, 1910, having expired, we are officially informed that the Board of Trade have made regulations, dated January 10, 1914, with re- spect to the constitution and proceedings of a Trade Board for those branches of the ready- made and. wholesale bespoke tailoring trade in Great Britain which are engaged in making garments to be worn by male persons, and for those branches of the bespoke tailoring trade in Great Britain which are engaged in making garments to be worn by male persons and in which at least three persons or two female per- sons (in both exclusive of cutters and trimmers) are engaged in making one garment. In accordance with these regulations a Trade Board has been established for the period of three years, commencing March 23, 1914, and thereafter until dissolved by order of the Board of Trade. The Trade Board consists or five ap- pointed members (who are persons unconnected with the trade and appointed by the Board of Trade)—namely, Mr. Ernest Ayes (chairman), ' Sir Shirley F. Murphy, F.R.C.S. (deputY-chair-' man), Mr. G. M. Booth, Mr. F. Tillyard, and Miss Constance P. Lewis, together with 22 repre- sentatives of employers and 22 representatives of workers. The representative members have been selected by the Board of Trade after con- sidering names supplied by employers and workers respectively. The secretary of the Trade Board is Mr. G. T. Reid, Old Serjeants' Inn Chambers, 5, Chan- cery-lane, London, W.C.

div.head: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.

Before Mr. IL C. Parr (in the chair), Council- lor If. Roberts, Mr. J. Rymer Young and Mr. W. Fairclough. Dogs Exempted.—The police objected to several claims for exemption from dog licences made by several farmers from Burtonwood and Sankey.—lt was stated in three cases where there were two dogs, that one was used as a yard dog and not for tending cattle.. In one case a man had only two head of cattle, and the dog was chained in the yard all the year round. Two Sankey farmers had neither cattle nor sheep.—The objections were allowed.
Mr. Charles Dukes' Attack on Liberalism.
PARR HALL MASS MEETING.
--3 ks

A largely attended meeting was held in the Parr Hall on Wednesday night to hear the case of the deportation of the South African Labour leaders first hand, from the mouth of one of the leaders, Mr. IL B. Waterson, general secre- tary of the South African Labour party.

Mr. 11. Wardman presided, and both he and Mr., Charles Dukes attacked the Liberal party., The seats at the back of the platform were occupied by the strikers from Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., and they arrived at the hall in processien, headed by a picked band. The Chairman was sure that every Labour movement, by whatever name they were called or whatever phrase they took up, were united on that occasion to protest, loud and strong, against the deportation of their South African comrades, and to demand their return to their homes. (Loud applause.) They were there not only to protest against the action, of the South lAfrican Government for the unconstitutional act they had committed, but to protest as Eng- lish trade unionists, and English men and women connected with the Labour movement,l because they knew if that kind of thing was allowed to proceed without protest, and allowed to be carried out in its entirety, their own trade unions would probably be attacked.
Right to Trial.

They maintained that those men had a right to a trial, a right that was allowed a criminal. The men had tried to raise the conditions of men and women of South Africa, and had been deported by order of an autocracy scarcely Over known in the history of the world. He moved a resolution, which welcomed Mr. Waterman and protested against the action of the South African Government in attempting to suppress trade unionism and demanding the return of the men.

Home Government Blamed. lie thought the British Government was not free from blame in the matter—(hear, hear)— for the action of Lord Gladstone had been con- doned by the British House of Commons, and he hoped the working men of Warrington would remember that at election times. If that thing had happened under a Tory Government the Liberal I'ress and platforms of the country would have rung about the wickedness of the Tories, but because it had happened under those who called themselves Progressives, the people on the platforms and in the Press were as silent and dumb as dogs. (Cheers.) In the course of a long effusion from the pen of Mi. Crosfield in the local Liberal weekly, the writer went out of his way to say some very strong things regarding Sir Edward Carson, for what- ever Sir Edward Carson had done was no more unconstitutional than the deportment of the men from South Africa. (Applause.)

div.head: OLD SOLDIER'S FATE.
div.p: OLD SOLDIER'S FATE.

Mr. Charles Dukes said those nine men had been deported for doing specifically what a few of them in England gloried in doing. He did not believe for a moment that they had been deported without an understanding between Smutts and Botha. lie could not dissociate the recent happenings from certain incidents that occurred here some fourteen years ago. They would remember then how the patriotism of the country was aroused, and they were told it was their duty to send soldiers to South Africa, ' and the duty of those at home to pay. Both phases of their capitalist political Parliamen- tary machine then stood upon the platform and confirmed the conventionalities, justifying the sending of troops by stating there would be Eternal Freedom. They spent £250,000,000 and left 30,009 men on the veldt. They fought that war for the " gold bugs." 1

After stating that labour should show its force, Mr. Dukes said it was not a matter of what their M.P. said, or what .the Government were likely to promise; they were not concerned with splitting the Progressive vote, and all that humbug, but the ways and means of obtaining a fuller and freer share of the interests of life. (Cheers.)

div.head: Fight in the Workshop.
div.p: Fight in the Workshop.

Their fight was primarily in the workshop. What was the history of the so-called Progres- sives? The Liberals were the early manufac- turers and they were the manufacturers to-day. After mentioning prominent Liberals connected with several firms, and of their exploitation of the workmen, he stated they had never known land to pay 331 per cent. They heard the call "back to the land" to people who would not know the right end of a shovel if they were sent back to-morrow. (Laughter and applause.)

The real trouble in South Africa was the ob- taining of cheap labour to extract the gold, and those men who worked for little money had to live under conditions which would not be toler- ated by white men. (Applause.) "We in Warrington have hundreds of workers to-day earning nineteen 'bob' a week," ex- claimed Mr. Dukes, and, he continued, "I do not blame the employers. They are not there, for fun; they are there for 'pelf.'" (Applause.). DEPORTE'S STORY. ••

Mr. Waterson, who had a great reception, apologised for the absence of his friend, Mr. McKerrell, who, he stated, was in a sanatorium, suffering from miner's phthisis. That would show them the brutality of the South African Government, for they had deported him— separated him from his wife and children— whilst knowing that it would mean shortening his life by a number of years. ("Shame.") This was one of the things for which he could never forgive them. Mclierrell was not a mil- lionaire, and if he died in England, as probably he would, he would leave a widow and three or four children dependent upon charity. That fact alone was enough to condemn the South African Government, for Mclierrell was one of the most moderate men in South Africa.
„..__ The speaker then detailed the events result- ing in the strike, the attacks by the police and troops, and the manner in which they were disbanded.

Referring to the attacks that were being made ,Inon the character of the deportes, be told the audience that three of them were total ab- stainers and two were non-smokers. The speaker was a town councillor in Boxborough, and was a nominee for the mayoralty for this year. He stated that to show they were just as good as the best men in the Botha Cabinet. The resolution was carried unanimously.
-- WOMAN SUFFRAGE—continued.

active movement. The women who responded to the call of the Republican leaders, and took an active part with the men in bringing about the overthrow of the monarchy, were naturally disappointed when the Franchise Bill of the new Government excluded them, in company with non-commissioned officers and privates, idiots and undischarged bankrupts. In response to agitation, the officers and privates are now en- franchised, but the Government has paid no heed to the plea of the women. Still many lead- ing men are taking up the women's cause and perhaps in Portugal the enfranchisement of women is not so very far off. ' E. W.

div.head: WOMAN SUFFRAGE.
div.p: WOMAN SUFFRAGE.
How the Cause Is Faring In European Countries. -

Di some of the Germanic countries of Europe the status of women is not so high as in those of the North. The Netherlands and Switzer- land have as yet no form of franchise for women, though the Queen of Holland has an- nounced in her speech from the throne a revi- sion of the Constitution. In the Dutch Parlia- ment universal suffrage for both sexes is cham- pioned by the Left, i.e., Socialists, Radicals, Liberals and Unionists, so the hope of the woman suffragists lies in supporting the Left in the next election campaign. GERMANY.

German women have the -local government franchise under very restricted conditions, and in most States can only vote by proxy. It is hardly surprising that they evince little inter- est in the elections, since they can exercise no kind of control as to whether the vote has been recorded as they intended. The situation is summed up in the classic phrase of the rural voter, "The woman's vote is extremely con- venient; you can use it, or leave it alone, just as it suits best." Even this miserable indirect vote is lost in most States by marriage. The Social Democrats, the largest single party in the Reichstag (Parliament) have already adopted woman suffrage as part of their political programme, but it is not so very long since the mere mention of the question was the signal for an outburst of merriment in the Reichstag.

AUSTRIA-HUNGARY. In the provinces which go to compose the Empire of Austria-Hungary, women are on a better footing. In Bohemia, indeed, they are allowed to vote, and are eligible to stand for election to the Provincial Diet. The Czech women are properly organised, and work ener- getically along with the men; it is said that they refuse to be misled by party tricks, and vote in accordance with their convictions. In other provinces women tax-payers have the franchise, though in some cases this ,vote for the Diet must be exercised by proxy. For the Imperial Parliament women are not enfran- chised, and there is one great difficulty in work- ing for their enfranchisement, in that in Austria the law forbidding women, minors and foreigners to form to be members of political associations still holds good, though Germany abolished it in 1908. In the meantime big street demonstrations must advertise the cause.

• THE LATIN COUNTRIES. These still exclude women from the franchise, though French women have some voting rights and eligibility for employment and educational councils. It is a sign of advance that feminism is no longer a subject for ridicule in French literature, but is seriously discussed by the most distinguished writers. In the case of Belgium, it seems probable that women will be enfranchised when the electoral law is next amended. The Catholic party are definitely in favour of the reform, so are the Socialists, but they wish to abolish plural vot-' ing first. Italy has no woman suffrage as yet, but in the big cities distinguished women carry on the campaign by means of congresses, meetings, lec- tures, literature and petitions. So far only Socialists and Republicans have made it a part of their party programme. In Spain the majority of women who do take an interest in polities are free thinkers, and they wish to oppose clericalism first of all, so there is really no suffrage movement as yet. div.head: CIVIL WARRIORS.
div.p: THE CIVIL WARRIORS.

The Government and the Opposition have come to closer grips this week than ever over the Home Rule question, and the firm stand taken by the PRIME MINISTER has exasperated the desperate party, whose only stock-in-trade has been finally reduced to threats of civil war, so that they have lost what little restraint remained to them. Mistaking the offer of con- cessions for signs of weakness, they went to work to extract from Mr. ASQUITH the full details of his proposals. Mr. Await, being too old a Parliamentary hand to give his oppon- ents details with whic., to play before they had agreed to accept his offer in principle, firmly declined. This and Mr. Ginincium.'s plain inti- mation that the limit of concession had been reached, brought about a climax and a vote 'of censure was tabled. It is difficult to under- stand the principles underlying the discussion upon that vote. Mr. BONAR Dow asked for a Plebiscite in Ulster at the end of the six years. and, as an alternative, for a referendum to the electors of the United Kingdom on the Home Rule Bill, as amended by Mr. AsotThi's con- cessions. The genuineness of these time- wasting requests will become apparent when it is borne in mind that Mr. ASQUITH has provided that Ulster will not be included if the Imperial Parliament interposes to the contrary. Before the exemption period comes to an end -two General Elections will give the people the opportunity of declaring which Government, a Liberal or a Tory, shall go to Westminster. If a Tory Government, there is a simple N'tly out, for Ulster—but the Tories, as we know, despair of getting back to power. If they fail, Ulster of course, goes to help to make a United Ireland. The game is to make progress diffi- cult in the meantime, and, if possible, to w- the whole Bill. By a majority of 93 the House decided that the Government method of pro- cedure was the right one, and their supporters in the country are heartily in accord with that majority.

Not His Fault.

Little Jack. attended Sunday school for the first time and was told that he would not be asked any questions, but that he must par close attention to all that happened. Later his father inquired who it was that killed Goliath. "I don't know, daddy," was the shame-faced answer. "I was sitting on the back seat, and I couldn't see."

An Impossibility. Little Willie was detected by his teacher in the act of stealing from one of his playmates. Instead of inflicting punishment she concluded to by a moral lecture. "Bear in mind, Willie, that these temptations, can be resisted if you turn a deaf ear to them. Willie's lip ti•embled as he replied: "But, teacher, I ain't got a deaf ear."

IMPRESSIONS OF MASCULINITY. Observations of a Woman Who Has Seen Her Thirty-f 11th Birthday. A married man either talks a great deal About his wife, or not at all. The man who talks to a woman about another woman never tells the truth. He is either try- ing to make the one of whom he is speaking better or worse than she really is. A man 'believes that it is unmanly to forgive a woman who has been untrue to him, but a Woman will forgive an unfaithful man 20 times over if he will only seem repentant. The temperature of a Man's affections can be accurately gauged by the amount of money he Spends on the object of his affections. Do not trust the man who begins his love letters " Carissima." He has written many before.

Lloyd George Made Them Talk. In a rural district, where Radicals are almost unknown, a correspondent says he discovered in a bar-parlour a portrait of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The landlord denied the insinu- ation that he was an admirer. of. Mr. Lloyd George, and protested that he had nearly ruined him. "Then why do you hang up his portrait?" he was asked. "Easily explained," said mine host. "Directly people come in here and see Mr. Lloyd George's Portrait, they begin saying things about him. And talking •about Mr. Lloyd George makes you thirsty, you know. And they go on saying things (and drinking), until closing time !"

Bargain Day in Our Viilage. - "Volk that do live in girt towns lucky as they mid think theirselves, can't hope to kip every- thing in their own hands these days. No fear. rhey mid have their drapers' sales spring and winter and crowds packed so close as eggs in h basket; but here .to our place, Hatch-on-the- Moor, nine miles from town as tes and ten from rail, we be to ha' a chance at a remnant now and again. Oh ay—to be sure ! Iss we be. There's a annual sale to Hatch now—twice a year. And really an' truly our summer zale do hap to vit in most wonderful convainient like. One ver'ly mid a'most a-thought the young man must ha' ranged it a-purpose, just along the middle of May, vull a wick or more avore the Anniversary and well in front o' Whitzun whenever that should hap to vall. What's the Anniversary? Why, when the chapel wur a-budded to be sure. And Whit- sun is when the club do walk."—Walter flay- mond in "Country Life."

When a man is in love he says, "How happy I am." When a woman is in love she says, "Are You happy?" The one thing a man cannot forgive \in a woman is strength. Many a man is unhappy because he has not married the woman that he loves. But often lie would. be infinitely unhappier if he had married her. A woman who can allure, yet keep herself always a little out of reach is always the most desirable to men. Many a man has beheld girlish innocence and sweetness where there wag only a baby stare and a vacant brain. The chap Who reads sonnets to a pretty girl has no chance against the fellow who sends candy and flowers regularly. Indeed, modesty ranks first among man's favourite attributes for women. The next is good nature and the next is neatness. Heaven help the woman who r.aarries a man given over to fads and fancies about his food. He is a worse life-companion than a pirate or a burglar with sound digestion.

div.head: WORKING MEN AND"THE,INFIRMARY.
div.p: WORKING MEN AND"THE,INFIRMARY.

One of the best meetings that have ever been held under the auspices of the Infirmary Work- ing Men's Committee assembled in the Council Chamber last Saturday under the presidency , of the Mayor, Councillor Peter Peacock. The re- sult of the year's work was extremely satisfac- tory, for in spite of some dislocations in the matter of organisation consequent upon the passing of the insurance Act, the contribution of the committee, to the funds of the Infirmary reached £1,215 17s. 5d., against c£1,248 18s. 10d. in the preceding year. 'lust this slight falling off was not much more serious is entirely attri- butable to the devotion of the committee and its officials to the cause they have at heart. They simply could not sit down and allow objections to the Insurance Act to injure the funds of the hospital, and the -men of the various works re- sponding willingly and cheerfully, the off was only a few pounds where it might have been hundreds.

Mr. lames Henry Smethurst, the -chairman of the Infirmary Board, remarked upon a strangely paradoxical state of affairs. The assistance forthcoming for the whole of last year from the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co.'s employes was £7 17s. 2d., against £lO5 in the preceding year. Before the passing of the Insurance Act the heads of this firm, whose employes make great'use of the Infirm- ary owing to the number of accidents that in- evitably occur in their large works, in addi- tion to the claims upori the institution for medical service by the dependents of those employes, were as actively interested as were their men in the work of this committee. Why, he asked, when both sides were so keenly in- I terested in the welfare of tne Infirmary, should this breakdown occur? The men, we under- stand, are still anxious to contribute, the staff are willing to collect the contributions, an offer has been made to pay the staff for this extra service, so that it will be no charge against the firm. Yet there is a deadlock that has not been overcome up to now. Surely, in a cause of this kind„ there is a way out? We are pleased to see that the contributions from Messrs. 'Viands Bros.'. employes stand at the same amount as formerly. Only One other firm has fallen back.

The Net of the matter is that firms and men, with very few exceptions, realise clearly that the claims of tilt Infirmary and the calls under the Insurance Act • are two totally different things, and that to mix them up is decidedly unfair. Under the Insurance .Act the men get value for their contributions by services to themselves in time of stress and trouble. For those personal services, or guarantee of ser- vices, they make a personal payment. Their subscriptions to the Infirmary are to cover ser- vices to 'themselves which are not covered by the Act, to their poorer brethren who suffer from sickness, or to their unfortunate mates who reach the ever-open door of the Infirmary In consequence of some sudden accident. It would be a source of great pleasure to all con- cerned if Itlessrs. Pearson and Knowles could devise a way to get into line with the rest of the works of the town.

div.head: MAYOR AND THE CONIA.IITTEE.
div.p: THE MAYOR AND THE CONIA.IITTEE.

- -- The Mayor. was so deeply impressed by the size of the meeting, its representative character and the enthusiasm which prevailed, that he has ,decided to invite the members to a garden party at the Town Hall in the early summer. The Working Men's Committee of the Nursing Association will be included in this kindly token_ of the Mayor's appreciation. .
CONTINUOUS INDUSTRIES.

---- To-day •we publish the last of a series of articles by Mr. A. li. Crosfield on the question of curtailing the hours of labour in continuous industries. Few who have followed Mr. Gros- field's arguments will have failed to realise how great a Change for the better would be effected if rational hours of work could be enforced throughout the civilised world, and how gredt is our responsibility in the matter of taking the lead.
SHALL WE GET THE ORGAN?

It really looks as though Parr Hall will get : its organ, and that Warrington will save itself from being styled one of the stingiest, if one of the .wealthiest, towns in England. To 'Mrs.' Parker, of Penketh, belongs the honour of showing the way out of the difficulty. On seeing what the state of things was she wrote the iMayor offering to subscribe £lOO towards an organ fund, if others would give the balance within a reasonable time. Miss Bylands, the Gables, Thelwall, seconded this effort by also promising ,tlOO and, as if to prevent the danger of ladies having all the credit for good deeds to them Selves, Mr. J. C. Parr has written to Mr. Reynolds, of the Musical Society, offer- ing another £lOO. Thus, in one short week, £3OO has been secured., The 'total needed is £1,600, so that the Mayor needs only thirteen volunteers at £l.OO a head to complete the scheme. Are there thirteen ladies or gentle- men, or ladies and gentlemen, in the district who Will, among them, complete this little amount?. Or are there twenty-six who will give There should- be little difficulty in raising, by this means even more than £1,600, in which ease a'better'instrument than the one contemPhded could be purchased. •

div.head: SHAKESPEAREAN PLAYERS.
div.p: SHAKESPEAREAN PLAYERS.
Teck

It is Opportune at a time when the Warring- ton Shakespearean players are preparing to place to of the works of the immortal bard before the public, that the interesting descrip- tion and picture of the first English theatre should be furnished to "The Examiner" by our contributor, Mr. Arthur Mounfield. Thi article, which appears on page 9, reveals an acquaintance with "the boards" on part, which almost rivals his knowledge of ancient "pubs" and the rules of cock-fighting. Whether our readers are theatre-goers or not, we think they will enjoy a description—to us very diverting—of the playhouse for which Shakespeare wrote his plays. Shakespeareans will be interested to know that Mr. Mounfield has made an effective little contribution to the literature of the acute Bacon- Shakespeare controversy. Those who have read Sir E. Ifurning-Lawrence's last book will re- member that the main argument is based upon' the frontispiece of one) of Lord Bacon's books,, in which a classical figure shakes a spear. Those who advocate the Baconian theory make great play with this fact, but the use of a figure shaking a spear has as little bearing upon the subject as most of the fanciful theories that have been pressed into the service of the tra- ducers of our greatest writer. Mr. 11,1ounfield, after various rummarrings among musty volumes, has shown that pates were used by printers in the 10th century for widely different books, and that the one sup- posed to have been designed by Lord Bacon w-as in use 50 years before he was born. This makes short i.vork of the enthusiastic Sir Law- rence and his elaborate argument. Mr. Moun- field's find has been handed over to the Shake- speare Society, Stratford-on-Avon, and will doubtless be utilised to the fullest ,extent.

div.head: GERMAN TRADE WITH THE BRITISH EMPIRE.
div.p: GERMAN TRADE WITH THE BRITISH EMPIRE.

The Berlin Chamber of Commerce calls atten- tion in its " Mitteilungen " (January number) to the movement of commerce between Germany and England. It shows that Germany's exports to Great Britain during the decade from 1903 to 1912 rose from £49,115,000 to £58,050,000, while its imports from that country rose from £29,700,000 to ,E 42,100,000. In other words, exports gained only £8,935,000, while imports rose £12,400,000. Taking the whole British Empire, the Chamber finds that Germany's imports from it amounted in 1912 to £100,000,000, while its exports reached only £75,530,000. The margin of difference is also becoming less favourable to Germany from year to year. In 1909 Germany's " unfavourable " balance of trade with the British Empire was only ,R 12,485,000 but by 1912 it had risen to £2475.25,000.

div.head: MARCH 21, 1914.
div.p: HOURS OF LABOUR.
Great and Vital Idfantages to be DeriTed from Rational Conditions.
halting the Triumph of Equitg and Cononsense.

To the Editor of " The Examiner." the articles . already pumislted in •• Examiner," I have drawn attention to some of the great vital national advantages to oe derived from the adoption of l‘ational 11011115 VV urK. Let me now, ere I. ieave the suoject, emphasise the international advantages which may, and 1 think must, follow as a result of this vigorous movement of reform. Latter-oay horrors. .

0 neuter as a result of the ever-widening sweep or the iiasu-iigut of the telegraph, or oc cue enterprise emu ceaseless vigilance of oui fress, whether through our being kept bettei informed of the events of our times, good, bad dud indifferent, or whether it be owing to the met mat there has been an unusual preponder- ance ot dismal, shocking and atrocious incidents in the history of humanity during the last decade or two, certain it is that in these lattei times the world has supped full of horrors. In the impenetrable forests of the Congo, and the Amazon, in the far recesses of the backwoods of South America and Central Africa, on the battlefields of China and the' Balkans, and a little more than a decade since during the pro- tracted struggle in South Africa, a tale of blood and tears and disaster on a vast scale has been written, which is uisuial and tragic and terrioie reading; and, as we saw recently during the wai in North Africa, and towards the end of the lasc century in the course of the hideous atrocitiee perpetrated on an appalling scale among the Armenians, cruelty is more deliberate, and hellish work the more ghastly where the conflict and the hatred are between men of different. colour. There is no problem so perturbing, Sc. sombre in its menacing possibilities, or so for- midable in its proportions as this problem pre- sented by the antagonism of men of different colour. Many a tragic chapter has yet to be written 'before that problem is solved, for it will not be solved before humanity is well on the way to completing the history Jf the slow story of its evolution, and of its efforts towards political emancipation and social regeneration. But if we must reflect with pity and horror on that half of human affairs, the other half is well calculated to maintain and strengthen our faith in the power reposed in mankind to work out its own sah,ation, and that a vise, noble and inspiring destiny. Years ago Sir Charles Dilke was fond of emphasising one great domi- nant fact in the world's foreign policy—the fat that the time had gone by when Great Britain and the United States of Ameriza would evei again consent to settle differences by the sw old Combined Onward March. We are on the eve of celebrating the mainten- ance for a hundred years in unbroken continuity of peace relations between our own country am. the great Republic of the West. But have wt not made further progress still in quite receet years? Are we not already in sight the time when it will be recognised that, how- ever acute quarrels and differences between any of the leading Powers of Europe may be, the settlement of those differences by the sword is a settlement which, alike for victors and van- quished in the struggle, is bought too dearly? Are not the interests of the mass of the demo- cracy at one end of the social scale, and the , powerful financier at the other, uniting in theft influence and leading us step by step, slowly but surely, towards a position which will mark an immense advance, which for all time will be one of the greatest and noblest landmarks in the on- ward march of human affairs? It is for the most powerful and most highly civilised nations in ; the world to set the pace and lead the way in this forward movement, just as ire must :ea' to them to advance the cause of indlistriol re- form. In both cases their ezampie will ir.bse. fluently—and in all probability fit no distant date either—be followed by the more backward ' States of Europe, so that in the long run we shall see the triumph of equity and common- sense throughout all the white races of the world. If it be permissible to peer into a dim and distant future, one may venture, with absolute confidence, to piediet that a time will come, and a day will dawn, ,when the same principles will be extended further still. Now it may be said, What has the cause of International Peace to do with the agitation for Rational Hours of Work in Continuous 'lndus- tries? A good deal, I venture to think. The one cause may, and assuredly ought to, help on the other. Teach men what international co- operation may achieve in helping to introduce more scientific, up-to-date and civilised ideas into our industrial system, teach them how it may conserve their health and energy and save their time, and it will not be long before they ask why it should not save their pockets, too. If we are justified in anticipating such a result, and if it is realised—if, in fact, once the indus- trial policy is fairly launched, the other great international question advances parri passu with it—how much more effective, satisfactory and permanent will such united action be than the spasmodic and sporadic efforts of any single, isolated nation. From every point of view the combined movement is infinitely to be preferred, whether it has the effect of simply checking the increase of total expenditure on armaments of all kinds by the great Powers, or whether it brings about an actual diminution of that enor- mous outlay. Possibilities of International Co-operation. In preceding articles I have made it clear that while the other continuous industries are speedily to follow, and while industry in its entirety stands to gain by the success of ou Ii undertaking, the efforts of the International Association for Labour Legislation—and wishthe we had a more compendious title—are in d first instance concentrated upon the Iron an Steel Industry. On that stupendous branch of the world's commerce the livelihood and well- being of millions of men, women and children depend. Every one of them would be benefited by this reform, which would effect a change so enormous that it would simply revolutionise their lives. Now, it is not a complicated pro- posal; it is a simple issue which all men may easily understand. What will be the effect on their minds—and I care not what their nation- ' ality—when they realise the possibilities of this: international co-operation? There will spring into existence a strong feeling of identity of ; interest, limited by no territorial boundary, of difference of language, uniting all men in the common purpose of a great achievement. May we not then fairly' ask the Home Secretary where we are likely to find a better way to mend the relations between people of different nation- alities, or a more simple? If it were some ; agreement as to wages we propose -one could ' easily imagine how, with the complexity of cur- rencies, and the infinite variety of the purchas- ing power of money in different countries, and different parts of the same country, we might ' lose ourselves in a labyrinth of conflicting claims which would baffle and defeat any body of men who sought for some common measure of inter- national agreement along those lines. Our proposals present no such difficulties They are Simple, as I hope has been made abundantly clear. They are also Urgent. In Germany the Imperial' Ministry has within the last two or three weeks been considering the question of over-work in this same Iron and Steel Industry. And they are Strong. Ne ' impartial man who knows the facts dealt with

in these articles questions the ,strength, one may fairly say the overwhelming strength, of the case for this reform; and yet with it all, and if we make the very, best possible use of our opportunities it will take years to carry. Long- continued propaganda work is an essential pre- liminary, even in the ease of the more enlight- ened industrial nations; and when they are in agreement some years of notice for employers of labour will be indispensable so that, though every effort be made (and the British Section of the International Association is ready and willing to devote both time and money to the further- ance of this reform) it will still take us many years to reach the end of our journey. Is it right, or indeed tolerable, that the Home Office should any longer prevent us taking the first step?
A. U. CROSFIELD.

div.head: DEPUTATIONS TO IRELAND
div.p: DEPUTATIONS TO IRELAND
The Latest Trip From Warrington.
IN BELFAST YESTERDAY.
Our Belfast correspondent, wiring last night, says:—

The Warrington deputation, which reached Belfast on Thursday, return home on Saturday evening. They were interviewed to-night by ' representatives of the Ulster Liberal Associa- tion and Belfast Trades Council, and had the case for the democracy put before them convinc- ingly. A reporter from one of the local Tory papers attended on behalf of the Unionist Council to take official notes of the interview, but the Liberal representatives naturally objected, since the proceedings were private, and the journal- ist withdrew.

Members of the deputation declined to make any statement to-night about the tour, explain- ing that that was due to the decision arrived at before they left home. A report would be drawn up in due course. We understand that the members of this deputation are:—Messrs. W. Woodcock, fitter; J. Payton, gas stove maker; J. Roberts, fitter; W. Hall, joiner; James Bramhall, wireworker; E. Davenport, wireworker; and E. Pester, printer. _
They are in charge of Mr. W. H. Bellian.

div.head: BELFAST TRADE UNIONISTS AND
div.p: BELFAST TRADE UNIONISTS AND
HONIE RULE.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—l am some distance from home, and have ' not got the correspondence by me to refer to. I am therefore trusting to memory in replying to a letter written by Mr. Ravenscroft in justi- fication of his deputation telegram respecting Ulster trade unionists and Home Rule. In the first place I would like again to draw his attention to the telegram, attributed to him, the accuracy of which I really questioned. It reads thus: " All trade unionist leaders here unite in condemning Home Rule." Had he said all the engineers, boilermakers, patternmakers, &c.: in the shipyards unite in condemning Home Rule, I might have doubted it, but should not have questioned it, and I accept Mr. Ravens- croft's word that all those he spoke to in the yards were against, as a matter of fact. After the recent exhibition we have had of their per- suasive and fraternal methods of dealing with the unfortunates who differed from them, any- one could be well forgiven for not being too exuberant in his expressions of Nationalism; and as for the Corporation employes, Mr. Ravenscroft must have forgotten be was not in Warrington, but in Belfast. If he will read my first letter again, I said I was quite pre- par-d for a great diversity of opinion; in fact, a 1. I,a majority in Belfast against Home Rule. But even Mr. Ravenscroft will admit that the trade unionists he refers to, large and important as they may be, do not constitute all trade union opinion in Belfast, neither, do they speak for the whole of Ulster, and whether they are represented on the Trades Council of Belfast or not—a point which I have not yet assumed, as I know nothing of its constitution any more than I do the constitution of the Trades Council of Warrington—yet I assume they represent some sections of labour, or their representa- tives could not have been present at the Labour Congress at Glasgow. If Mr. Ravenscroft will read the London "Daily Chronicle" of Friday, rebruary 27th, he will see a statement by Mr, D. R. Campbell, president of the Belfast Trades and Labour Council, Who, favouring Home Rule, and op- posing the exclusion of Ulster, claims to speak on behalf of 15,000 workers. I would thank Mr. Ravenscroft to point out where I have ever men- tioned even the Liberal party, much less any association with the Trades and Labour Coan- cil or party. Their future policy, whether for good or for bad, is entirely a question for them- selves, woilld consider it an impertLnence On my part to offer an opinion. Again, I have not questioned the bona-fides of Mr. Ravenscroft as a Liberal either before or since he went to Ireland. From my standpoint, his political: convictions are his own, to change or maintain I just as his own judgment and conscience dic- tate. I questioned the accuracy of the tele- gram sent in his name. I do now, after it has I taken a fortnight to remember that he and his colleagues spoke to some official members in the shipyards; and I assert still that he has not justified himself or the telegram. And if he still has nothing to withdraw or retract, I am afraid we both differ in our appreciation of the value of language. With respect to Mr. 'Bellian's letter and strg- gestion, which I only saw by reading the local papers, I have sent on copies of the Warring- ton "Examiner" and Warring,ton "Guardian" to my Belfast correspondent, with Mr. Bellian's letter marked for special perusal. It remains for him to deal with it according to his disposi- tion or judgment, although I don't quite see why the name and address of my friend is necessary. He writes as one of the Belfast Trades and Labour Executive. Mr. Bellian has only to put himself in touch with Mr. D. R. Campbell, the p rcelosfni dchleeunsti endorses.o n Is thhe emppuwodshsi aiabtt el ysm more we d ee- fmr friend g afnudrthheirs. does he require?
PATRICK O'BRIEN. 125, Wilderspool-road.
P.S.—I have just heard from my friend, Mr. D. R. Campbell, that he has written to Mr. Herbert Hayes direct.

div.head: PARR HALL ORGAN.
div.p: THE PARR HALL ORGAN.
Mayor Receives Handsome Donations and Encouraging Letters. TOWN MEETING MAY BE CALLED.

The Mayor's remarks about the Parr Hall organ, and the difficulty to get money for the purpose, is meeting with a ready response. Up to yesterday afternoon he had received £3OO, as the following letters show : Penketh Lodge, near Warrington, March 15th, 1914. Dear Mr. Mayor,—l notice with regret that your appeal for funds for the Parr Hall organ- has so far been unsuccessful. Having gone so far, it would be a great pity that the matter should be dropped, and a great loss to the town, both from' the educational and the pleasure-giving points of view, and I sincerely hope that your own efforts and the admirable letter from Mr. J. Reynolds may meet with some response. Possibly someone will now come forward and offer a sum bearing some substantial proportion to the amount required. I have great pleasure in promising one hundred pounds („e100) if the amount call be raised within reasonable time.—Yours very truly,

div.p: irELEN PARKER.

Dear Mr. Mayor,—l have much pleasure in promising one hundred pounds (X 100 towards the Parr Hall organ fund, to which. I believe, Mrs. Parker has already offered a similar amount.
Wishing you every success in obtaining the require(' sum,—Yours faithfully, • (Miss) M. G. RYLANDS.

Illness of Councillor Taylor. Councillor S. Taylor, we regret to say, is lying dangerously ill at his home in Manchester-road. A specialist was called in during the week, and an operation was advised, but has not yet taken place, owing to the patient's present weak state. Great and general anxiety has been dis- played, among the callers yesterday being his Worship the Mayor.

A Boundary Battle. Major C. E. Norton will, on behalf of the Local Government Board, begin an inquiry at the Manchester Town Hall on the Ist of April, on the proposal to re-adjust tile boundary be- tween Lancashire and Cheshire. Warrington Guardians and Rural District Council, Lynam District Council, and the Parish Councils of Grappenhall and Thelwall will, amongst others, be represented, in addition to Lancashire and Cheshire CS)lllity c94nCilS, • A Ray to Remember. There will be a splendid miscellaneous bill, including "Raffles," from Mr. Gerald Alexander's Company, and the War- rington Dramatic Society in "The Deal Departed," by Stanley ikaglitOtt•

div.head: Printers Make Merry.
div.p: Printers Make Merry.

To inaugurate the Warrington Branch of the Typographical Association a successful tea and Iconcert was held in the Norton Arms Hotel on Saturday evening, and the men of type spent a merry, time. The gathering numbered ovei 70. Mr. W. Robinson (president of the War- rington Branch) was in the chair, and he was supported by Mr. French (the president of the Typographical Association) and Mr. Skinnei (general secretary of the T.A.). These two gentlemen addressed the gathering upon topics of interest to the branch. Various toasts were proposed, and an excellent vocal and instru- mental programme was rendered by talented artistes.

The Mothers' Union held their annual soci4l gathering at the Institute on Alonday evening. There was a splendid muster, and a very happy evening was spent, thanks to the entertainment provided by the following ladies and gentle- men Mesdames A. Landon and W. Bibby, jun., the Misses Pollett, Bates, Lister, Miller, Hughes, Tanner, Brown and McCollom, and Messrs. A. Davis, G. Lloyd and T. Hughes. The Misses Pollett and Jones were the accompanists. During the evening fight refreshments were handed round. The ladies responsible for the arrangements, which were admirably made, were Mesdames Gandy, Atherton, Armstrong, and H. Landon. The gathering was presided over by the Incumbent.
