Bewsey-road Ladies' Concert. In connection with the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church an excellent and well-attended concert was given by the ladies on Monday evening, Mr. James Bennett, Padgate, presiding. "See the dancers" was the part-song rendered in so admirable a manner by the choir, with which the programme was opened. Other numbers given by the choir were "Gipsies' laughing trio," "Mountain call," "Killarney," "Bells of Aberdovey," Rule, Britannia," and "Even. ing song." The sketch, "Valentine's Day," by 1 the Misses N. Light and M. Turner, was very diverting, and was given skilfully. Miss Win- statiley pleased with her rendition of "Come: sing to me," and other pleasing items wev. given by the Misses E. Turner, Wardle, Jones, L. Nock, and Maddock, and Mr. Patrick O'Leary. Miss M. Plinston was an efficient pianist and trainer.

Warrington Photographic Society. Perhaps the pleasantest evening of the wintei session comes when all the leaders of last sum- mer's outings are called on for screen pictures taken during their particular ramble. Last summer the journeys extended from Bangor, Llangollen, Prestatyn, and Chester, in the West, to Millers' Dale, in the East; from Darwen to Eddisbury, Pettypool, Vale Royal, Rostherne, Arley, Dunham Massey, and Aston Hall were nearer places reached by cycle or train, and most of these were illustrated by voice and pic- ture on Tuesday evening. The humorous side, however, is the most popular. To see how the snapshotter was snapped, and what contor- tions of face and body a photographer under- goes in the course of his art, to see how you look, getting over a stile, or under a fence, in tying your boot lace, or lying full length in sleep, or pretence of sleep; to see how miserable a group of holiday camerists look huddled undei a sun blind to keep out of the rain; or to see how happily similar cameristes can pick choco- lates out of a bag—all these and many othei funny bits kept the audience in a ripple of merriment from opening to close of the evening.

div.head: An Expert in Salesmanship.
div.p: An Expert in Salesmanship.

Mr. Harry llaintith, 83, Hood-lane, clerk in the export department of Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., has just earned a conspicuous distinction. Entering a competition open to the United Kingdom for a prize for the best essay on salesmanship, he was successful in carrying off the trophy, a solid silver rose bowl, offered by Sir John Barker, and presented to him on Monday at the Kingsway Hall, London.

- - - Mr. Daintith, who is the son of Mr. William Daintith, wheelwright and smith, Sankey Bridges, was 24 on Tuesday. He received his edu- cation at the Wycliffe School under Mr. Alfred Corney, his principal class teacher being Mr. JefforY. the present headmaster. Prior to entering, the service of Messrs. Crosfield, 18 months ago, he was employed by the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co., Ltd., and by Messrs. W. D. Iloughton and Co., Ltd. Although a serious student of trading methods, Mr. Daintith has some outside interests. He is, for instance, secretary and treasurer of the Sankey Cricket Club, and he took a small part in the recent performance by the Crosfield Operatic Society. lie has been warmly congratulated upon his success.

div.head: Warrington Dramatic Society.
div.p: The Warrington Dramatic Society.

The annual meeting of the members of the abore-named society was held at the l'atten Arms Hotel on Monday evening, Mr. Arthus Browne being in the chair. It was reported that no stage production by the society had taken place during last season owing to death having been very busy amongst several impor- tant members, which made it absolutely impos- sible to complete a cast, and thanks were due to Mr. Loader and Mr. Warburton for filling up the week for which the society had engaged the , Royal Court Theatre. The Honorary Treasures produced his accounts, showing a satisfactory ' credit balance in the bank. Mr. W. P. Rylands was unanimously re-elected president for the ensuing year, and Mr. Sidney Wallhead was re- elected stage manager. On the election of the honorary treasurer, Mr. Charles 11. Wood asked Mr. Browne how many years he had been hon treasurer, and the reply was 21 years. Mr, Browne was unanimously re-elected, as was also 111 r. J. W. Bullen as honorary secretary. The committee, consisting of Messrs_ George Wil- liamson, C. H. Wood, Stanley Wright, H. G Mosley and H. M. Ashton, were also unani- mously re-elected. Mr. Arthur Norman Browne was elected a member of the society.

There was a large congxe.gation in the Parish Church yesterday afternoon., when the Rev. B. Heywood, Vicar of Swinton, Manchester, gave an address to women on "The Influence of Woman." In the evening a large number of men congregated, and the reverend gentleman preached on the subject, "The Folly and Sin of Gambling." Ile dealt with the extent, sin, folly and cure of g‘ambling, and after referring to horse-race betting and other forms of gam- bling, he said that although not technically being a forth of gambling, a good many news- paper competitions, strictly speaking, were. In regard to the cure of gambling legislation was ' proposed, such as Lord Newton's Betting Inducement Bill, and the Bill introduced by' Lord Loreburne. Legislation, said the preacher. could not of itself cure the mania, for that could only be done largely by individual action, creating public opinion, and by the provision of other means—more innocent—fo satisfying the natural instinct in the people for excitement and amusement. Whilst denouncing gambling, he supported manly sports, and also othei interests of a literary and artistic nature. If their in was full of what was good they would have no room for evil.

The Mayor and Temperance. The Band of Hope in connection with the Brick-street Mission has had a successful session and there was a large attendance in the Schools on Thursday evening, when the final concert was given. The Mayor presided„ and was sup- ported by the Mayoress, Councillor Shaw, and Mr. Laws (Police Court Misaioner). The Chair- man said he hoped the children would take to heart the teaching they received week by week, for they must remember that they would con- stitute the nation of the future. He urged them to keep good company, always avoiding bad companions If they were temperate in their habits, as the Band of Hope taught them to be, they would be well on the way to good eitizenshfp. (Applause.) Mr. Laws dealt with the principles of temperance and spoke of the effect the home life of a child had. If every- thing was all right, and the children were happy and contented in the home, there was a strong influence working for good. (Hear, hear.) An excellent programme had been arranged by Mr. Bradley, and the various artistes con- tributed enjoyable items. On the proposition of Councillor Shaw, a hearty and comprehensive vote of thanks was passed.

Free Chareh Boys' Brigade. The quarterly brigade service was held on Sunday evening in the Golborne-street Baptist Church, when the service was conducted by the Rev. T. S. Chedburn, the president of the Bri- gade and also the Senior Chaplain. There were four companies in attendance, namely, Latchford Baptists Working Men's Mission (Bank Quay), Hill Cliffe, and Golborne-street Baptists. In all, about 100 boys and 12 officers turned out to the rally. The whole Brigade was under the command of Colonel Grounds, who led the boys smartly through the streets, and the bearing of the Brigade reflected great credit upon his leadership. The form of service was unusual and extremely interesting. The Rev. J. S. Chedburn's keen interest in and ability to help lads is well known, and the strength of the movement is in no small mea- sure due to his never-failing interest. Ile had I secured an excellent electric arc lamp and illustrated his address to the boys and congre- gation by the aid of the powerful lamp. The subject he considered was the story of the Prodigal 'Son. His first picture illustrated the , home life of the prodigal. There he was gathered I with his father and brother, and the servants of . the house, in the family circle. His home asso- ciations were of the best. His father's relation to his children was such as should ordinarily lead children to live a straight and noble life. But the development of children has a strange way of eluding all man's methods, and setting at naught the most balanced calculations. This young prodigal was determined to see life. He had a false estimate of what constituted life. Thus, in spite of a noble heredity, in spite of the best of environments, in spite of the most exalted teaching, this young prodigal went I astray. The preacher made this application ' to the present day. The boys of the Brigade might have the very best of homes, their train- ing in such homes might be all that an idealist could wish, they might have the best of instruc- tion in the Sunday School, but unless they were willing to give themselves to the highest and , the best, the seductions of the .modern world , were such that they would be drawn away from all early influences, and would wander as the prodigal did in a far country. Other beautiful Slides illustrated the prodigal's gay life. He was surrounded by a multitude of friends; then lie was shown in the abject plight of a wan- derer, glad even to fight with the pigs for a meal; then finally the father receives him, a sadder, but a wiser son.. During the evening the boys of the Golborne-street Church rendered two special hymns, having been under the training of their Senior Officer (Captain Davis). It was agreed on all hands that the service had been helpful, and especially were the boys im- pressed by what was a most blessed, but serious service. After the service the boys marched, under the command of their respective officers, to their own headquarters.

div.head: MARCH 21, 1914.
div.p: COMMITTEEMEN'S PAY.
The Insurance 7/- Per Week Discussed and Adjourned.
MEMBERS DO NOT WANT PAYMENT.

The question as to the payment of Insurance Committee members was again raised at a meet- ing of the committee in Trinity Chambers on Wednesday evening, when Councillor Roberts presided. The following item appeared on the minutes of the previous meeting: "That the Commis- sioners be asked to approve of payment of 7s. per attendance at all meetings of the committee and sub-committee."

NO DESIRE TO BE PAID. The Chairman, referring to the particular minute, said he had no keen desire to be paid in that matter. In fact, he would personally pre- fer not to be paid. He had never received money I for public work, and he was rather old to begin. If the practice of payment to members obtained through the country, he would not object to his colleagues taking their share, but personally he would not take any at all. He thought it extremely improbable, in face of the present financial condition in the admin- istration of the Act, that any matter of that kind would be entertained at present. There was a just claim for recognition in County Insurance Committees, where the men had to go a long way to the meetings, and the finances being small he thought the money would be [distributed for cases of that nature. In view lof the fact that the amounts paid out, particu- larly in regard to women, whose illnesses had exceeded the amount provided, it was a littk , too premature to begin suggesting payment to gentlemen Who worked that great measure, and they sho•ald wait until sufficient time had elapsed to ascertain the true financial position of the whole administration.

div.head: NO PAYMENT SUGGESTED.
div.p: NO PAYMENT SUGGESTED.

The Mayor said they did not suggest they should be paid. There was a certain amount of money allocated for that purpose, and they had to put themselves right by making a suggestion as to the amount. They knew they would not get the amount the committee passed. lie knew in seine instances it was absolutely necessary that members should be paid. Some of the members who attended that night had lost a " turn." The Chairman said there were individual cases where it was too much to expect men to lose wages, or part of them, to attend meetings of that kind. But in the naain it would not apply to the majority of their members, and he, thought the bulk of them would prefer to re- main as honorary workers. There was a great deal of splendid work done on committees of

that character on a voluntary bans, (Hear, ' hear.) No man should be expected, however, to lose money in attending the meetings, and he thought the money should go to euch men, rather than make the payment a general thing. He was prepared, however, to leave the matter on the minutes,

div.head: WAKES WEEK SCHEME.
div.p: WAKES WEEK SCHEME.
The Mayor in Communication With Employers of Labour.
MESSRS. PEARSON & KNOWLES' EXAMPLE.

The scheme to have a Wakes Week for War- rington like what obtains in other Lancashire and Yorkshire towns, originally mooted in "The Examiner," has advanced a step further. This week the Town Clerk, on behalf of the Mayor, sent out the follo*ing circular-letter to employers of labour in the borough :

Dear Sir,— His Worship the Mayor has received a request from the Trades and Labour Coun- cil to call a Conference for the purpose of arranging a Local Wakes Week if possible. Before taking any further steps in the matter, his Worship would be glad to have your views upon the question of local holi- days, and whether, in your opinion, any alteration is desirable. Yours faithfully, J. LYON WHITTLE.
Up to last evening some fifteen replies had been received from the firms circularised. The Mayor will probably call a Conference at an early date of the persons interested in the proposals.

MESSRS. PEARSON AND KNOWLES' EXAMPLE. We have received the following communica- tion from Mr. J. Elwell, Council member for the Warrington district of the Associated Iron and Steel Workers of Great Britain:—
Re question of Wakes Week for Warring- ton !ITT pjstrict I b to state that rEzre-
. _ sentatives of the workmen interVieW6he employers of the firms of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, and Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., last year, and _an agreement was

_ arrived at whereby the workmen engaged in the manufacture of iron at the above firms should have the week following Walk- ing Day as an annual holiday week. The men on their part agreed, if orders were pressing, to work Easter Monday and Whit-Monday. I have sent a copy of this to the Mayor, who I wish every success in his effort. ' Yours faithfully, JOSEPH ELWELL.

div.head: PADGATE VICAR DEAD.
div.p: PADGATE VICAR DEAD.
The Sudden Passing of the Rev.
G. W. Dickinson.
A FAMOUS ATHLETE.
The news of the sudden and unexpected death of the Rev. G. W. Dickinson, vicar of Padgate, came as a great surprise on Thursday to all who know him.

The first intimation of the Vicar's demise was the announcement posted on Thursday morning on the Vicarage Gate, which notice simply stated:— " The Vicar passed away at; 2.30 this .morning,!' A painful surprise was created by theoiiitelni- gence, both in l'adgate and Warringttin.• The majority of the people were not, aware of; his illness, for he had pre.a.uhed: on' the previous Sabbath. On. Sunday- Ike ocafiliteted the early morning, cortiitianion aild a children's afternoon service attWitcilkton, preached a,t his own church in the morning, and for the evening service exchanged pulpits with the Rev. G. C. Briggs, of Christ Church, Latchford. He was taken ill soon after, and during Sunday night his ill- ness made itself more apparent, and life slowly ebbed away during the succeeding days. until his death took place on Thursday morning as stated.

div.head: HARD WORKER.
div.p: A HARD WORKER.
He was a hard and persistent worker for all the parochial undertakings and ventures con- nected with the church, but his sympathies
were not absolutely exhausted upon them, for he took a keen interest in everything promoted for the general welfare of the village and the district.
In Warrington he was well known and highly respected, and it is significant that his last sermon was delivered in the town.

The deceased was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge. In 1891 he was successful in ob- taining his B.A. degree, and in 1905 he gained his M.A. He was ordained in 1896, and his first curacy was at Walton-on-the-Hill, where he remained for two years, during which time he was created a priest. I He came to Warrington in 1898, as a citrate under Canon Willis at the Parish Church, and Ihere he stayed until 1905, when he accepted the I curacy of St. Oswald's, Chester. Leaving there the following year, he went to Southport, where he laboured until 1908 in the Holy Trinity Parish. In May of that year he received a call to Padgate, where, as Vicar, he had laboured so conscientiously ever since.

div.head: SATURDAY,
div.p: SATURDAY,
'FAMOUS HOCKEY PLAYER.

- The deceased Vicar, who would have reached his 46th birthday on Monday, was a follower of the majority of outdoor games. In his younger days football, hockey and cricket re- ceived due attention, but these were superseded latterly by golf. On the hockey, field he achieved his greatest success as an athlete, hav- ing played on several occasions for Lancashire County, and in his prime was considered one of the finest exponents of the game of hockey in England. He was a bachelor. The funeral will take place to-day.

div.head: COUNTRYSIDE
div.p: THE COUNTRYSIDE
About the Sweet Violet, the Daffodil and Other Early Flowers.
SPRING DAY.

Spring begins to-day with the vernal equinox, that is, the time in Spring when the 24 hours are divided equally between the night and the day. Henceforward the days will gradu- ally lengthen and the nights will shorten, till we reach Midsuromer. Then we shall go on towards the Autumn equinox, and beyond that we shall travel, by ever-shortening days and lengthening nights, to the shortest day in Mid-winter.
But we are now leaving Winter behind, entering upon Spring and anticipating the Summer, with its long days and all that is bright and hopeful.

How could we better approach the part of the year that is most associated with hope and promise than in the way Mr. Dunlop invites us—by considering the early flowers that come to give us object-lessons in the perpetual • glories of life?
Mr. Dunlop will be a frequent contributor to "The Examiner" during the coming months, when Nature will be revealing her beauty at its best. There are few better fitted than he for the task.

This month the array of the Rowers begirt their yearly march through the meadows and the woodland groves and glens, over the moors and the mountains, and along the seashores Already several of the advanced scouts have if spying Out the land. Foremost and daintiest of them all, in spotless white, graceful and strong, the lovely little Snowdrop has appeared on the scene, a full fortnight in advance of its fellows. The Snowdrop, though so delicate and fragile in appearance, affords ons of the most striking examples of the power of growth in plant life. On two occasions I have seen this flower making its way into the world under the most adverse circumstances; once it was forcing itself through an asphalted garden walk, and another place, near High Legh, a macadamised country roadside, well-worn and hard, was not sufficient to restrain its exuberant life. A contemporary of the Snowdrop has already appeared in meadows and parks in cer- tain localities, and, like it, still remains with us to cheer on the advancing host. This is this Winter Aconite, one of the Buttercup order of plants, a low-growing plant with a bright yellow flower, and large leaf-like bracts circling round the base of the blossom, giving a pretty study of harmony in gold and green. The plant is not plentiful in the Warrington district, but is frequently met with in gardens.

The Advance Guard. Should the weather be mild and east winds not too keen, many of the advance guard will soon make their appearance. Most of them are already well on the way, and only await a few hours' genial warmth to show their heads. The first to break into flower is almost sure to be the 'Yellow Crocus, and its relation, the Purple ' Crocus. Both these flowers are better known in our public parks and private gardens than in the wild state, yet in some parts of England. they are very common. In former years the Yellow Crocus was found along the banks of the Mersey in Latchford. The ovary of this plant is quite underground, hidden amongst the bases of the leaves, out of the way of the frost. IWhen the pollen grain reaches the stigma it send's, out a pollen tube, which will have to travel five or six inches 'down the style beforc fertilisation can take place, a journey which occupies from one to three days. After the formation of the seed the stalk below the ovary .elongates and pushes the fruit out of the ground for the-sun to ripen the seeds. That feathered wanton, the Sparrow, plays havoc amongst the Yellow Crocuses in some districts by pulling the petals to pieces. What is the reason of this? There seems to be some purpose behind this vandalism. It seems hard to think that the bird acts out of pure spite. A curious fact is that both Field Mice and House Mice show the same preference for the Yellow I Crocus. These rodents will in a night visit a. ' garden border, choose all the yeliow flowers, and, passing over the blue ones, dig up the corms and devour them. In the morning a number of little pits will be found where the destructive little navvies have been at work. The naughty Sparrows may act under the same occult attraction of the yellow flowers, but are not sufficiently industrious to finish their work, or are prevented by frequent interruptions from getting to the buried food store. It is very remarkable that it is invariably the yellow plants which suffer, because it has been found that the Yellow Crocus corm has a more pleas- ing taste than that of the Purple Crocus. So far as the human nose can discern, there is no , difference in smell between the two colours, but it is. of course, quite possible that the keenei scent of the Sparrow and the Mouse may detect. I one.

Another favourite which will be emerging from its long winter's sleep and wafting its fragrance on the balmy air is the Sweet Violet. It still escapes the rapacity of the " penny-a. root" hawker in some sheltered districts, and may be found on woody banks, usually with a southern aspect. As with many other Violets, there are two. colours of flowers—blue and white. What is the real cause of this albinism in plant life no one has yet discovered. Many theorie.,, have been advanced, but none seem conclusive. But what is stranger still, is fault most of tlic Violets, besides having flowers of two colours, bear two kinds of flowers, one with the usual coloured petals, and another, later on in the season, entirely without petals. The petaloid flowers seldom develop seed, while the petalle:sf, flowers, which NEVER OPEN, produce seed in abundance.

The Daffy-down-dilly. The Daffodil is, par excellence, an early Spring flower. It has many names. It is the "Daffy," the "Iffy-down-dilly," of village children in the Midlands, the " Glen" of Ayrshire, and the "Lent Lily" of Cornwall. It is a flower of the woodlands, and a lover of shade. The plant must not be confused with the Narcissus of Greek poetry, which has a sweet-scented white flower. The tube-shaped corona in this flower is an "extra," not found in many British plants. Of the six outside floral leaves the three outer ones are sepals and the three inner ones petals. In the "double" varieties, now so abundant in the florists' windows, all the stamens have been transferred by the art of the gardener into petals. The double flower does not produce seed, the essential organs having been traded for show. The Coltsfoot and the Butterbur are two plants of the composite order which may be found in flower this month, the former in rough waste ground, and the latter generally in abundance in damp places by banks of rivers and brooks. Neither plant has the graceful beauty of the •Snowdrop or the Daffodil; their beauty is that of proportion and mass rather than outline. The growth .of the flower stem in both plants between the fading of the flowers and the ripening of the fruit is well worth observing. The elongation of the flower-stalk is a contrivance to lift the fruit above the sur- rounding vegetation (including its own immense leaves, which at this stage develop very rapidly) so that the wind may have full play upon the feathery pappus and transfer the seed away from the parent plants.

_ In the copses and shady hedgerows, if there is warmth and wind, the Wood Anemone will be sure to show the passer-by its white star-like flowers. The more the wind blows the wide/ will they expand, a habit which has given the plant the name of "Wind-flower." The Anemone belongs to the Buttercups, and it is an interesting object for examination. The underground stem, the single flower-stalk bear- ing leaf-like bracts, and the apparent absence of sepals, tell something of the relationship be- tween habit and structure. Many Spring ! flowers, usually white or some pale colour, have ! a tendency to become more or less red. Amongst these we find red specimens of the Anemone.

div.head: CANADIAN MINIBUS.
div.p: CANADIAN MINIBUS.
Mr. J. T. Shaw Writes of Climate
and Conditions. '

Mr. -James T. Shaw (eon of Councillor James- Shaw), to whose experiences in Morse (Sas- katchewan) we referred a fortnight ago, has written a letter home, from which we give the following extracts : Tho snow is so thick out in the country that the farmers have a terrible job to get through it. In places it is sft. to 7ft. deep.- The weather for a time has been very severe, our lowest temperature being 58 below zero. It might be worse, but when it is I hope I am out of it. I can stand cold as well as anyone (bar Esquimos), but I am quite content at 58 below zero. With , a slight wind it is impossible to face it and run .100 yards without freezing the nose or cheeks. It feels very funny—something like iubbing menthol all over your face and then blowing a cold blast on it. That is as near to the feeling as I can get it, for the face seems to lose all blood and go stone cold. To try and walk 200 yards with ears uncovered is madness, for one 01 both will be bitten, and they swell up like a big thick mushroom, and if they are not at- tended to promptly they will drop off in time. But as I have said before, "It is a lovely climate."
A Lot of Distress.

There is a lot of distress throughout the country. Every town has its portion, more or less. Bome of the big cities hare their thousands of unemployed. Montreal, for instance, has Isome 10,000 out of work; Morse Jaw has 8,000; Calgary, 6,000; Vancouver, heaven knows how many. I don't think they do in Vancouver. They have put an embargo on all labour, and forliidden anyone without so much capital from entering, and it goes like this all over the Dominion. More or less every town has its ' charity works. Even in this small place we have six families living on charity, and I am expecting two or three more before long. It is madness for young people to come out to this country for the next two years. The conditions at present are due to extravagant speculation in real estate. people with big money invested big, and the ordinary man that had 75 dollars per month and 30 dollars per month to spare, invested the 30 dollars per month in a lot of land, never allowing for hard times. Thus when it did come they lost, their all, or had to put money into it that ought to have bought clothes. Many of the big money men have had to live as poor men to meet the big sums due for payments on big speculations. This has crippled the country financially, as there has hardly been any money stirling, only for real estate and necessities. No doubt this ' year will be a lesson to them all, and the coun- try will benefit by it in the future. But it has been a hard knock, and it will take a year or two for her to get over it.

div.head: Gamble.
div.p: A Gamble.

Undoubtedly to give up any kind of a decent ' job and come out to Canada at any time is a big gamble, that is, if they came, like I did, no friends, jobs, affluence or influence. It is a thousand to one against the chance of success. Even so far as I have got, my advice to anyone thinking of coming out is, Don't come this or next year, for there won't be much growth of any towns in comparison to recent years, for private pockets, corporations and all have been hit heavily up to now, and it will be a year or more before they have the same confidence, although the Canadian and Yankee are bigger gamblers by far than Englishmen, "as a rule." This is where ray luck has come in. I have taken chances, and then worked hard to make a success of them. My letter will help anyone to decide sensibly before coming out and then doing the thinking here, for it is too late. The homestead business is not what it seems.' The Government .will grant a quarter section (240 acres) of land for 10 dollars to any able-bodied man. But he has to live six months out of every year, for three years, on the homestead and put in so much improvements or ploughing, &c. There are not ten out of every 100 that haven't 1,000 dollars capital to start with, but what are up to the eyes in debt. There is so much machinery for ploughing, reaping, sowing, &c., to be bought that it means running into debt for 1,000 dollars to be anything like equipped. These things it is no trouble to get; in fact, they will push them on to him. But the interest on the money is so great that in the end farm, tools, and everything go to the implement man, for horse food and others have to be bought to work the machinery. And these are half cash, and the.balance in the fall (autumn). This is ' when he receives money for his crop, and if he doesn't pay the horseman, back go the horses. The implement man knows better; he stands by and lets everybody take all the cash they can get. When the poor fellow is tied up, and doesn't know where to find a dollar, up comes "Mr. Na!)" lind asks for his share. It can't be paid, therefore he makes no fuss, plays the good Samaritan, renews the note 50 per cent. heavier interest, takes a chattell mortgage on the farm and machinery. By this, whatever articles are in this mortgage no one else can touch until the machinery man has had his fill. From this time onward the farmer is a servant to him, and a poorly paid one at that. There are more lunatics come off these farms 'than anywhere else in the world. I believe homestead insanity they call it. Through the " quietness " they say. The lively time, I should say, for he won't get much time to worry over anything else, only working for one or other of the implement firms and getting noth- ing for it only insults. These are facts that I have come across personally, and not guess work.

div.head: COUNTRYSIDE—continued.
div.p: COUNTRYSIDE—continued.

This red tint is more prevalent in bleak spring, and in exposed situations. Red colour has the power of absorbing heat rays from the sun more than other colours, and this in cold springs helps to protect the young flower inside the unopened bud, from the biting winds and cold. Full Parade.

- Towards the end of the month the snowy white flowers of the Blackthorn will be claiming our attention by their beauty. A large solitary bush in full bloom in a hedge is a very striking picture with the white flower mass set off against the black leafless branches. In the Craven district of the West Riding, especially at Kettlewell and round Grassington, where the hedges are almost entirely composed of Black- thorn, the sight of the long lanes of white- topped hedges is one of the very finest in Eng- lish landscape.

Among the trees, in thicket and hedge, the Hazel's erect and slim male catkins will be lengthening, opening out and becoming pendulous, shedding their abundant pollen in the breeze over the tiny crimson star-like female flowers below. By river and stream the Aldei has opened its long, dangling male catkins, full of pollen, and the more slender upright female catkins will be swaying in the wind. On the same tree the dried, hard, brown cones of the previous year may still be seen clinging to the twigs. What the fierce blasts of winter could not accomplish will soon be done by rising new life within the tree, and, one by one, the dead cones will soon be left lying under the tree. The flowers of the other catkin-bearing fs. - the Willow, the Black and White Popla- the Aspen will be fully developed befort days have passed. Then comes the burst varying tints of green leaf o'er woodlan and Aik meadow, bringing gladness and joy to wearY eyes. Battalion after battalion and brijade after brigade will he marching with quick otep over the landscape till the middle of May, %%Tien the Spring flowers will be on full parade. G. A. DUNLOP.

div.head: FLETCHER, RUSSELL'S GOOD YEAR.
div.p: FLETCHER, RUSSELL'S GOOD YEAR.
- t

At the 22nd annual meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd., gas stove manufacturers and iron founders, War- rington, Manchester, and London, held at Warrington on Wednesday, a very satisfac- tory report was presented upon the results of last year's business. A dividend of 5 per cent., with a bonus of 5 per cent., was de-
The strike at the works was discussed, the Chairman asking the meeting to support the directors in their efforts to manage the busi- ness in their own way and free from outside interference.
Mr. Rude, the secretary, was made a director, an acknowledgment of his interest in, and knowledge of, the business.

Igfr. George Perkins (chairman) presided. The following directors were also present: Mr. W. Russell, Mr. W. Fairhurst, Mr. F. G. Rowson, Mr. Charles Clare, Mr. Thomas Settle and Mr. F. P. Bayley, with the Secretary (Mr. W. 11. Rndge). Mr. Thomas W. Fletcher was absent. to the deep regret of all present, having had to go away for the benefit of his health.

THE CHAIRMAN AND THE STRIKE. No Outside Interference. The CHAIRMAN said: Before dealing with the accounts, I think you would like me to say a fey( words with regard to the strike at the works. The men have emphasised the fact that at one time they were allowed to approach the firm by deputation. During the past year several deputations of workmen .have been seen regarding complaints, which have, generally speaking, turned out to be of a frivolous char- acter, and could easily have been dealt with by the foremen. We therefore put up a-notice in the works that any man having any complaint to make must mention the matter to the fore- man of the shop in which he worked, and the same, if reasonable, would receive considera- tion. Many of you will have read that the men at a mass meeting decided that unless the right of deputation was conceded work would be sus- pended. It might interest you to know that the meeting referred to could not by any means , have represented the views of the majority of our workmen, as the room in which the meet- ing was held only accommodates at the outside 300 men, and, as you are aware, we have about 1,000 employes in our works. Moreover, a num- ber of the men present at the meeting referred to were not employed by us, and yet they were allowed to vote for a strike in our works., I ven- ture to think that if a ballot of our workmen had been taken there would have been a large majority against a strike. I can assure you that the men have.no genuine grievance, and it is hoped that your directors have your support in their efforts to manage your business in their own way and free from outside interfer- ence. (Hear, hear.)
Concentration and Economy. The directors have pleasure in submitting the
t
I
iH ,ii
Cr,

report and balance sheet of the company for the year ending December 31st, 1913. They are still continuing their policy of organisation, concentration and economy, and think the share- holders may congratulate themselves on the re- sult of the year's working, and on the ample evidence of the decided improvement in the position of the company, financially and other- wise. A larger business has been done, which also makes for the satisfactory results achieved. During the past year repairs and general up- keep have received the directors' most careful attention, and the works are in very good work- ing order. Turning to the balance sheet, it may be noticed that before arriving at the profit shown in the accounts, large depreciations have been allowed for, including extra depreciations, espe- cially in the pattern values, Pendleton property and King's Cross depot. These were absolutely necessary to a sound financial condition of the company.
The Year's Profit.

In the profit and loss account you will find that the balance (after charging depreciation), from trading account, interest on investments, cottage rents and transfer fees, amounts to 45,952 18s. If you deduct the debenture inter- est paid and what was due to the end of the year, amounting to .23,920, and also the direc- tors' and debenture trustees' fees, namely, .2887 16s. (which makes a teal of £4,807 165.), it leaves a balance of .221,145 2s. Add to this balance the amount brought forward from last year, namely .23,057 35., and you arrive at a total of 44,202 ss. 4d. Deducting the interim dividend paid on the preference shares at 6 per cent. per annum for the half-year ending June 30th, 1913, .21,500, you have left a balance of .222,702 ss. 4d. With that sum the directors now recommend that a final dividend be paid on the preference shares for the six months ending December 31st, 1913, which will absorb .21,500; a dividend of 5 per cent. be paid on the ordinary shares for the year, which will absorb .25,000; a bonus of 5 per cent, for the year be paid on the ordinary shares, absorbing .25,000; that the sum of 026,919 16s. 6d. be transferred to the reserve fund, as per the Articles of Association; and that the bal- ance of .24,282 Bs. 10d. be carried forward to next year's account. According to the Articles of Association, it . _

is nOcessary to transfer to the reserve•fund .250 per cent. of any surplus profits which are avail- able for further dividend, after payment of the preference dividend, and .25 per cent. on the ordinary shares, until the amount of the reserve fund shall reach .220,000, so that the directors to-day transfer £6,919 16s. Gd. to the reserve fund, making that fund .215,163 16. Gd.

Value of the Property. Turning to the balance sheet, the total value of the property, as shown on the asset side, bas decreased from last year's total by the sum of .6200 1%. sd. The additions during the twelve months, including new foundry exten- sion, new warehouse, new hydraulic moulding plant, new power-house, new painting machines, new overhead runway, new cupola bridge and stage, new motor-house and plumbers' shop, are .e 8,561 us. id., and the depreciation and writ- ings off .£:8,762 10s. 6d.; thus. the amount of 19s. sd. just mentioned is the difference between the additions and the depreciations, and extra depreciations.

The sundry debtors show a decrease of £3,559 54. gd., as compared with the total debtors shown at the end of last year. Stocks on hand show a decrease of £1,331 Os. od. The cash in hand and at banker's has in- creased by £4.293 is. 3d., due partly to de- crease in the sundry debtors. The bank ac- count is a very satisfactory feature of the bal-

ange sheet, especially when you notice that the sundry creditors are £9,283 13s. 9d. less than last year. There is an increase in the sundry in- vestments of .2525. The directors have pur- chased 17 of the goin-Pany's debentures as an investment for £1,660 15s. 10d., making with the 30 bought during 1911 and 1912, 47 deben- tures at a total cost of £4,385 16s. 10d. The arrangement made by the directors with regard to the fund to meet compensation cases for accidents is still working .satisfactorily, and there is a substantial balance in hand. The National Insurance Act gives us a deal of extra clerical work to do, and cost us over £940 last year. div.head: FOUR-YEAR COMPARISON. Who Makes The Profit?
div.p: A FOUR-YEAR COMPARISON. Who Makes The Profit?

Mr: EDMUND ROWSON, in seconding, said he thought he ought to offer some congratulations to the directors for what had happened during the past twelve months. He wished to make a comparison to the position of the company In 1910 and at the present date. In 1910 the cash in hand was £143, whilst to-day they found it amounted to £28,300. Yhe company had gar- chased 47 debentures, and the profits in 1910 were £2,535, whilst to-day they were £21,145. Those figures were all the more startling when he recollected a remark made at a strike meet- ing that the men made the profit, and i that they should have it. He was of the opinion that t was the men at the head of affairs, and not the workmen, who made the profit. Last year he alluded to the labour questiofi, and congratu- lated them on' the fact that during 1912, although there was a strike in Lancashire and in the Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and North o üble. He was sorry to say allocro. fha England, no glan tdr, o that most contagious disease had attacked their works. The shareholders could congratulate themselves that there were no such loathsome things as insanitary workshops on their prem- ises, or that the wages were inadequate or un- fair. The whole question, he understood, was that of recognition of the union. He thought the objects of trade unions had somewhat altered during the past ten or twelve years. He did not wish to discuss the merits or de- merits of trade unionism, but how on earth recognition was going to compensate the men for their loss of wages he could not possibly understand. Whatever opinion they might have regarding the strike, he thought they would be unanimous that it was unfair, unEnglish and unsportsmanlike. He thought that the conduct of men who interfered with men who honestly wished to work and called it peaceful picketing must receive the condemnation, nqt only of that meeting, but of everyone associated with the company. He hoped that shortly the men would return back to the work they had so unfairly left. (Applause.) The motion was carried .'unanimously.

div.head: FIVE PER CENT. DIVIDEND AND FIVE PER CENT. BONUS.
div.p: FIVE PER CENT. DIVIDEND AND FIVE PER CENT. BONUS.

On the motion of the 'CH-AIRMAN, seconded by Mr. J. Mills, a resolution approving of the pay- ment of the interim preference dividend at the rate of six per cent. for the half-year ending June 30th, 1913, was passed. The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. FOSTER JACKSON seconded, and it was carried, that a final divi- dend on the preference shares for the six months ending 31st December, 1913, be now declared.
A dividend on the ordinary shares at the rate of five per cent. and a bonus of five per cent. were declared.

div.head: DIRECTORS' REMUNERATION.
div.p: DIRECTORS' REMUNERATION.

Mr. GAULD proposed that a sum not exceeding .R4OO be placed at the disposal of the Board of Directors for the purpose of extra remunera- tion to the ordinary directors (other than man- aging directors) as the Board might think proper for their services during the past year. He referred in complimentary terms to the splendid results which they had achieved) and they were deserving of this extra remuneration. Alderman BENNETT seconded, and the resolu- tion was carried.

div.head: SECRETARY MADE DIRECTOR.
div.p: THE SECRETARY MADE DIRECTOR.

Messrs. George Perkins (chairman), Charles Clare, William Russell and Thomas W. Fletcher were unanimously re-elected directors of the company. The CHAIRMAN moved that Mr. W. H. Rudge (secretary of the company) be elected a mem- ber of the Board. He said this was the direc- tors' recommendation. Mr. Rudge had been connected with the company since its incep- tion. He was intimate with most of the cus- tomers and knew the business. Personally, Mr. Rudge had been a great help to him, and he thought that he was a very desirable gentleman to be introduced on the Board. He was sure every member of the Board would be pleased to receive him. (Applause.)
Mr. J. WHITEHEAD seconded, and the resolu- tion met with the hearty approval of the share- holders.

Mr. BUDGE returned thanks for the honour, and said he would do his best to merit the con- fidence they had reposed in him. (Applause.) Messrs. Edwin Guthrie and Co. were re-elected auditors. ' Alderman BENNETT, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, expressed the hope that the labour difficulties would soon be set- tled. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: AN OVER-WORKED COMMITTEE.
div.p: AN OVER-WORKED COMMITTEE.
Request Made for More Assistance.

The School Attendance Sub-committee of the Warrington Education Committee complained at the meeting on Monday that they were over- worked, and to remove the cause of their " sweating" they asked that the following reso- lution should be passed: "That it be a recommendation to the Educa- tion Committee that the Chairman of the School Attendance Committee, together with six mem- bers to be chosen in rotation, viz., one member of the School Attendance Committee and five members of the Education Committee not al- ready on the School Attendance Committee, form a Rota Committee for the purpose of in- quiring into cases of absence from school." Mr. PLINSTON said it was difficult to get mem- bers to attend, and he thought it was work in which all the members of the Education Qom- mittee should take a share. Father WILSON thoughtlt was only right that all members should take a share in the work. Mr. I.lPsbx asked how a magistrate could sit oLatthe committee when he would have to adju e on cases when they came before the Bench. Councillor Roszzas said he had once been challenged as Chairman of the Education Com- mittee when a school case came before the Bench, and now he never adjudicated in such cases. • The resolution was adopted.

Joseph Hynes (32), of Garrett-street, Oldham- road, Miles Platting, Manchester, was crushed by a crane at the Bradford-road Gasworks of the Manchester Corporation. He was removed to Ancoats Hospital, where he lies in a serious condition.
EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1914.
Lymm Ward.
and 11. Thomas; T. B. Parry and J. Whitby; G. Warburton and H. Jones; P. J. Peters and L R. Barnes; G. H. Howard and W. Rouse; W. Boond and B. Elliott.
James Jolley, file cutter, Pepper-street, Lymm Proposed and seconded by G. Moston and G Eccleston.
_ William Kenneth Kershaw, farmer, "North- wood," Grammar School-road, Lymm. Pro- posed and seconded by H. S. Saville and C. Glea% e; Tames Gould and T. Ardern. Mr. C. E. COWPER'S CANDIDATURE.

_ Mr. C. E. Cowper is making a strong fight in the Booth's Hill Ward, where he is particularly well known. His election address clearly sets forth his views, and this address will be found advertised on our front page. Dealing with the gas question, he describes the gas supply as "a disgrace to an enlightened community." He promises to secure for the public the maximum of advantage at the mini- mum of cost, and to insist upon proper housing accommodation for the workpeople.

div.head: MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
div.p: MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.

, Efforts to Retain the Ceremony. ' Lymm, wake up !—your throne is in danger, for, owing to the lack of interest taken by the inhabitants in the May Day revels, the May Queen Festival Committee are not at present a very happy band. Although the village is becoming more and more up-to-date, it would be a pity if this old-world festival was discon- tinued, for no other reason than that Lymm's natural surroundings are quite in keeping with this ancient custom. With a view to re-kindling enthusiasm, a meeting is to be held in the Parish Schools on Tuesday, 'March 24th, when all interested are invited to be present The situation will be discussed, and a strong effort will be made to establish a sound financial basis. The officials consider that it would be a pity if the proceed- ings cannot be sustained, for there is not the slightest doubt that the children derive great enjoyment.

The festival is quite non-political and non- sectarian, so that all the village children par- ticipate. Besides being the means of providing pleasure, the festival, directly or indirectly, affects the tradespeople, as it is estimated that about 73 was spent in the village last year in preparations, and that a considerable sum was spent by visitors in refreshments. It is highly desirable that all the public-spirited men should show their love for quaint Lymin in doing all they can to keep the May Queen Festival afloat.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

Three Men in Trouble.—At an Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, John Thomas O'Kelly, James Finn and Martin Watson, no settled addresses, were charged with having been found on enclosed Premises at Hrappenhall Hall on Monday for an unlawful purpose.—Evidence of arrest was given, and Inspector Breese asked for a remand till the 24th inst.—This was agreed to.

div.head: TEA AND POLITICS. Liberals Spend a Pleasant Evening, With Speech, Mirth and Music. AVENUE OF POLITICAL PROGRESS.
div.p: TEA AND POLITICS. Liberals Spend a Pleasant Evening, With Speech, Mirth and Music. AVENUE OF POLITICAL PROGRESS.

• Mirth, music and pointed speeches combined to make the social gathering of the Orappe..- hall Liberals, held in the Methodist New Assem- bly Room, on Saturday night, a great success. A most enjoyable evening was spent. Addresses were given by Mr. P. M. Oliver and Alderman Middlewood (Bolton). At the splendid concert Which followed the tea, Mr. J. Kenworthy pre- sided. Mr. OLIVER had a hearty reception. He jocu- larly remarked that their tea reminded him of the Duke of Westminster's £l,OOO banquet, in- augurated to help the fuuds of the Tariff Re- form party. Ever since the banquet that cause had dwindled smaller and smaller, until now it had almost disappeared. Whether the banquet was responsible he could not say. (Laughter.) The latest scheme so far as he knew was that Mr. Boner Law proposed to put a ten per cent. tax on all manufactured goods and a larger tax upon luxuries.

To Make It Popular. That was an attempt to make Tariff Reform popular. By taxing the luxuries of the rich they were trying to cover up the old history of Tariff Reform, and the taxing of the food of the people. The Liberal party had a better way of taxing the rich. If they wanted to make wealth pay its share ,to the country they didn't want to tax luxuries which the rich man might buy or leave untouched; they taxed the rich man himself, and this the Liberal Government had done in the Budget of 1909. Referring to the Irish question Mr. Oliver spoke of e concessions which had been made by the Li .a.l Government during the week. It was neces yto remember that the Liberal party were in power, and Mr. Asquith had only to raise his finger to set the machinery in motion and the Home Rule Bill would go through as it stood that day. Not only were they in power, but they believed the measure to be a just one, for they had introduced safeguards against every conceivable fear that Ulster might have. Therefore, having the power, and believing in the justice of the measure, they could certainly drive it through, especially if they followed the example of their opponents.

Tories Did Not Consider. The Tories did not consider the Nonconform- ists in the Parliament of 1900 during the dis- cussion of the Education Bill, for they trampled Upon their feelings, and although they (the Tories) looked for the support of Ulster Non- conformists to-day, they thought as little of them as they did of the English Nonconformists. However, that was no reason why the Liberals ! should not seek ft settlement, and when Mr. Asquith made his concessions they expected that those concessions would be met in the spirit in which they were made, and if the Con- servative party refused them, them Home Rule would go through whatever might be the conse- quences. (Applause.) The question of Home Rule was practically settled, and they had to look into the future.

Avenue of Progress. The avenue of progress was made up of step after step in one continuous advance. Old age pensions had dealt with pauperism among the old, and National Insurance tried to deal with pauperism among the rest of the people, especially in the crusade against consumption, for it had been stated that one out of every three persons who died of consumption died in the workhouse. Mr. Sidney Webb had esti- mated that one-seventh of the whole expenditure of the Poor Law was caused directly or indi- rectly by consumption. The Insurance Act led to the housing question, and that in its turn led to the land question, for if they wanted houses they wanted land, and they wanted land where the people needed it, and at a price which the people could afford. Thus, through 'old age pen- sions and National Insurance there was a con- tinual advance to housing and land reforms. (Cheers.)

THE ENTERTAINERS. Mr. OLIVER proposed a comprehensive vote of thanks. This was seconded by Mr. NELSON and responded to by Mr. KENWORTRY. The excellent programme was well sustained by Mrs. J. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

People areleaving the Heath. The Swing Bridge is said to be The cause of so many removals. Thus have the "Heathens" got another grievance. • "When is the Parish Meeting to be held?" So inquires an interested resident. It is to be held on Thursday. A pretty tug boat race was seen • • Upon the Ship Canal the other day. • The beats had to slow down for • The bridge before the race was decided. Our local Sherlock Holmes made -A -discovery as a ship passed the bridge. "" Oranges!" he exclaimed, as the vessel passed, •• Making several prodigious sniffs of the air. He was right, for a reference to the Sailing list showed that the ship had come From a Spanish port, and her cargo Consisted entirely of boxes of oranges. Such a keen scent is wonderful. "Come back to Erin" a "Heathen" was Heard to warble in the early hours of Wed- nesday. He was coming home from St. Patrick's Ball. "What is it that can go up a spout down, "But cannot go down a spout up?" This is the latest conundrum which has been Testing the brains of a good many of the "Heathens." The answer is simple when you know it— Merely an umbrella, and if you don't believe, try it. A football match is to be played for charity. This takes place at the West-avenue ground On the morning of Easter Monday, and the "gate" Is to go to the Stockton Heath Nursing Asso- ciation. The contestants are Stockton Heath and Orford St. John's. Such a great match - well deserves a • great "gate." It has been said that Penketh holds a record, In that a bunch of roses was gathered in mid- December. Several gardeners in Stockton Heath, however, Gathered posies of roses on Christmas Day. Cah Penketh claim to equal this record?

Parish M eeti ng.—The long-awaited Parish Meeting ha.s been summoned for next Thursday evening, when the free and independent rate- payers are expected to pack the Church Room, which has been engaged for the meeting. Coun- cillor Whitley, chairman of the Parish Cbuncil, will preside, and the meeting is timed to start at 7.30 p.m.

Son Follows Father.—At a meeting of the managers of St. Thomas' Day Schools on Thurs- day evening, Mr. James Richardson was ap- pointed a manager in succession to his late father, who held the position for a considerable time. Amongst all classes of people in Stock- ton Heath the appointment will be appreciated as Mr. James Richardson is very popular.

Road Improvemdnt.—Several of the newer roads in Stockton Heath are now being made as promised by the District Council. Tar macadam is being 'chiefly employed, and when completed the roads will be. a marked improve- ' ment, and the customary grumbles beard at the Parochial Committee meetings will be heard no more.

Hospital Sunday.—Two of the Stockton Heath Nonconformist Churches celebrated Hospital Sunday last week-end.—the Independent Metho- dist and the Wesleyan. At both churches there were good congregations, morning and evening. At the Wesleyan Church the special preacher on Sunday evening was the Rev. W. A. Beckett, the Superintendent Minister of the Warrington Circuit.

Richmond's xtensions.—The announcement made in last week's "Examiner" that Messrs. Richmond are to take a section of their works to GraPPenhall and may finally remove all theft works to this side of the Canal aroused much interest amongst profierty and land owners in Stockton Heath. With a large number of workers at Grappenhall it is thought a great percentage would live in Stockton Heath. One builder is reported to have 'considered the ques- tion of building working-class cottages in the event of Messrs. Richmond developing as pro- ' mised, and it has also been mentioned that an effort may be made to get the trams extended to Grappenhall from Victoria-square. What thc, residents of the Grappenhall-road villas would say to that is another question.

A Hopeless Case.—At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday Herbert Wood, Stockton Heath, was charged on remand with obtaining food and lodgings to the value of 14s. from Mr. W. S. Roberts, 57, Wilderspool.causeway.—lt was alleged that prisoner said he was a clerk at Crosfield's. One morning, Mr. Roberts, being suspicious, accompanied the man from the house °ll the way to work. They met clerks from ! Crosfield's, and Mr. Roberts ascertained that he was not working there. Sergeant Holland received the prisoner into custody, and he said "Yes; it's true, but I will pay it. when I get work." His Parents were highly respectable people, said the Chief, and every effort has been made to make him lead a straight life. He is quite a hopeless case, although only a young man. His parents can do no good with him.— The Clerk: Have you anything to say?—Pris- oner: I am not working, you see, sir !—The Chairman: You don't want work.—The Chief: It is not the first or second time you have done this thing.—Wood was sent to prison for one month.

The body of a child aged five, named Veronica Flanagan, of Goodier's-buildings, Clayton- street, Ancoats, was recovered from the Roch- dale Canal at Manchester. It is believed that she fell into the water when washing her hands.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM YMM.

The Police Court was a record. There were, only two summonses. Is this due to the police "rest day "? Perhaps Lymmites are .becoming very good. If this state of affairs continue the Magistrates may yet get white gloves. The justices were surprised to learn That sheepdogs are good for ratting. Their doggie education seems to have been neglected. Collies often prove better ratters than terriers. The May Queen festival may be continued Despite the rumour -that it was to be stopped. An appeal has been issued td the good Lymra- ites To lend their aid in continuing the festival. Let the appeal meet with a strong response.
On the Bench.—The magistrates at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday were the Hon. J. E. Cross (in the chair), Mr. E. G. Groves and Mr. S. Davies.
Police on Short Time.—There was a very small court at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday, when only two summonses were heard.
New Police Sergeant.—Sergeant Davies, who is to succeed Sergt. Washington in the 1,9111 m Police Force, is expected to take up his duties on April let.

Cycling Offence.—At- the Lymm Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday, a young man named James Griffin was fined 2s. 6d., including costs, for rid- ing a bicycle on a footpath in Warburton on March 12.—P.C. liilditch proved the case.

Hospital Sunday.—The annual sermons and offertories in connection with Hospital Sunday took place at the Lymm Parish Church on Sunday. The Rev. F. C. Bozman, of St Alban's, Broadheath, preached to a large con- gregation at the evening service. The offer- tories amounted to £l5 17s. 10d.

Lads' Club Concert.—There was a good attend- ance at the Drill Hall on Thursday night on the occasion of the entertainment in aid of the. Lymin Lads' Club. The whole of the pro- gramme was provided by Messrs. Edward 11. Lingard and Nelson Thorn. The former artiste is a well-known entertainer at the piano, and his contributions consisted of a large num- ber of humorous songs, monologues, whistling solos, and anecdotes. Mr. Nelson Thorn gave some clever exhibitions of conjuring and ventri- loquism; his impersonating or shadowgraph item being also well executed.

, .Matiiiee Concert —Many of our readers, we ' think, will have received invitations to the concert which is to be held this afternoon in the Baptist Schoolroom, Higher-lane. An excellent and varied programme has been arranged, provided by artistes who are, in most eases, well known to Lymm and district, and we feel confident that a really enjoyable formance will be given. We wish the promoter of this concert every success. The proceeds a the silver collection which will be taken up are in aid of the Baptist Sustentation Fund. The concert is to commence promptly at 3.15 p.m. Collies as Ratters.—Richard Willow, of Mas- sey Hall Cottages, Thelwall, was charged at the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday with allow- ing two dogs to be on the road with collars with- out the name and address thereon. He pleaded guilty.—P.C. Atherton stated that on February 17 he was on duty in Thelwall when he saw two dogs wearing collars minus name and ad- dress, and as he was taking them to the Lymirt Police Station defendant followed him and claimed the dogs.—Defendant stated that he had loaned the dogs to a neighbour for ratting. The dogs were collies.—The Clerk: Sheep dogs for ratting?—Yes.—Defendant was fined is. in each case.

- ----- Christian Endeavour Anniversary. The Primitive Methodist Christian Endeavour Societies held their anniversary services last week-end. Mr. A. N. Shimmin was the preacher at the Sunday morning and evening services. His text on the latter occasion was "That I may know Him and the power of His resurrec- tion," from which he preached a powerful ser- mon on progressive endeavourism. On Monday evening Miss Welford presided over a public meeting, which was addressed by Mr. Sandford, of Liverpool, on the subject of "The Floating Christian Endeavour Movement." In giving the reason for the formation of this branch of endeavour work, the speaker said that there was no class of men more neglected by the Christian Church than the Christian seamen. Their isolation from church association, in the case of Navy men, for periods abroad of even five years, called for some•organisation which would link up the seamen in Christian comradeship. Mr. Sandford claimed that this was the main object of the Floating Christian Endeavour Movement. Letter writing is one of the prim- ary methods by which this is achieved, and the speaker testified, both from personal experi- ence and letters he read, to the value of Christian correspondence. Miss Eva Tonge contributed the solo "If any little word of mine." Police Sergeant Retires.—References were made at the conclusion of the business at the Lymm Petty Sessions 011 Wednesday to the ser- vices of Sergt. Washington, whose retirement is pending._ -Tne Hon. ,y. E. Cross, on behalf of the justices, said how very much they on the Bench regretted to lose the sergeant, but at the same time they could heartily congratulate him upon the work he had done, and into his retirement he carried their good wishes. He understood that was the last time they would have the pleasure of seeing him on duty. The sergeant had kept Lymm in order sometimes under very difficult circumstances, and they considered the place had been thoroughly well looked after, and lie had carried out his duties with fairness and justice to all. They wished him long life and happiness.—The Clerk (Mr. H. L. Harris), on behalf of the officers of the Court, added his Praise. The officer had been of considerable help in the performance of the duties of the Court.—Mr. John R. Newton, farmer, Warbur- ton, spoke on behalf of the agriculturists in the district, who had been looked after very closely by the worth); sergeant. They were sorry he was to leave them, because whenever he had to do with infectious diseases he was always ready to help the agriculturists, although he kept the law to the letter.—Supt. Sutherland said he was sorry that Sergt. Wash- ington was leaving, because he could always be assured that Drat police section was well organ- ised. In his private life the retiring officer had always been an example to other men, and a credit to the constabulary. He was glad he was not leaving the district.—Sergt. Washington thanked them for their expressions, and their good wishes. A native of Middlewich, Mr. Washington was first stationed in the Wirral Peninsular, where, after spending a short time at New Brighton and Egremont, he was transferred to Mottram- in-Longdendale. After a brief term at the latter place he passed on to Dukinfield, where he stayed eight years. A period of five yearr. at Hazel Grove next followed, and then, after serving for a short time as Acting-Sergeant at Booth's Hill, Lymm, he was made sergeant at Altrincham, a position he ably occupied for nearly eight years. Lymm was the next move.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—The usual meeting was held on Thursday evening, when an interesting and instructive paper on " Cornish Scene and- Cornish Story" was given by Mr. W. A. Birchen, of Leigh, formerly a resident in the Padgate neighbourhood, and a devoted workei in the church. Mr. Newton presided.

Death of Mrs. John Hamblet.—Mrs. llamblet, of Summerfield House, Padgate, who had been ailing for a considerable time, passed away last week. The interment took place at Warrington, Cemetery last Friday afternoon. The Rev. E. Morgan conducted a service in the Wesleyan Chapel, Padgate, prior to proceeding to the Cemetery. The hymns used were "There is a land of pure delight" and "Brief life is here our portion." Amongst those attending the funeral were: Mr. John Hamblet (husband), Mr. Richard llamblet (son), Messrs. div.p: PEN K ETH.

American Tea.—The members of the Ladies' Sewing Meeting connected with the Penketh Wesleyan Church held an American tea on Thursday afternoon in the Wesleyan Sunday Schools. After the tea an entertainment was submitted, and the following took part, viz.: The Misses Dodds, Murray, Moston and Piggott (Warrington). The proceeds realised the hand- some sum of ..t.22, which is to be devoted to the School Renovation Fund.
WINwICK.

Swine Fever Outbreak.—An outbreak of fever has occurred on the main farm a't wick County Asylum. Only a few pig!, affected, but as the disease is very coot' it was decided to kill the whole herd, culls of 160 pigs.
Ex-Asylum Steward Dead.—The death place on Monday of Mr. Henry Ellis, of penhall, who was steward at the County Asylum from the time it was c until his retirement in 1913. The funerb

and was conducted by the Rev. H. V. Fig° Asylum Authorities were represented b Dutton, the clerk and steward; Dr. 13. c deputy medical officer; the Rev. F. W. C. wick, chaplain; and Mr. Davies, the ele engineer. Wreaths were sent from the officials at the Asylum.

SHAKESPEARE'S COLLEAGUES. Let us. take a closer view of the men who figure on the Shoreditch tablet, and see wherein their fame and glory rest. To James Burbage, carpenter, belongs the honour of building the first English playhouse. rravelling players ad moving shows there had been before, but never before a building that by any kind of accurate speech could be called a theatre. Here, at Shoreditch, assailed by Puritans and clergy, and wall the Lord Mayor appealing to the Privy Council to suppress the evil thing. Burbage braved oppoSition and gave the multitude what it wanted. One definite achievement stands to his credit. He gave status .to the actor. The "stager had been in England pretty much what he was in the Roman Empire, a pariah and an outcast, classed with rogues and social pests. James Burbage, by getting a Royal patent for his company, lifted his players to a new social level, and it was not long before Queen Elizabeth was visiting Shoreditch to see them. Burbage's two sons were chips off the old block. Cuthbert became his partner in theat- rical ventures, and Richard took to the "beards" as a duck takes to water. When young Will Shakespeare came to London and :drifted into the theatrical world these were his companions and friends. When he took to writing plays they were written for Burbage's wooden barn, and took shape accordingly; and the ,first man to play "Othello," " Daudet," and "Richard III." was Richard Burbage. Much more unlikely names for an ecclesias- tical tablet are the trio that conic next. William Somers was Court Jester to henry VIII., hated of Wolsey, yet loved of the poor, a quaint figure 'done up in scarlet,and green, whose first stage was the steps of Henry's throne, and whose last was that of the Globe Theatre. Richard Tarlton was born later and was fun- maker to Queen Elizabeth. Not indeed as Court jester, but as one of her players. The 11 original of Yorrick, Dick Tarlton was, by com- mon absent, the cleverest humorist of the day. The face pushed through the curtain was :enough; "he made the people laugh exceedingly . when he peejit out his head." Gabriel Spencer • was an actor of the :Rose Theatre, and was killed by Ben Jenson in a duel. Of William Sly and Richard Coivley we know little, save that they were players at the Globe. THE GLOBE THEATRE.
We may follow this brief and very insufficient glance at some of Shakespeare's colleagues by a

Juliet would first look down upon Romeo. At the back of the stage hung a curtain cut ' with numerous slits, and hearing over each opening a label containing a name. The names were those ox the characters in the play. Thus in " Othello Jago would alWays enter through um own slit and Desdewona through hers. The label told the audience the name of the actors as they ,appeared. . A Very good point of vantage in the theatre was the end of the stage. This was usually occw pied by the dandies of the hour, who lured stools and sat, dressed at their best, in full view of the audience. IA the picture they smoke and jest while the actors shed imaginary blood not half a dozen strides away, * There were no waits in the 'Shakespearean -theatre. And as more than half the audience were standing, there must be no dull patches. A trumpet blast announced the beginning and the play moved steadily to the end. Of course,-there was no scenery to shift and no ;orchestra to beguile blank moments. The construction of Shakespeare's plays is hereby explained. It will be noted that there is generally a sub-plot carried through by separate actors. The acenes alternate with those of the main story, and give the chief actors a little breathing time. Women were not allowed upon the stage •in Elizabethan times, and their -parts were taken, by boys. May not this explain the fact that Shakespeare • gave so little prominence to his women? It has been said that though lie has delineated wonderful men, his women are all alike, expressing, us a rule, simple things and ordinary sentiments. But what really great Part could be placed upon a boy? If women had acted, and there had been a female counter- part of Richard Burbage, who an guess what characters would have adorned. his already matchless plays: But if Shakespeare had to manage with makeshift queens upon the stage, he had the compensation of a real queen in his audience. Elizabeth often sat where the picture shows her,- in the centre of the gallery. With the queen among the auditors it was legitimate to adorn the Wall with • a Hercules, a Globe, and the Royal letters " Ell." The actors' days of vagabondage were over. A new era dawned, and Will Shakespeare made money. •

A Memorial to Dick Burbage Suggests a
Description of the Globe Theatre.
HOW SHAKESPEARE'S PLAYS WERE STAGED.
By ARTHUR

If ghosts have ears there would be a cheery company of the disembodied ones in the neigh- bourhood of Shoreditch last Monday morning, for, in the presence of a brilliant throng, Sir George Alexander unveiled a memorial in the, Parish Church to the memory of some of Shakespeare's fellow-actors. Perhaps the reader had better be introduced ' to them in the stately language of the mural tablet. Here' is the inscription :

" This stone is placed here to the •Glory of God and in acknowledgment of the work done for English Drama by the players, musi- cians, and other men of the theatre who are buried within the precincts of this Church, and in particular to the memory of those who are named below. JAMES BURBAGE (d. 1597), a joiner by trade and the head of Lord Leicester's players, who in 1576 font in Shoreditch the first English playhouse. CUTHBERT BURBAOE (d. 1636), his son, who in 1599 built in Southwark the famous Globe playhouse. RICHARD BURBAGE.(d. 1619), also his son, the great tragedian, and the first actor to play the parts of Richard 111. and Hamlet. WILLIAM SOMERS (d. 1560), Court Jester to Henry VIII. RICHARD TARLTON (d. 1588), One of Queen Elizabeth's players, and the foremost comic actor of his time. GABRIEL SPENCER (d. 1598), a player at the Rose Theatre. . WILLIAM SLY (d. 160, and RICHARD COWLEY (d. 1619), players at the Globe Theatre. Erected by subscription in 1914. Stewart D. HeaCam, Chairman of. Committee, Lon- don Shakespeare League."
It is safe to say that whatever else their own age might have expected, it would never have expected to see those names upon a tablet in

survey of the famous theatre, where they " fretted their little hour," and ,amused: Eliza-, bethan London. Of ..the Globe Theatre we are able to give a very interesting picture. It is shown: in its palmy days, when royal purple adorned the gallery and Queen. Elizabeth watched the play. A knowledge of the building will be of great help to those who desire to understand Shakes- peare. Elizabethan theatres, it may be ex- Plained, were built of wood, or lath and plaster. The wooden walls, resting on a. brick founda- tion, were carried up forty or fifty feet high, and would be as beautiful as modern bill-posting stations.. There was no roof, but curved rafters bent inwards at the top of the walls and gave some little protection from the weather. This portion was covered with thatch, and there was a projecting thatched roof to cover the stage. A gallery was carried round three sides of the building. ,This accommodated the gentle folks, who sat between partitions in what were called " Twoe pennie roomes" (places) and "Gentle Iloomes." The gallery folks, in return for their lordy twopences, enjoyed some protection from the weather. No so "the pit." The centre was open to the sky, and the multitude must take the chances of bad weather. , There were no , seats, but there were rushes to stand on, and a play a Shakespeare's on the stage. The ad- mission fee .was a penny. It would have been ungracious to grumble.

The stage was a broad platform projecting into the "yard." ' There was little attempt at scenery. A large label, to be deciphered in our Picture, was unfurled to, tell the audience whether the scene was laid in a palace or in the open field, and their imagination was ex- pected to. do the rest. div.head: FIRST INTERPRETER OF SHAKESPEARE.
div.p: THE FIRST INTERPRETER OF SHAKESPEARE.
Perhaps ,there is room to quote the speech of Sir George Alexander (for we are in the new era, in which actors get knighted), made at the unveiling of the mendirial last•Nlonday.

Sir George said "that to be associated with that honour and reverence paid to the Eliza- bethan actors whose bones lay there, and more especially to James and Richard Burbage, was to be associated with the very core and essence of his craft. They could not say how great Shakespeare's chief players were, and it was certain that there were others of whose memory as actors posterity thought more. But in the history of acting as a profession and of the theatre with its growing dignity and rttpute these men were pre-eminently important. " James Burbage (lid two things. By securing a Royal patent for his company—` The Earl of Leicester's servants '—he took the first impor- tant 'step- in transferring the actor from the positioh of a rogue and vagabond in the eyes of society into a citizen like other citizens, entitled like the rest to the respect of his fellows as long as his conduct deserved it. The other thing James Burbage did was to build and keep going, in the face of every, sort of discouragement, difficulty, sacrifice, and loss the first enclosed theatre in the country. It was also his great good, fortune, to work for and with the greatest dramatist and poet the world had known. Ile wondered sinnetimes if he had any idea of the privilege or whether he took Shakespeare into a corner and picked holes in hi's work as some present-,day actor-managers were said to do with the leading authors. It was the great luck of his son to be the first interpreter of Shakes- peare's; genius, so that James and Richard Bur- bage, and in a lesser degree the others whoM they commemorated, were closely associated niith the art and the work of the greatest genius
