div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS
div.p: WORLD OF LETTERS
Literary Gleanings.
THE ACT OF UNION. ~..

There was no mandate for the passing by the Irish Parliament of the Act of thiion. The Irish Parliament, which was elected when there was no question of a Union, transferred its own rights and the rights of its constituents to an- other Legislature, and the Act was hccomplished without any appeal to the electors by a disso- lution. In the Scottish Union debates it was strongly urged that the members of the Scot- tish Parliament had no moral competence to destroy their Legislature. The objection was met by the statement that the last Scottish Parliament was summoned by proclamation in- timating that it was to treat of a Union, and that " being sent up for that declailed purpose by their `constituents there remained no occa- sion to demand any other instructions from them."--J. G. Swift Mac Neil, M.P., in the March " Contemporary Review."

div.head: NORWAY'S ANXIETY.
div.p: NORWAY'S ANXIETY.

I find myself possessed of a message from the Norwegian people to the West of Europe, which it seems my duty, to convey. The heart of that message is that Norway, in common with Sweden and the other little peoples of Northern Europe; is at present over- shadowed with a deep, grave and increasing anxiety as to her national security. That , anxiety is not so much official as national, and I found it more in the people than in the Gov- ernment. But it pervades the whole life of Norway, and unless something happens to allay or remove this anxiety it may Shave deplorable results in the diversion of the national energies from her present splendid industrial and social developments.—Harold Spender, in the "Con- temporary Review" for March.

div.head: MOST FAMOUS SONG.
div.p: THE MOST FAMOUS SONG.

Therecannot be the least doubt whatever that the most famous song in the world, judged by its being known in the most lands and by the most varied nations, and by its being one of the oldest and most widely sung ditties ever known, is that which has for its first line, " Mar Through s'en va-t-en gnerre"; which, if we were to give the English version of it, instead of the older French words, would be, " Marl- borough goes away to the war." n But you say, " That the most famous song in the world? Why, we must be dreaming! We never even heard of it! What about our grand old ' Home, sweet home' ? What about 'God save the King' ? What about 'Auld lang sync' ? And what about .the ' Marseillaise' ? Why, we've known and sung these all our lives, so sto speak, and they are heard in every •coun- try ; whereas that song you've just mentioned —bless us, we don't even know the first line of it !" Yes, it does sound funny, doesn't it? But wait till you've read this; then we'll see what YOU say! There can be no doubt that if you took any hundred people in England. and asked them what was the most famous and best-known song in the world, they would all select one of the four you yourself spoke of just now. The Scotsman would swear by " Auld tang vile," and would have some good reason on his side; the Englishman would probably go solid for " Home, sweet borne," finding the Scotsman willing to put that second; the. Frenchman would plump for the " Marseillalse"; whilst both the English and the Scots would acknow- lec:ge that the great French song might well claim high place. But nobody, not a: single man out of all the hundred, unless he were a specially knowing person, would ever venture to suggest that " Marlborough " was the most famous, the most widely known. the most often sung, and hind by far the most glorious traditions amongst all the songs of the world's many and varied countries. Yet it unquestionably is so; and that you've acknowledged yourself many a time, though you've not known it! Yes, you have! For, I repeat again, there has never been such a popular song as " Malbrook," and you your- self have agreed to this often and often when you have sung so enthusiastically and heartily the song's splendid refrain: For he's a jolly good fellow, For he's a jolly good fellow, For he's a jolly. good fellow,
And so say all of as! —From " What is the World's Most Famous Song?" in "Chambers 's Journal."

div.head: APOLLO BELVEDERE.
div.p: THE APOLLO BELVEDERE.

We do not feel like assigning this statue to Praxiteles, and compared with the great Hermes of Praxiteles it becomes a lesser thing; but many believe it to be the-work of a contempo- rary of Praxiteles, one of the same school; and working with the same ideals, but without quite so masterly a touch. The statue is to studied especially' for its sense of movement. In studying the Victory of Samothrace we noticed, too, the effect of movement, the swift victorious movement of a figure just alighted on the prow of an on-bearing ship; but the movement shown in the Apollo Belvedere is of another kind. Look at the sculpture carefully and you will see that it steps and glides; it walks; the left foot raised, the right foot not heavily borne upon. but only lightly, so that there seems no strong centre of balance in the marble itself; this has much to do with this peculiarly lifelike effect of walk- ing. Also, the length of the legs, a little too long, you think, for the slender lifelike body, adds to the effect of motion and easy gliding. But note, too, that this is not the walking of mortal being; it is not walking as you and I would walk; it is the easy progress of a being of some superior race; a peculiar gliding ease, as though the feet touched the ground because they would—not because they must. This adds singularly to its effect, not only as' a statue, but especially as a statue of Apollo, as we shall see later. . .

'The two hands are restorations. They are generally thought to be too long. The original sculptor, it j believed, purposely made the legs of the Apollo longer than those Of a natural body, so as to heighten the sense of motion- and gliding; but the restorer, missing this point. has made the wrists and hands longer, better to correspond with the length of the legs. To most of us the Apollo would seem more beautiful if the hands were slightly smaller. The. pose is that of an archer; the left band holds the stock of the bow; the right has just sprung back from snapping the bowstring; the arrow has just flown. The head of the god is turned in the direction of the arrow's flight, and his eyes follow it with interest; but the pride' of the wbele face, especially of the lips. and the whole lift of the head, leaves us no doubt the arrow has flown true to its mark. A more human archer might bend forward a little to make sure, but this greatest of all archers, whose shafts are the very light of the sun itself. needs 110 such assurance; he well knows the arrow has flown true. The statue" is wonderful in the beauty. the pride, the assurance, the poise of the whole cx- ull isite figure.—" The Girls' Paper and Women's Magazine."

div.head: HOW CONJURERS REHEARSE.
div.p: HOW CONJURERS REHEARSE.

There is an old saying among conjurers that it is impossible for a performer to know a trick thoroughly well until every- thing that can possibly go wrong with it has gone wrong—in front of an audience. Robert Houdin, the famous French conjurer, used to say that the chief test of a conjurer was his ability to get out of a mishap. At such a time the conjurer must not Ehow that anything unusual has happened; he must bring his trick to som3 sort of conclusion even though the climax of the trick turns out to be quite different from the correct one. THE APPARATUS.

With this knowledge in his mind the con- jurer starts his rehearsal. We will suppose that lif3 has decided upon performing a cer- tain trick, with the secret ot which he is more or less familiar. His first step is to make him- self acquainted with the machinery of the apparatus that he is going to yea. Some of the most effective tricks, to the general pub- lic., are quits simple "to work," but only a highly finished performer can present them in such a way that they seem to be really mysterious. It is quite possible, therefore, that this business of finding out "how the wheels go round" will not occupy much of the conjurer's time. Having learned the purely mechanical part of the business the conjurer leaves the appar- atus alone for a little time while h sets to work to think out the best way of presenting the trick to an ordinary audience. There is a great art in getting every little bit of effect out of a trick. In other words, the trick should be shown in such a way that the youngest and dullest inembor of the audi- ence will understand, without any effort of the .mind, exactly what the trick any to be.

In the hands of a clever and original per- former a small, insignificant piece of magic may be made to appear as an unfathomable mystery, for in conjuring, as in some other things, it is not so much what you do that matters as what you can persuade other peo- ple that you do. This part of the conjur- er's rehearsal—thinking out the best way to show the trick—will test his abilities as a "showman." Many conjurers are excellent , performers so far as the manipulation of such things as coins, cards, balls, etc. are eon_ cerned, but they will never be brilliant per- formers, never at the top of the tree, be- cause they do not know how to present a tricic in such a way that it is thoroughly nteresting to an audience from start to fin- ish. Sometimes a conjurer in a big way of business (he usually calls himErlf an illur sionist) will call in the services of an expert " producer "to assist him with suggestions during this part of the rehearsal.

div.head: GOOD "PATTER."
div.p: GOOD "PATTER."

Next comes the question of "'Atter "—the words that the conjurer is going to say when he is performing. Good patter is half a trick. The amusing little witticisms which a good conjurer appears to he making up on the spur of the moment are all caretully thought out beforehand and learned by heart. The careful ,performer also .has a little spare "patter" to be used in Case of emergency, when some mishap may occur. At such a time the conjurer needs all his wits to extricate himself from the difficulty, and if he were compelled to think of something to say when he was also trying to cover up his mistake he would probably end by remaining silent and giving the trickaway. Having got all his words written down the conjurer studies them just as carefully as an actor studies his part, but with one great difference of method. The conjurer has to de- vise his own stage directions. These, as will be seen, are 'very important. One of the axioms of ccrnjuring is that there is a weak point in every trick; it is the time when the trick has really been accom- plished, although possibly the audience will not be aware of anything having happened until some minutes afterwards. Our best con- jurers are such good actors that the weak points of their tricks are never noticed by their audiences; they succeed in distracting people's attention just at the critical mo- ment, although they may not appear to be doing anything of the kind. 'iheir move- ments are all quite natural, and they never give one the idea that they are trying to hide anything. Lastly, when the conjurer is thoroughly ac- quainted with the mechanical part of his trick or, if the trick is one of pure sleight of hand. with the manipulation of the arti- cles used in the trick, and knows all his "patter" thoroughly, he performs the trick an speaks the words at the same time, lie usually does this in front of a looking-glass so that he may correct any m'stake as he gees along. Still better than a glass is a friend who knows something about conjuring but who is ab'.e to look at ji trick from the point of view of an ordinary member of an audience. The friend must be trustworthy, capable of keeping a secret. The rehearsal of a trick in this way may oentinue for hours, for the performer must not rest content until the mechanical part of the trick works smoothly, and he can oper- ate it without having to think of what he is doing. Also, he must know his "patter" so well that he can deliver the lines with pro- per effect and exactly at the right time. A conjurer who is going to perform before children will prepare himself for all kinds of interruptions during a trick. Children are much quicker than adults in discovering just "how it is done" and unless they are. re- strained by their elders they will not be slow in imparting their newly acquired knowledge, in shrill voices, to the rest of the audience.

div.head: IMAGINARY REHEARSALS.
div.p: IMAGINARY REHEARSALS.

When once a trick has been thoroughly learned the conjurer can have several "imag- inary rehearsals" while he is out walking or riding on a 'bus. To do this he has to see the trick, in imagination, and to go over all the movements and whisper all the patter to himself. The late Charles Bertram used to rehearse parts of his new tricks while he was walking in the streets, and in his own room he would often "run through" a trick without using any of the apparatus, but of course few conjurers of to-day have the abili- ties of Bertram, and not all those would get much benefit by rehearsing in that way. As a rule, the "imaginary rehearsals" that are carried on in the street must always be sup- plemented by the most strict rehearsals at home. during which the tricks are presented exactly as they will be before an audience. When a conjurer has learned a new trick thoroughly he will try and discover what parts of it are liable to go wrong. He has to prepare himself for emergencies. Some- thing may break at a critical moment. What is he going to do then ? Something may not "act' exactly at the right moment, or an assistant, out of sight of the audience, ma's be careless with his work, and, unless the conjurer is fully prepared for such a mishap, the performance will be a ludicrous failure. ,How is the conjurer to remain with a smiling •face before his audience, and finish the trick in some other way, and leave the audience in ignorance of the fact that they have not seen the real trick? It will be seen that the rehearsal of only one trick, lasting, periaaps, only five or six will get together a number of tricks over and over again. He is able t minutes, may occupy a good deal of time, and it is for this reason that few conjurers trouble to alter their repertoire of tricks. A scoamnjenrterrioks ov dbceiecsa because he hhe „au ssrtunaililyy rehearses has a and will content himself with performing the audience at every performance. Still, as every conjurer must keep his tricks up to date bye has to make a few chances oee,"ionaily. auld I thr:e new tricks and substitutes same number of o:der tricks, rthem for the ycl:henthhies would go through the hard, grinding conjurers learning an entirely new programme work of all, no rehearsal is of the same After conjurer as a performance of a vta.ue to the aa audience, and it is for this r rick before reason that a man's oldest tricks are usually which he scores his areatest those with arsedsiff:nre.onoort

div.head: ONLY ONE WEEK MORE.
div.p: ONLY ONE WEEK MORE.

My Dear Children,— I would like to remind you that our competition closes to-day week, when all essays must be sent in. The subject is: " What I would like to do during the Easter Holidays, and why." I hope to have a large number of !essays sent in. One has already reached me as I write, but I expect many more, and if you have not written your essay please do so and send it not later than next Saturday. Below I. publish a few conundrums from Nephew Fred Shelley, for which he is thanked.
Your loving

div.head: UNCLE JACK.
div.p: UNCLE JACK.
SOME CONUNDRUMS.
Dear Uncle Jack,—Will you please oblige me by putting these riddles in the " Children's. Corner," if room?
What three words did Adam use to introduce himself to Eve which read backward and for- ward the same? Madam, I'm Adam. When is a bonnet not a bonnet? When it becomes a woman.
FRED SHELLEY.
ALBERT'S QUEST.
Albert was sent down by his mother to get some horse-radish" which she needed for her pickles.
After quite an absence, he came back home, tired and empty-handed. , "Well, where is the horse-radish?" asked his mother.
" Why, mother, I went to every livery-stable in town, and they didn't have a bit," mur- mured Albert, with a weary sigh.

div.head: MY OLD HOME.
div.p: MY OLD HOME.

_ The waves of time may roll in a fast increasing tide, And the sorrows of the years come flooding far and wide, But a sweet, undying dream comes before my eager gaze, A vision of my home, of my childhood's happy days.

The brown thatched cottage nestling 'mid the verdant Devon With the little latticed window, near which the blackbird trills, And the honeysuckle blossom that kissed the tiny pane, All whisper of the old home I ne'er shall see again.
The crimson rambler roses that clustered round the door, The broken flagstone path, with the pansies nod- ding o'er, The little wooden gate that swung idly to and fro,
Come before my eager fancy as the days of long ago.

The peat smoke rising softly to the azure sum- mer sky, From the little blackened chimney round which the nestlings fly, And oh ! the hills !—I see them now, where often I have lain By yonder brook and watched around the golden fields of grain,

Where the ripened beads were swaying at the fancy of the wind, And the summer shadows sported with the play- things they could find, And the drowsy hum of insects had lulled me oft. to sleep, By the little babbling brooklet, where the frog and lizard creep.

And far amid the hills comes an echo, slow and clear, Froza the bells at eventide as they ring o'er marsh and mere. And the sweet chimes through the trees, how they softly come and go, Bringing back the olden times, the days of long ago.

A COUNTRY FAIR. In the beginning of August, I had the pleas Lire of journeying to that lovely summer resort, St. Andrews, and while there had the great pleasure of witnessing a real, old-fashioned country fair. This fair commenced in real earnest on Saturday night, and lasted till Tues- day, the fun waxing long and merrily. What with cinematographs, hobby-horses, motors, donkeys, lighthouses, boxing booths, shooting ranges, swinging boars, sweetie stalls, and hostg of other good things, the streets were both lively and picturesque.

On Saturday and Monday nights the streets were packed with merry-makers, but Tuesday eclipsed these nights altogether, for into the "Market" (as it is called) trooped the ,coun- try gentlemen, farmers and ploughmen, all in- tent on enjoying themselves. Looking along the streets anyone who has never seen this fair before is amazed, for as far as the eye can see are carts, bearing troops of laughing-faced chil- dren, men and women, from the smallest child to the oldest grandmother, all bent on making the most of this public holiday. After stabling their horses they are to be seen wending their way to " Logie's-lane," where the young men and women dance to the musical strains of the city band. By-and-bye a young ploughman linked up with a blushing servant lass, will make his way through the crowd, and after paying the small sum charged for each dance, join in the Scotch reel or other dance with the greatest of good humour. Having danced a good deal of leather off their shoes, away they will go, along South- street or Market-street, as the case may be, stopping to try their luck at the shooting ranges, hoop-la, or with the Japanese sailor quoits, los- ing more money in a cbuple of hours than they could earn in a couple of weeks. Soon after they adjourn to the motors, hobby-horses, don- keys, and lighthouses, all of which receive a goodly share of the ploughmen's hard-earned money, esPecially the donkeys, over whose heads many of them are thrown. Turning from these, the first thing they hear " Hi! hi! hi!" and looking round they see a negro in the act of eating a lump of coal, wash- ing that down with a draught of paraffin mixed with sawdust, pins and needles. div.head: HOUSEHOLD CAVALRY.
div.p: THE HOUSEHOLD CAVALRY.

The Household Cavalry consists of three regi- ments, two of which, in scarlet, are the Life Guards, the third being the Royal Horse Guards. The horse Guards are not the Life Guards, and the Life Guards are not the Horse Guards, as we frequently hear them called. In precedence they rank first in the British Army; and they are, and always have been, worthy of their position. The Life Guards originated in the two troops of exiled cavaliers formed by Charles the Second in Holland in the year before the Restoration. These were the King's Troop and the Duke of York's Troop, and to them were added the Duke of Albemarle's, which soon became the Queen's Troop. To these the Scottish Troop was added at the Union of England and Scotland, and the four troops be- came two in 1746. In 1788 the Horse Grenadiers, dating in their earliest form from 1678, were amalgamated with them, the First Troop of Life Guards and Horse Grenadiers becoming the First Regiment of Life Guards; and the Queen's Troop of Life Guards and Second or Scottish Horse Grenadiers became the Second Regiment of Life Guards. Both the old Life Guard troops distinguished themselves in the campaign of William the Third, and the second was at Walcourt under Nlarlborough in 1689. There is an erroneous notion that the Household Cavalry have only begun to be sent abroad during recent years, but their duty as the Sovereign's bodyguard took them to the Continent in their early days. In 1812, squadrons from each regiment were attached to Wellington's army in the Penin- sula and continued with it until the close of the campaign in the South of France; and in a similar way they were represented at Waterloo in the following year, in Egypt in 1882, and in South Africa during the Boer War. They abandoned cuirasses in 1698 and went without them for 123 years, when they were reintroduced at the Coronation of George the Fourth ; like those of the Horse Guards, they have never been worn on active service. The cuirass, it may be interesting to know, weighs 101 b. 120 z., and the helmet 31b. 70z., the horse appointments, with the cloak, weighing Get. 1111 b.; and not so many years ago, when the average weight of the troopers was 12st. 91b. 70z., the horse carried 3171 b. 14oz. That is no longer the case, how- ever; heavy cavalry are not now so heavy, the horses being lighter in build and the men lighter, the biggest men being not in the House- hold Cavalry, but in the King's Company of the Grenadier Guards.—W. J. Gordon in "The Boy's Own Paper."

div.head: NATURALISTS' AMBITIOUS PROJECT.
div.p: NATURALISTS' AMBITIOUS PROJECT.

At a meeting of Lancashire and Cheshire Naturalists at the Manchester University on Saturday, it was decided to form a committee to take steps for the collection and publication of records relating to the fauna of the two coun- ties. The natural history societies and field clubs of Lancashire and 'Cheshire are to be asked to undertake a systematic survey of the district covered by 'their activities, and to col- lect and preserve regularly the various forms of animal life found. It is hoped that all the local museums in Lancashire and Cheshire will be- come possessed of a series of authentically named specimens of the fauna of their district.

The death is announced at Walshaw, Burr, of Mr. Richard Nolllett, for several years police superintendent at Bury and for 44 years a mem- ber of the Lancashire County Constabulary, and who retired in 1910.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21, 1914.

death. Jack speedily found out where the trouble lay, and set to work to free him. But he also found that as fast as he freed one part another would get entangled, and all the time he had a growing conviction that the conditions at that depth were very different from any he had experienced before. The great pressure of the water made itself Felt more and more, there was a singing in his zars, and he began to suffer from headache. I Presently, when he thought he had nearly freed Herron's lines, he suddenly discovered that his own bad beome entangled. Then there began a terrible fight for life— for his own as well as for Mat's. As fast as he disentangled the lines or tubes in one place the swirl of the current carried the"' against wreckage in another, and the Wel st. bad to be commenced all over again. Ms - worst of it was that Herron, who was up on the deck, while Jaclewas now working below him, was so situated that he could not help at all. He dared not move, but had to remain in the one place hour after hour, watching and waiting, while his would-be rescuer toiled and strove, wrestled with the difficulties of ' he situation, and persevered with eeemingly tireless persistence in his endeavours to save Jack Gale understood now, for the first time, why all the other experienced divers had not volunteered. He perceived why it was that even the rich rewards held out by the owners had failed to tempt them, and he began to feel sore against Mat, considering that it was his greed which had led to their both being in this awful peril. More than once he debated with himself whether he should make a hauling-line fast round the old man and himself, and signal to those above to haul him up, and then cut the air-tubes and lines, trusting to their both being hauled up before they were suffocated. But each time the idea occurred to him he decided that it would be too perilous. His head began to feel as if it must burst, and once or twice it seemed to swim and he nearly lost consciousness. And then, at last. when he had almost given up all hope, 114 foinid that the tide was slackenin. He ha" be en working down there so long that the ebb was near, which meant that the current would practically shortly fall away altogether. Revived by the hope that this put into him he started with fresh energy, and at last had the satisfaction of getting all the tubes and lines clear and finding that they remained so. Tluzel he gave the signal to haul up, and from ibat moment lie remembered no more till he came to himself on board the barge, and found a doctor whom he knew bending over him. While he had been working so heroic- ally below those on board the tug had pro- vided for possible emergencies, by going back to the harbour and bringing off a doctor. "Ha! You're better now, lad," said Dr. Robins, as lie saw Jack's eyes open. "And Mat—what about him?" Jack gasped out. The doctor shook his head. "Poor fellow, I fear the worst—l am afraid ne is done for. He was bleeding at the nose and mouth when we got him aboard, and he's still unconscious. It was folly for him to offer to go down to such a depth at his age. It's been touch end go with you, I can tell you; and you were not down nearly so long as he was, they tell vie. Herron was still unconscious when he was carried ashore, taken to his cottage, and put to bed. As he lived quite alone, Jack, although still very shaky himself, went with him to look after him. It was not till late at night that the old man opened his eyes, and after a time re- cognised his rescuer. Jack would have had him remain quiet, but all his cautions were vain. .

" Ary lad," he said, "I feels as if I ain't got much more time in this world. My cable's a'most run out, so it doant make much difrrence -whether I talks or not. Any wiLY, theers that t' be said as must be said, so I Wants you t' listen an' t' gi' me your solemn oath as you'll do as I asks ye to.' "I'll give you my word—my 'solemn Pro- nlise, Mat, if it is nothing against my cos' science."

' Agen yer conscience? No; it be t' other way about; it be t' right a wrong—a crool wrong—that's what I wants ye t' do. "It be about four or five year agone as 1 wur tempted by the devil. Up t' then I'd allus tried t' do me dooty—but—well, I went through 'ard times. I 'ad a boat—a fine lugger—an' she wur lost, an' she wern't in- sured. Then my whoam, that I had then, was burnt down about me ears, an' I onnly just crawled out wi' me wife an' our darter. Be- fore that I'd given up divin' work, thinkin' I wur gettin' too old, but I 'ad t' go back to it when I lost me boat. „ - .

" A'most—tice"Kst-Tol; I got arter I started agen wur one very much like this one +l4 'a bin too muen fur me. I WAS asked t' go down t' a wreck as lay very deep; but 'twasn't fur the owners nor 'twasn't fur the underwriters. 'Twer for a private matter. A gent came an' offered me a tidy sum o' money if I'd try t' find the body of a passenger who'd bin aboard her, and recover whatever I could belongin' to 'im. I found the poor feller right enough, and took a belt from round his waist. Now belts like that be some- times filled wi' gold; but this 'ad only papers —a lot of 'era, clone up tight in indja rubber, so 's t' keep 'ern from gettin' wet if anything 'appened. "Now I somehow guessed as the man who wanted them papers 'adn't no right t"em— an' I wur tempted t' read 'em in order t' see if I couldn't make 'im gie me more 'n he'd n bargained for. Sure enough it turned out so. I didn't unnerstan"em all exactly, but I guessed at a good deal, an' seem' as he wur so anxious t' get 'em I made 'im gi' me a good round sum for 'em—quite snuff t' set me up agen. But I warn't satisfied wi' that. I says t' meself, P'eaps some day more mis- fortins an' I may want more money.'may come about, So I kep' back some o' the papers, an' he never knew but what he 'ad 'em all. " Now, me lad, let this be a lesson to ye. It never did me no good. I didn't come t' want money agen, it is true; but I had ne luck other ways. Our darter died, an' thaw me wife died, an' I wur left alone in the world; an' I saw as I'd bin wrong, an' I cursed the day when I sold them papers to a man as I knower.' 'ad no right to 'em an' helped t' keep another—as I believes now— out o' his rights. Since I saw things in that light, I've bin doin' me best t' make reste- tooshun. I've worked, an' saved, t' get snuff t' send out advertisements, an' pay lawyers or somebody, t' find the chap as ought t"ave had them papers. D'ye see? Now will ye swear t' me solemn as ye'll do this fur met Ye'll find theer'll be 'nuff money over t' pay yerself lib'ral—an' I b'leeves I can trust t' yer honour t' carry it all out honest." " do that, Ma,t, my friend," said Jack, in earnest tones that carried comfort and con- viction to the heart of the repentant diver. "But I can't take any money payment for it beyond bare expenses. I couldn't bring my- self to make any profit out of such a trust. Tell me the names, and give me some idea how you want me to set to work." "Get out the box from under the bed, an' gi' me the key ye'll find in the- drawer over yonder. It takes a load off me mind t' hear ye promise so hearty—but, lad, it would take a greater load off if ye could find the right man afore I die, an' I could hear 'im say as he'll forgive me!" Jack found the Mx and the key, and - little later he was engaged in looking over papers. Suddenly he uttered a startled cry, the blood rushed from his heart to his head and then back again, leaving his face deadly pale. I "Mat!" he gasped, in a voice that seemed half-stifled. " Mat! What is this? Surely it cannot be! The name can't be Elsworthy?" Herron stared at the questioner in surprise. I*Aye)" he said, feebly, "that be the name. Do, ye know it!' "
"know It? Why—it's ours. That is, I mean that my mother's name was Elsworthy. Was the ship you went down to named tho Tasmanian?"

"Aye, aye, but,--" -"Mat, you have here the papers we want to prove my title to the Elsworthy Estates! I am the heir to them! My father was lost on that ship! Ile had been out to Australia to try to secure these very papers, and was re turning with them wheis the vessel was wrecked. It was from his dead body that you took the belt! Where—is—he—buried? Unclei what name?"
" Ife wur took ashore an' buried wrout nc name," was the shamefaced answer. "Be tause, ye see, most of the people on board was drowned wi' him, an' nobody seenicA t know' Wahl!' - .

div.head: COMPLETE EXAMINER STORY.
div.p: COMPLETE EXAMINER STORY.
"Aye, T sec!" cried Jack. "You and this other man between you had stolen everything by which he could be identified, and so—so— you left him to be buried in a pauper's grave, nameless and unknown!"
Jack had risen to his feet, his eyes flashing with anger and indignation, and he was point- ing an accusing finger at the shrinking figure on the bed. _

_ "Haven help me! I know I've bin wicked, wicked, wicked!" groaned the diver. "An' what makes it worse fur me be that you, that ve wronged so, have nearly lost yer own life this day a-tryin' t' save mine! What shall I do? How shall I die? I wanted ter make some restetooshun, but now—now--" The voice died away in a hopeless, despairing moan. Jack, who had begun to pace restlessly up and down the little room, stopped and gazed hard at the diver. And in those few moments many thoughts passed through his mind. He had thought this man greedy and miserly. But had he been? If he had been scraping, and saving, and denying himself in order, as the poor fellow quaintly put it, to "make restitution," why, then, there was much to be said on the other side. That his repentance had been sincere was evidenced by the trust he had proposed to place in Jack's hands, by which he was to use the money thus scraped together to find out the true heir, and do the best that could be d,one to remedy the wrong in which he had aided. And after all, Jack reflected, the man who had tempted him had been most to blame.

Jack went to the bed, and, leaning over it, took Herron's hand in his. "Mat!" he said, softly. "Mat, cheer up! Lei there be no bad feeling between you and me! You have dealt honestly by me in trying to teach me all you could, and it is thanks to you that I, a mere 'prentice hand, have been able to earn as much money as older men, and so have had some over to send home. I am not going to forget it, and if I say that I for- give you— Mat roused up, as though there had come to him a fresh lease of life. "Ye forgives me?" he exclaimed, incredu- lously, staring hard at the young fellow. " Say it agen—say it agen I carn't b'leeve me ears!"

Jack said it again, and more, too, while Mat lay there listening hungrily to words that sounded too good to be true. And, strange to say, spite of what the doctor had feared, Mat did not die. From the moment when the terrible burden that had so long lain on his mind had been lifted, and he felt that he was in very truth forgiven, he began to mend, and finally recovered. But neither he nor Jack did any more diving work. When the latter, in due time, took the place in the world to which he was entitled, Mat went to live in a trim little cot- tage on his estate. And Jack, and his mother and sister, and Mat, are now all great friends, much to the wonderment of the gos- siping folk of the countryside. But that is be- cause Jack keeps his own counsel, and has never told those curious people this strange story of the Diver's Secret.
:THE END,I

THE DIVER'S SECRET.
BY FENTON ASH
Author of "The Radium Seekers," "The Black Opal," "A Trip to Mars," "The Broken Sword," d-c.

As the grey dawn was stealing over the harbour of a south coast town one autumnal morning, a tug-boat might have been seen making its way out towards the English Channel which lay beyond. It was a fussy, snorting, grimy, self-suffi- cient-looking craft, this tug. b'rom the sooty top of its funnel it poured forth almost enough black smoke for a man-o'-war, and it was tooting with its shrill, chirpy siren as though it were a Cunarder at least, and ex- pected everything afloat to clear out of its path. It was towing a barge, and as it threaded its noisy way amongst the crowd of other vessels, large and small, many of those on hoard them turned to stare after it. It was not that the pair were unfamiliar objects, for it was known to most mariners thereabouts that the tug was the Otter, and that the barge carried a party of deep-sea divers and their outfit. " Theer goes 'Mat the Diver,' " a sailor oso board a schooner lying at anchor remark-.. to a mate. "He be a-goin' out after gold to the wreck o' the Dolphin, as was run down t'other night in the fog. They do say as it be 4, mighty risky job, fur the wreck inw twenty- four fat'homs deep, an' what makes it worse the tide just theer do run uncommon strong. Nobody else would tackle it, not even for the big price as be offered. But 1 heered yest'day as Mat Herron's took it on. I s'pose if lie's lucky he'll make a tidy bit a& on it— but I'd rayther him try fur it than me!" This voiced the general opinion in the port; and it is no matter for wonder, therefore. that the start of the diving party was watched with more than ordinary interest and curiosity. On board the barge, Mat himself was talk- ing to one of his assistants in a fashion which showed that he was fully aware of the un- usually dangerous nature of the undertaking he had in hand. He was a man advanced in years, with a weather-worn visage which habitually wore a stern and forbidding ex- pression, and he was at all times rough and curt, and reticent of speech. The assistant he was addressing was a contrast to him in al- most every way. Though working under Mat for the wages of a working diver, everyone who knew him was aware that he must origi- nally have been one of a very different class from that to which such men usually belon. His name was Jack Gale; but amongst his fellow-workers he was more commonly known as Gentleman Jack—a fact which almost ex- plains itself. It tells at once of some young fellow who has been well educated and brought up amid very different surroundings, and who has manfully thrown all pride to the winds, and taken to the first honest work which offered itself in order to avert starvation. This had been Jack Gale's position three years before, only that in his case it was a question of starvation not merely for himself alone, but for an invalid mother and young sister in their home in the North. So when the crisis came which had cast him suddenly upon his own resources, he had paid the little money he had been able to serape together as a premium to Herron the diver to take him on as his assistant and teach him the work. Jack's people knew not that the money he sent them every week was earned at so risky a trade. He had kept them in ignorance upon that point, fearing that they might otherwise refuse to accept it. It was enough for him to know that he could not have learnt to earn so much in the time in any other way. Great was his surprise, this particular morning, at what Mat Herron was saying, and the singular change in the diver's manner. For though he and Herron had got on fairly well together on the whole, and Jack knew him to be plucky and skilful at his work, he had always appeared a sombre, reserved character, with little to say, surly and unsym- pathetic in manner, and greedy and grasping in disposition. The latter quality it was, in Jack's estimation, which had caused him to attempt the recovery of the boxes of gold on the wrecked vessel—a task which every other diver in the district had declined, spite of tbs tempting reward offered. "This is what I wants of ye," Mat was say- ing. '°Th case annything 'appens t' me. Under the bed in my room ye'll find a box, a:" the key be in a drawer. I wants ye t' open it an' t' read the papers in it, an' a dociment as I've writ out after a good deal o' thought an' trouble. Yell find some money theer too, an' I wants ye t' apply it t' the purpose I've set down in that dociment, d'ye see—all but what ye'll see yere t' keep fur yerself fur yer trouble."

As may be supposed, Jack stared as he listened to these details of the strange task thus unexpectedly Qtrust upon him. More particularly did he wonder at the confidence it implied, and that he, of all the diver's acquaintances, should have been selected for the trust. He put this point to Mat, but the man turned it aside, and in response to Jack's objections only stuck doggedly to his request. Evidently the old man had recognised in his own mind the difference between "Gentleman Jack " and his fellows, and had decided that he would rather trust him than anyone else he knew.

As argument proved fruitless, Jack at last gave the required promise. But he made mental reservation that it applied a to that par ticular time only. If, as be hoped, they suc- ceeded in the task before them, and returned in safety to the shore, he was resolved that b. would make the diver draw up 3 proper instead of the informal "dociment" which had been spoken of, and insist upon somebody else being appointed to carry out its provi- sions, whatever they might be. . N!.... In due time the two vessels reached the scene of the wreck, and there the barge was moored, the tug remaining near, to be at hand in case she was wanted. Jack and his fellows helped Mat into his diving-suit and and a little later IT went over the side an disappeared from view.

As Jack watched him sink beneath the waves a feeling of ' depression stole over him such as he had never felt before in similar circumstances, and which he could in no vise account for. Certainly the scene was dreary and depressing enough. Overhead the sky was grey and lowering, arounsl there was no- thing to be seen save the grey-green waves rising and falling, nothing to be heard save the peculiar sucking sound as they pattered continuously against the sides of the barge, or the desolate cries of the sea-birds as they wheeled and circled in the air above. Jack felt some consolation in the fact that he could talk to the diver and ascertain from him all the while how he was progressing. ort-htoe-dapparatus was of the best thean d whole most up Mat carried with him a telephone with which he could communicate with those on the barge. For a time all went well. Mat reported through the telephone that he had found no difficulty in climbing on board the wreck by the bow, and later that he had fixed a laddei there to facilitate his return. A little late, still he had made his way into the captaim& cabin, and had reached the boxes of gold which he had been told he would find thee Then came the news that he had dragged one of the boxes up on to the deck ready for a rope to be attached to haul it up. For a while after this therewvas silence; and then came the ominous information that while the diver had been in the cabin the tide, which at that time was increasing in agaostrength,is had forced his life-line and air-tuho t the bow, and got them tangled up round the anchor and a mass of loose wreck- age which lay there. minutes which followed were anxious ones, and then came the announcement from Mat that the current was too strong to allow iwofan his h is setting his lines free, and that ho The owners' o agent, go do irvi calledhe a heart for a volunteer t bounded within him as he saw that the other and I d Jack'sfo r rl men, who by reason of their seniority were t rten ; 11 asked first, hung back. While they hesitated he volunteered and was accepted; and, as quickly as was possible, he' donned a diving- suit and went over the side,

He made his way to where Herron was standing, and found that he was : Fraid to stir, for the position was such that any movement on his part might have broken or ruptured his air tube. v,itich would have meant certain

div.head: DEATH OF COLONEL PILKINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF COLONEL PILKINGTON.

Colonel Windle Pilkington, head of the glass. making firm of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., St. Helens died on Sunday afternoon at Cannes, where he and members of his family were on holiday. They left home three weeks ago, and Colonel Pilkington was taken ill with influenza, which developed into congestion of the lungs. Dr. Kerr, of St. Helens, was summoned to Cannes, and a specialist was also called in, but Colonel Pilkington's condition gradually grew weaker until tile end. He leaves a widow and four children, two sons and two daughters, the eldest son, Austin Pilkington, being on his way home from California, where he has resided four or five years owing to the state of his health. The other son, Mr. Cecil Pilkington, is actively engaged in connection with the glassworks. The death of Colonel Pilkington is a loss to the town, where he had spent the whole of his life. He was in his seventy-fifth year.

A French Campaign Against
Immodest Fashions.

div.head: DRESS AT THE COURTS.
div.p: DRESS AT THE COURTS.

The Buckingham Palace Courts this season are more remarkable for the beauty of materials than for artistic design of the dresses worn. However cleverly arranged, bunchiness and in- artistic bustle draperies do not make for ele- gance or true beauty, and the world of fashion would welcome a return to "La Ligne." The curtailment of trains has made a perceptible difference in the time occupied by presentees passing before their Majesties, but it has not had the effect of shortening the Courts to the extent that was predicted. The fashion for narrow skirts makes it difficult to execute the deep obeisance with the grace that distinguished the ladies attending Queen Victoria' 4 Drawing Rooms, and the curtse3-8 have consequently lost a little of their stateliness.

The Protest Against Immodest Modes. The Patriotic League of Frenchwomen who have inaugurated a campaign against indecorous fashions, is a most aristocratic and influ‘ntial body. The public protest they have raised against sensational feminine modes should not therefore be altogether in vain. The churches have not been silent on this subject, but where they have failed, a fashionable society crusade may succeed, or at least prevent the notoriety fashion-hunters from going to further extremes. It is true that modes which are entirely lacking in self-respect, appeal only to a small minority of women, but no one can deny that there has been in the last few years too much tendency to transfer to the streets the licence allowed on the stage. Whether the initiative in this de- velopment belongs to French or American women, it is time to call a halt, and everyone with a proper sense of the fitness of things will welcome this new crusade against immodest fashions. The New Skirt.

Some of the new modes that have so far been allowed to see the light appear to indicate the passing of the hobble skirt, which has had an unusually long reign. The new design is simple and elegant, for it follows the line of the feminine figure, as did the Greek draperies— complicated as they were—from which it has been chiefly evolved. Some of the new models Show skirts of afternoon dresses flounced from waist to hem, the material being pinked out at the edges of the flounces. There is, however, no superfluous fullness, the skirt follows the lines of the figure, but it is moderately wide at the hem. The peg-top effect has disappeared from the creations of several leading houses. Whether this new silhouette ' will take the popular fancy remains to be seen. Spring Materials.

The fickleness of spring weather and the un- certainty of the coming su,mmer make the choice of materials for new sults a difficult matter. It is impossible to know beforehand whether thin silks and muslins or woollen homespuns will be required. Happily in these times there are numerous materials that are admirably adapted to these various contingencies. Smart, well-cut tailored suits in shantung, tnsiore, or thin suitings, look well in any state of the weather. The great thing is to choose a light- weight material in wool, and the name of these is now legion. The new heavy flax linens may he considered in this connection. They are rich in appearance, very like silk in fact, and quite warm enough for spring wear, or for a chilly summer day. They are made in all the new and beautiful colodrings. For warmer weather there is a new and very handsome make of ben- galine, and silk gabardine has also much to recommend it as a spring material.

The Fancy for Capes. Ttoe,lal have t have e successfullyhe cape mayhro u truly s f; f he saidrialsag scored a triumph for feminine styles in these days of masculine adaptations, for it has with- out any doubt " arrived " and will remain throughout the summer. In design it varies eiceedingly. Some models are fussy and frilly in the extreme, others are of an almost nun- like severity. Sometithes very wide frayed-out ruches take the place of frills, but these should be we'll only by the slim, nor are frills to be ad- vised for the short or stout. The fussy cape is full from the neck, has a V-shaped opening in front, trimmed with a wide frill, and is lenge' in front than at the sides. A full frill finishes the hem of the cape, and outlines the shoulder also. Much variety is obtained by different col- lars, the Napoleon and Robespierre in particu- lar affording a wide choice. Sometimes the fronts are slightly drawn into the figure by means of ribbon velvet and bow. This style of cape is at its best in taffetas, and in black com- pletes a taffetas dress most charmingly.

The Newest Millinery. The Louis XVI. plateau hat, perched high Upon the raised coiffure, is worn rather for- ward over the face or it is raised at the left side. A curious feature of the new straws is their extreme brilliance, giving the impression that they had been subjected to several coats of varnish. After the dull straws that have been so long in use, the contrast is almost dazzling. Equally so are the highly varnished leather flowers that in some instances trim them. Even the ribbons used on these straws are treated in a way that gives them the same brightness of surface that differs altogether from the usual sheen of silk. The larger the plaid the better milliners appear to like it, and checks and stripes vie with each other. ,Watered moire ribbons and materials are also greatly favoured by milliners this season.

Ornaments Made of Hair. The high coiffure is making headway, and the latest invention of the coiffeur is the cheek curl, which does not hide the ears altogether, and is decidedly prettier than the coiffure that was drawn down the side of the face. The hair is worn quite low over the face, and waved at the sides. A new comb, called the "monoplane," is used for the fashionable high coiffure. The latest thing, however, in ornamentation for the head, and far more sensible than the aigrettes that have been so much worn on evening coiffures, are beautiful flowers, delicate feathers and mounts, made of human hair. The flowers are most realistic.

div.head: VICTORY FOR WARRINGTON "A."
div.p: VICTORY FOR WARRINGTON "A."
A Good Game at Wilderspool.

The Warrington Combination team made amends for the reverse they experienced at the hands of St. Helens Recs. by trouncing the lads from Pemberton to the tune of 2 goals 5 tries (19 points) to 2 goals 1 try (7 points). The score might even have been greater had the Wilderspool lads taken all the chances which came their way, but the rather slippery nature of the ground may be some excuse for the number of forward passes and " knock-ons" which were a noticeable feature of the game. The Wilderspoolians, however, were full value for their victory, and Pemberton were fortunate in retiring with only 19 points against, them. Thirteen of these were piled up in the first half, tries being scored by Baker, Naylor and Howard Davis, while Critchley landed two goals, the one from Baker's try being a particularly fine effort, almost from the touch-line. Pemberton, during the first moiety, were unable to pene- trate Warrington's defence, although Smalley and Taberner both made dashing runs, but Bramhall was found at his best and avoided disaster. In the second half Warrington again mono- polised most of the play, but were only able to add two tries to their score, and Pemberton replied with two splendid penalty goals and a rather "soft" try. Green put on the flecessary finishing touches to the work which led up to the first try, and Baker was responsible for the second, but Critchley, somehow or other, must have lost his goal-kicking boots, as he could not steer the ball over the bar on any Occasion , during the second half. Pemberton made one or two attempts to break through, but they were no match for the nippy Warringtonians ancl a good game ended as stated above.

• BRAMHALL AT HIS BEST. was a pleasure to see Bramhall "come out It of his shell," and he played .the best game I have seen. him since he joined the Combination team. He kicked with good judgment, and his following-up and dodging was quite a feature of the game. The threequarters all did well, ' though Baker was undoubtedly the pick. He used his speed well, and fully deserved his two tries. On the other wing Shakeshaft showed he has got plenty of speed, but he is not quite up to the finer arts of the game, though with a little more "coaching" he ought to develop into a useful wing. Howard Davis and Steele both did well at centre, and were very often in the picture. , The half-backs--J. Brown and C. Brown—did not strike one as being an ideal pair, and •certainly could claim no advantage over the Pemberton halves. At times, however, they did some smart things, and with a little more practice may understand one another's play better. The forwards all did well, and none were more prominent than the "old war- horse "—Naylor--who received quite an ovation when he got over for his try. Critchley and Harmer were hard workers both in the tight and in the loose, the kicking of the latter being a notable feature.

div.head: RYLANDS' FINE WIN.
div.p: RYLANDS' FINE WIN.
Defeat of Wardley.

On the Moorhouse-lane ground, Rylands' won a fine victory in the League Competition. Mor- ris kicked off for Rylands'. Wardley pressed through Mooney, Tlorrocks,kicking dead. War- ren had to retire hurt. Good play by the Ward- ley left wing nearly brought a score. Warren returned and the " Wiremen" at last got to busineA. Warren, picking up in the loose and dodging his opponents, passed to Griffiths, who scored. Morris failed at goal. Welsby next had hard lines, being brought down -on ,the line. llalfAirne arrived with the score: Rylands' Recs., one try (three points); Wardley, nil. Wardley commenced the second half up the slope. For obstruction. Warren kicked a goal. Mooney scored for Wardley. Rylands' scored again through- Griffiths, the goal kick failing. Further tries were scored by llorrocks and Slater, Warren gosling each time. A grand passing and repassing movement by Poynton and Mooney ended in Poynton scoring, the same player goaling. The game ended in favour of Rylands' by three goal four tries (18 points), to Wardley, one goal two tries (eight points).

div.p: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM. Pithy Pars About the N.U. Games.

Warrington did not get their due In the match played at Dewsbury. They were simply swamped in The flood of Dewsbury's kicking. Sweet will be the time of revenge. This comes along on Good Friday. With the venue at Wilderspool there Should be no question as to the result. What went wrong with the team? They seem not to have recovered yet From the result of the Batley cup-tie There is no use of living on regret.

div.head: 00000 C
div.p: The dear neighbour of Batley—Dewsbury— Will now give themselves airs and crow Over the Batla laad3 something like this: "You of Batley could only beat A'arrington by "Ono clear point—we of Dewsbury have -Defeated them by thirteen clear points, "Therefore we of Dewsbury are the better team?! . Anyone who knows the two rival towns Will know that such is just likely to happen. Both can have all the praise they like, but When Dewsbury come to Wilderspool They may have a different tune to pipe. "Ruddick," said a Dewsbury critic, "is one "Of the best players on the Warrington side." Dewsbury critics do not give any Praise where it is not at all due. Waywell was another active worker. Young and Nicholas did well at half-back, Only they were over-weighted with work. What came over the Warrington forwards? They have been playing erratic of late. George Dickenson tackled without fear. Brookes also played a useful game, but The team as a whole was not up to par. ()coo ee

The Warrington "A" men did very well. They defeated Pemberton rather easily. Bramhall was the life of the winners. He has shaken off the past "nerves." His dodging was the feature of the game. Baker showed a fine turn of speed. He is coming on as a threequarter. Slip.kesbaft also gives much promise. A -little more coaching will bring him out. 'Howard Davis has come back to form. The two Browns, if not brilliant At half-back, were very reliable.

div.head: COOCCO
div.p: COOCCO

Runcorn—the same old tale. Still another defeat to be recorded. Well may the supporters of the club ask, What on earth is wrong with the team? The Workshop Competition is a record In point of the number of entries received. There are 20 more teams than last year. Yet we have been told the N.U. game is Fast losing its hold in Warrington. Will new talent be discovered in the competi- tion? Warrington team are resting to-day—nb match. Some folk think the rest will do good.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
STOCKTON HEATH v. WESTERN.

Stockton Heath completed their list of home fixtures on Saturday, when Western were the visitors, and after a moderate game won by 3 goals against nil. At Eccles, Stockton Heath won by 6 goals to 2. The ground was in a very bad condition and neither side could settle down to good hockey. For the first 20 minutes Stock- ton Heath had most of the play, but could not sore, the forwards being continually ruled off- side. A fine run by Bainbridge brought the goalkeeper out, and passing back to Baxter, the latter had no difficulty in opening the scoring for Stockton Heath. Western now played up strongly, but poor shooting prevented them from scoring. Half-time: Stockton Heath, one goal; Western, nil.

From the bully the visitors got into the home circle, but again their shooting was very poor, and at no time were they really dangerous. Play was now practically confined to midfield until about ten minutes from time, when the home team rallied, Bainbridge getting through and scoring, Richardson adding a third imme- diately after. Stockton Heath continued to press, but could not add to their score. Re- sult: Stockton Heath, three goals; Western, nil. Stockton Heath are away to Chorlton to-day.

LATCHFORD VICTORIOUS. Latchford first eleven defeated Sale "A" after a dull and uninteresting game last Saturday. The visitors were kept mostly on the defensive, but owing to Latchford's front line finishing' poorly, the score was only 1-0 at half-time in favour of the home team, Pearson shooting through from a corner hit. In the second half the Sale backs were kept busy, Beresford in particular playing well. Starkey scored a second goal from close range, and Pearson, with one of his best efforts, put on a third. Sale ; made several attacks, but their forwards were worse than the home team The strongest ,1 point of Latchford's team was the halves (Albin- ! son, Wilkinson and Knight), and better use should have been made of the opportunities they gave their forwards.

This success put more life into the homesters, and. cheered on by their supporters, they were soon attacking the visitors' goal. Amidst great ex- citement Denny equalised. Both teams were now working hard to gain the lead, the home players being more prominent in their methods and were keeping the.visitors well in their,own half, when Smith was brought down just inside the penalty area. The referee awards,d the penalty kick, which was entrusted to Stubbs, and he drove the leather past Williamson and placed the home team in front. During the closing stages play was of a scrappy nature, and no further scores were made, the result being: Stockton Reath, three goals; Crosfield's Reserve, two goals.

Second Division. ' Bank Quay Recs. v. Warrington Excelsior. Played on the Bewsey-road ground. The Rees. made an attack on the home goal, and Eccleston, when in a favourable position, shot over the bar. This gave relief to the home defence and even play followed in mid-field. Then the home forwards, by adopting close methods, missed many opportunities of scoring. Hughes missed an open goal. Berry, during this period of attack, was the most prominent player in defence, and saved his goal from down- fall on several occasions. The interval arrived without any score being made. The second portion opened very fast, and each end was visited in turn. The forwards on both, sides were very erratic in their final shots at goal. Crozier, of the Rees., sent in a long shot from mid-field, which hit the inside of the up- right and beat Rigby. The homesters now Played strenuously to get on level terms, but Berry proved too good for the attacking forces, and the home team had<to retire defeated Result: Bank Quay Recs., one goal; Excelsior, nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON RUNNERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON RUNNERS.
Good Performances in the National Cross Country Championship.
TWO IN INTERNATIONAL TEAM.

Warrington runners made a good fight in the National Cross Country Championship at Chesham, Bucks, on Saturday, amidst a deluge of rain and sleet, and as a result F. Antrobus and W. Bolton have been selected for the Eng- lish team in the International to be run at Chesham, but over a different course from that ,of last Saturday. The 26 teams entered turned out, and, facing the tempest, 269 runners broke away without the starter's signal, and could not be brought back. Glover set a hot pace, and the tail was 400 yards long when Ruffen and Yost!, went to the front at the end of the first mile. Before two miles! Glover met with a mishap, and the battle be- tween Hallamshire and Warrington was now all against the "Blades," and "Wire" predomin- ated over all. At 3-1 miles Vose and Ruffell were followed by Wooton, Wilson, Stanton, O'Neill, Hughes, Antrobus, Cook, Hutson, Holmes, Bolton, and the next 20 included the other six of Warrington; 80 runners, including Sanderson and Wallach, had retired, and Nicholls, Southern champion, was just in front of Warrington's eighth, Gregson, therefore, the team chance of Warrington looked rosy, and Vose was now the fancy of the cognoscenti. At four miles Warrington had their first mis- fortune by losing Burgess when running 14th. At 5-1 miles the storm abated, but the water had carried away the loose soil and what was soft going in the first round was now a track of flints. On to these the first 20 (six of Warring- ton) dashed, and, except Ruffell, everything within 900 yards appeared to wither; soaked pump tops were torn like paper and the iron (spikes) left the soles of the shoes and entered the souls of the wearers. The opinions of the first nine to finish, supplemented by those of Cottrill and Cooke, Hallamshire; Vose, Turton, Holbrook and Hanson, Warrington; Hinkley, Derby; Lloyd, Herne Hill; and Bryant; Bolton; would make interesting reading, even without the military expressions of the " Connaughts." With 'Pinion carried off and Vose barefooted, Warrington had only six left, and thus they dropped from first to ninth team before they got going again.

div.head: Leading Results.
div.p: Leading Results.

At seven miles another 40 runners were miss- ing, and that 138 actually completed the dis- tance is a poser for people who talk of decadent Britishers—they must have had grit other than in their pumps (what was left of them) to do it. Official result:—

div.head: IN arrington Workingmen's Association.
div.p: IN arrington Workingmen's Associa- tion.
N.A. CENTRE.
THE CLOSURE.

Last week-end saw the finish of coarse fishing until June 16th, and a very poor finish it was, for those who visited the Gowy. As far as Warringtonians were concerned only one mem- ber took fish, and this was of no consequence. Now is the time for the older members to take the new ones to this stream to show them the different haunts of the roach during close season. When eels are fairly on the run it is an ideal place to take the novice. There are two roving matches, to take place in May by the N.A. clubs of Warrington, and although nothing yet has been definitely settled, there is no better spot than the Gowy for such contests. We pre- sume the reason that the places for the matches for 1914 are not yet chosen is because secretaries are waiting results of the Northwich Joint Ang- ling Association to offer terms to them. The rules sent out by them do not at all meet with approval, and other arrangements are not to HEADQUARTERS' SPECIALS. Season 1914. The following list is not yet complete and others may appear later. The list is quite independent and apart from the usual yearly set board prizes, which will be raised according to the progress made during the year. Prizes ranging from 10s. to 2.8.
