THE TUPWS TREACHERY.
BY G. E. BURGIN,
Author of "Tomalyn's Quest," "Gascoigne's Ghost," 'Judge of the Four Corners," "Tuster's Little Maid," "Old Man's Mar- riage," &c.
("Mid pleasures and palaces, though we may roam,' or even Armenia, there's no place like home," sang Totnalyn Crane, as he gave his wearied mule a prod in the ribs.

"Thank goodness there ain't, sir." said Smith, the chief's servant, lie struggled up beside Tornalyn, who was young, and the chief's secretary. "As ley sings at the dear old Gaiety in the Strand: From the garret to the base, it is sich a beastly place, That I never wish to see it any more, any more.' * "Ali," said Tonialyn, betokening a very languid interest in Smith's vocal efforts, as the members of the Commission crawled on through the grey after- ii(X)n, and the snow began to fall thick and fast. "Ah, that's all very well for you, Smith; but I had such a good time in Constantinople before the chief was appointed the head of this beastly Com- mission and sent down here to report on everything and everybody. I'd arranged to go as the hind legs of an elephant to Demetri Pasha's ball, and now the front legs will have to go by himself." "You're much better out of it, sir," said Smith cheerily. "I went to one of them masked balls as a good old Robinson Crusoe once, with a real parrot and goat, and-----" He paused reminiscently. "Well?" languidly inquired Tomalyn. "I got that there parrot from a man in the har- bour," said Smith solemnly, "and the langwidge it made use of was awful, They was going to turn me out, but the goat charged the crowd and the parrot got away on to an old lady's head-dress." "Do you think we shall ever find anything to eat to-day? " Toinalyn wistfully inquired. "l'd give all my hopes of a Turkish decoration for a plate of roast beef, with floury potatoes." "It's very few taters we'll get, sir," said Smith, "till we reaches Kharpoot. Them American mis- sionaries at Kharpoot has taken to growing taters, and if we're lucky, we might sneak a few. Just look at old Said Pasha, sir, he hates us, and is always on the look-out to play us a dirty trick, since I gave his black servant a hiding. Cheering, ain't it? My teeth is loose already from taking so much quinine in cigarette papers every morning, and it makes 'em worse when I see that old villain grinning at me."

Said Pasha turned round and muttered a grave "Inshallah " as he heard his name pronounced. "Take care, Smith," said Tonialyn, somewhat apprehensively. "He understands English, and may play us a nasty trick." Subsequent events justified Tomalyn's prediction,' for, as the cortege wound slowly up the mountain, the Pasha's negro servant, after a brief colloquy with his master, got off his mule ostensibly to tighten its girths, and allowed Tornalyn and Smith, who were the last of the party, to precede him along the narrow path. The horses had given out liang ago, and both Tomalyn and Smith were mounted on ordinary pack-mules, which, from sheer forte of habit, hugged the edge of the precipice in a manner which would have made both Englishmen shudder with terror had they not gradually grown to under- stand that the mules did 60 lest their imaginary packs should strike against the wall of rock on the other side of the path, and dash them to the bottom of the abyss. . _

As Tom-alyn rode in front of Smith, his head sleepily falling forward on his breast, the latter turned round just in time to see the negro mount his mule, dig the spurs into the animal's sides, and make a rush between Smith and the wall. It dawned upon the ex-hussar in this moment of supreme peril that his life was not worth much ; for the object of the wily negro was to get his animal between Smith and the wall and thrust the Englishman over the precipice. A sudden cry, a thud-thud on the rucks below, and there would be an end of the matter. Such accidents were by no means uncommon on the mountains of Armenia. Toinalyn could see nothing (he was just turning an angle in the path) and the others were half a mile ahead.

But the old hussar was not to be caught napping. In a moment, he had drawn a revolver from his breast, there was a solitary "ping " as the weapon dropped to the line of fire, and the next moment the negro's mule, shot in the forehead, swerved round and fell over the precipice, taking his rider with him. Smith could hear the bodies striking against the rocks as they disappeared in the gathering night. Smith leisurely thrust the revolver into his pocket and rode on after Tornalyn. "I thought I heard a revolver go off just now," said the latter innocently.

'"Let's get near the others and see if they heard it too," Smith huskily replied. Now that the danger was over, his nerve began to go. But when they turned aside from the path and debouched upon an open plain, Said Pasha slept peacefully in his saddle, and Tonikins Pasha, the chief, alone rode with soldierly erectness at the head of the straggling cavalcade. The other members of the commission were all more or less demoralised by cold, hunger, and fatigue. They wanted something to eat, something to smoke, divans whereon to rest their weary limbs. It was the Pasha's vengeance that Smith dreaded; and he was perfectly well aware that if Said once knew his servant's fate, the taking off of himself would be speedy and sharp.

Smith drew a long breath of relief. "If I was you, sir," he said significantly to Tomalyn, "I wouldn't remember anything about hearing a revolver go off just now. You must have been dreatui pg. Tomalyn loved Smith and trusted him. "I understand, Smith. I didn't look round at all. Smith's countenance cleared. "What surprises me, sir," he said, with a wink, "is the ingratitude of these beastly niggers. There was that fellow of Said Pasha's riding his master's best mule, and I shouldn't be surprised to hear he's cleared off with it and will never turn up again." "Oh, you think he won't turn up again?. "Not till the Day of Judgment." Tomalyn shivered a little in spite of himself. 'He didn't hurt you at all?" "No, sir; but I was only just in time. He'll never trouble us aga-- What's tha—at ? Smith nearly fell out of the saddle as he spoke. They had gone round the other side of a huge snow-covered mound in order not to be overheard by the rest of the party, and something lay crouched under the hollow of a huge rock. Its shadow on the snow was not unlike that of a man. To Smith's excited imagination it seemed as if the negro had climbed up the side of the precipice and was lying in wait for hint. "Don't you go a-nigh him, sir; he'll knife you," he cried, as Tomalyn stumbled down from his mule.

Tomalyn's heady laugh reassured him. "Come on, and don't be. an idiot, Smith. It's only a dog; he's half dead." Ile dragged the animal out and felt for his whiskey flask. Even in the dim light, Smith could see that it was a beautiful brown and white Persian greyhound. Unlike the English breed, it had long silky hair, with large flapping ears, and feathered stern.

Smith began to laugh, as he helped Tomalyn to revive the beautiful animal. "lie's worth a lot of tin I should say, sir," he remarked. "Some sweirs been gazelle hunting, and the dog's funked the cold and hidden himself out of the way of the wind. They can stand anything but cold. Here's some crarabic nonsense on his coat, sir."

dog had a square of silk fastened over his loins, and, by the aid of a match, Tomalyn deciphered the word "Janonm " embroidered on it in Turkish characters. "He's probably been stolen by some Kurdish rascal, who won't care to claim him," he said. "The chief will be delighted." "It's a lucky find for us," said Smith, picking up the dog, and laying it across his saddle. "We've got a good excuse for stoppling behind. Now, sir, let's go and tell old Said all about it." And Said, waking from his uneasy slumber, apparently mused the luck of the Giaours in finding such an animal. Presently it dawned upon him that he had lost a far more valuable one in the shape of his own mule—a beast whose hide had been decorated with various patterns and which was reserved exclusively for ceremonial processions. Instead of flying into a rage and bewailing his 1.49, the old Pasha simply shrugged his shoulders and rode on. It was kiamet. What would be, would be. It had been written on his forehead bit hi should lose this milli Why should he din
ptb the decrees of Allah! Still, if these mote iiapeks (infidel dogs) had anything to do with it, Let them beware!

A. collection of little huts suddenly rose ur gainst a background of snow. In a few minute' the moon came out; so did the village dogs, and scented the ristocratic stranger in Smith's arms. He was sufficiently revived to snarl angrily at his foes as Smith drove them away. Half-an-hour later Tomalyn had found him home food. That night Janoum shared his rug.

Janoum's gentlemanly manners endeared him very much to Tomalyn and Smith, and he accom- panied them everywhere except at official receptions, where his presence would have been regarded as an insult. demi= was a thoroughly happy, light- hearted, gentlemanly dog, with a kind of airy !gaiety which impressed Smith tremendously. The only thing which upset him was cold weather. It became necessary to carry him whenever there was snow on the ground, as he had an invincible repugnance to getting chilled, and would simply make for the shadow of the nearest rock. He was no match for the big Kurd dogs, with their iron- spiked collars. These magnificent brutes always attacked him in packs, and, as each of them could easily have tackled a wolf, Janourn's chances would have been small had not the watchful Smith come to his rescue. But the dog was plucky, and took his punishment with a philosophy which made Smith look upon him as a phenomenon. The chief petted him, and both Tomalyn and Smith felt that Janoum afforded them a good deal of pleasure. His temperament, his light, inconsequential way of looking at things, made a welcome relief from the gravity of the Turkish cut-throats who accompanied the Commission.

But one ;day, a rascally Kurd who had been con- demned to life-long imprisonment by the Com- mission for slaughtering Armenians (this meant that directly the Commission had left the place he would be released) was so impressed by the chief's indifference to bribes that, after a hurried con- ference with Said Pasha, he brought him down another beautiful greyhound called "Hanoum." Hanourn was much bigger than Janoum, who greeted him with an effusion to which the other ,failed to respond; but when Janoum went and sat down on the right hand of the chief, Hanoinn lay on his left and slightly lifted his upper lip. There was a peculiar, yellowish slime on his jaws. Janoum looked at him with an air of light inquiry. "pen't you comfortable ? " his manner seemed, to imply. 'We're travelling, and have to rough it a bit ; but I'm told we shall be all right when we get to England." Hanoum's sulky, saliva-stained lip went higher. "You're not going to get to England if I can help it," he said. "Who are you, any way? I've half a mind to give you a jolly good hiding just to take the cheek out of you." Janoum yawned. "Gentlemen don't fight before the chief. We'll be let out for a run presently; then, I'm at your service if you are such a sulky cad. Your mother must have thrown back a bit when you were born." Smith regarded his favourite a bit anxiously, for he was not favourably impressed by llanoinn's manner. It seemed to him to lack repose : the animal did not appear to to be in good health. When the dogs were let out, he kept Janoum at his side. Presently, however, Hanoum sneaked up, grapped Janoutn by the hind leg, and commenced to .chew it. It was. all Smith could do to get his mouth open. He gave Hanoum a kick in the ribs which , considerably astonished that saturnine animal and carried Janouni back to his own quarters. . "That there Hanoum don't fight fair," he said indignantly to Tomalyn. "He's a dirty Turk all over. I believe he's been put up to it by the old Pasha."

janoum looked up gratefully. "Of course the fellow's a bounder,' he said, with an eloquent wag of his tail; "and he's bigger than I am. How am I to get even with him when my leg's well." "Smith," cried the chief at that 'moment, "don't interfere with the dogs. They'll soon settle down and become friends. They're bound to have one good fight first."

"All right, sir," said Smith respectfully, "but 'tain't fair. "This here sulky beast (pointing to Hanourn) is & good deal heavier than t'other ; and now Colonel Blakely's left me his black greyhound, Missie,' to look after I only want a kennel and a red coat to be complete." It was a great delight to Smith that Missie would have nothing whatver to do with Hanourn, who became more morose than ever. Twice Janomn gallantly tackled his saturnine foe, and was hope- lessly beaten on each occasion. Missie, the bone of contention, looked on as if unable to under- stand how Janonin could make such a mess of it. She soon found out, however, for the surly Hanoum, with unwounted lack of, chivalry, turned upon Missie, after some cutting remark of hers which had sent Janoum into fits of canine laughter, and bit a piece out of her glossy side. Janoum came to her rescue, but was kept back by Smith, who separated the belligerents and reported to the chief that it was impossible to keep the three dogs together. "Then one of them will have to go," said the chief. "Hanotun's the better dog of the two, we'll keep him. He looks as if he wanted physicing though." 1 Crane. They Smith walked away. He did not intend to part with Janoum, neither did Toma 3 Hamm loved the dog as much as they disliked ,w •'a Smith, with it wink, "I leave it to me, sir, said Pasha got Hanoum given to who had no redeeming qualities whatever: ;lot; Said sort of dog ours was, and abesli,ecvaeastehalitatearew wanted it chewed up. I don't speak the langwidge of these here Kurds, but I'll make 'mu understand if you'll give me a handful of copper money, sir. We're going to lay up this afternoon, so you just keep quiet when the Pasha's having a nap, and see what'll happen." amid, with the assistance of an interpreter, That afternoon Smith got hold of a Kurdish understand that he wanted a couple of reihmedpeh ehrit wolf-collars, such as the sheep-dogs wore. When lie had purchased these collars he eat down and fitted them to the necks of Missie and Janouni. His next proceeding was to sharpen the iron spikes inchasstlucankceotpitoifnrtosm. eNcollars e suntilhan ,ttheybauleo-aegs,s, wkehe rtiiieads tulpaatkh the f ted ro gtsh. a ell'vvees daoan'xet all I hummed, and theyeda,as he time Hanoum goes for 'em. He'll get his teeth broken if he ain't careful." Smith and Tomalyn went for a walk along the bluff which overlooks the valley of Kharpoot. There was an ancient castle on the extreme edge of the bluff, from which the Saracens had amused themselves by throwing down doughty crusaders, armour and all. Tornayln lay on the edge of the bluff and peered over, whilst Smith held his heels. "It's enough to make one shudder," he said, as he rose to his feet. "I can't imagine a man falling over here under any circumstances. I'd rather be burnt alive at the stake ; " and he turned to go hack to the village.
Suddenly Smith caught his arm, with a wild cry. "Get behind me, sir! Get behind! That beast's gone raving mad. I knew there was something wrong with him."

itranouin e,atne at them full tilt, with head low, jaws dripping foam. Janoum and Missie, who had broken their fastening and sneaked out to join Tomalyn and Smith, were racing to cut him off. Totnalyn was unarmed, Smith had a revolver. "It's no use, we can't do nothing, sir," said Smith. "They'll be up with him in a moment. We must look out for ourselves. I meant 'em to lick him this afternoon, and they're going to do it now. There's one on each side of him. Ah-h-h I They've got him. lieep your gloves on whatever you do, sir." • He ran forward a few feet as the two dogs pulled Hanoutn down., snd the sharp-iTikefl tv.llars protected their throats from his frenzied assaults. Smith ended the fight by putting a bullet into the unfortunate brate. Then he tied Janoum and Missie tightly together by their collars and, with tears streamin; down his face, led them to the brink of the bluff.

What tue you going to do with them?" cried Tomalyn. "What's the matter?" "They've been bitten more'n once by that brute," said Smith, pointing to llnnotun's dead body, "and there's no chance for either of 'em. Old Said Rohs knew the dog was going mad, so he had him given to us on purpose, just out of revenge for the loss of his servant.' Filled with horror at this incredible villainy, Tomakyn came up to the dogs, who licked each sther's wounds and looked in the beet of spirits. "What are you going to do ? " "Say good-bye to 'em and go back," said Smith. 3lt's always my luck, sir. I'm as fond of these Jogs as if they was my own children. Just give em a pat, and cover your eyes while I do it." Tomalyn turned sick "as he gazed into the four ' rntle, brown eyes upturned to his. janoutn saw lotnething was wrong and put out his paw wist- ully. Missie did the same. Tomalyn shook the ikon MITI sad turned sway. .

LANCASHIRE .EA STER Q MUER SESSIONS. 'NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS OF THE PEACE for the County of Lancaster will be holden at the Castle of Lancaster on Monday' the 6th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the forenoon; and by adjournment at the fol- lowing places and times, viz. At the Court House, in Preston, on Wednes- day, the Bth day of April next, at Ten o'clock in the forenoon. At the Assize Courts, in Manchester, on Wed- nesday, the 15th day of April next, at half-past Ten o'clock in the forenoon. At the County Sessions House, in Liverpool, on Tuesday, the 28th day of April next, at half- past Ten &clock in the forenoon. The Solicitors engaged in Prosecutions at the said Sessions are requested to take notice that all Depositions and instructions for indictments are required to be sent to the Clerk of the Peace's Office seven days at least before the said sessions respectively. COUNTY COURTS INQUIRY. The committee recently appointed by the Lord Chancellor "to inquire into the distribution of the work and business amongst the County Court Judges of Lancashire and neighbourhood" held its first sitting for the taking of evidence on Saturday last at the Assize Courts, Manches- ter, under the presidency of the Vice-Chancel- lor of the Duchy. The proceedings were held in private. The Warrington County Court is concerned in the matter. Judges Thomas, Stanger, Sturgess and Spen- cer Hogg and Mr. Alleyne Brown, .Registrar of the Court at Ormskirk and Southport, attended and were examined by the committee.

FIVE "PUBS" TO ONE CHURCH. "You have 48 places of worship in Wigan and 260 drink shops," remarked Mr. (1. B. Wilson, secretary of the United Kingdom Alliance, at a temperance demonstration held at Wigan on Saturday. " The proportion seems somewhat unfair," he added. "In 1912 there were 295 pro- ceedings for drunkenness at Wigan. I doubt very much whether that represents the exces- sive drinking that has gone on ill this town. It seems to me it cannot be so with all the facilities that are provided for you." Wigan's share of the drink bill was at least A:6,000 a Week, calculated on the expenditure over the whole country. PASSIVE RESISTERS AT WIDNES. At Widnes, on Thursday, the Fey. Alexander Harvey, a local Baptist minister, represented several persons who were summoned for the non-payment of that portion of the poor rate devoted to educational purposes. He said that it was the tenth time be had appeared in the court, and the situation was still the same. They protested, not as a matter of tactics, be- cause if that was the case they might be drill- ing. (Laughter.) They felt they were suffer- ing an injustice. After formally making the protest they were williug to pay. •

CRICKET. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT JUNIOR CRICKET LEAGUE. Any junior cricket clubs in Warrington and district desirous, of joining the Warrington and District Junior Cricket League should apply im- mediately to Arthur Boyle, 333, Wellfield-street, Warrington. EMMANUEL CRICKET CLUB. The annual general meeting of the Emmanuel Cricket Club was held in the Institute, and a good number were present. The President, the Rev. W. T. Jaye, occupied the chair. The secretary gave a very satisfactory report of the previous year's sport, and the treasurer sub- mitted his accounts, which were adopted. The following officers were appointed for the year 1914:—President, Rev. W. T. Jaye; secre- tary and treasurer, Mr. R. Lees, jun.; captain, Mr. W. Bibby; sub-captain, Mr. S. Hughes; committee, Mr. T. Hughes and Mr. P. Broad- hurst. A vote of thanks was accorded to Miss N. Gandy, the donor of last year's medals for the best batting and bowling average. These were won by Mr. T. Hughes and Mr. W. Bibby respectively.
